practice_items.explanation: Reviewers have little time; a few deep case studies show process better than many thin ones.

practice_items.prompt: You have no measured outcome for a student project. What should you show?
practice_items.explanation: Honest evidence and a measurement plan show judgement; invented numbers destroy trust.
options: Test findings and how you would measure success

practice_items.prompt: What best shows design judgement in a case study?
practice_items.explanation: Reviewers hire for decision-making; trade-offs and reasons show it far better than final screens.
options: A long list of tools used
Explaining alternatives and why one was chosen

practice_items.prompt: What should appear at the very top of a case study?
practice_items.explanation: A summary lets a busy reviewer understand the project in seconds and decide to read on.
options: A short summary of the problem, your role and the outcome
A list of the fonts used

practice_items.prompt: In a whiteboard design exercise, what should you do first?
practice_items.explanation: Interviewers assess how you frame the problem; clarifying first shows structured thinking.

topics.title: C++ basics for problem solving
topics.summary_md: Use fast input/output, know the integer sizes (int is 32-bit, long long is 64-bit), and pass large objects by reference to avoid copies. Prefer vector over raw arrays and string over char arrays.
key_points: Use long long when sums can pass about 2 × 10^9.
Pass vectors by const reference: const vector<int>& v.
ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr); speeds up input.
learn_items: Skeleton: #include <bits/stdc++.h>, using namespace std, int main() returning 0; know what each line does
Output: end lines with a newline character rather than endl, which flushes the stream and is slow in loops
Integer types: int is about ±2.1 × 10^9, long long about ±9.2 × 10^18; write 1LL * a * b to multiply in 64 bits
vector: vector<int> v(n, 0), push_back, pop_back, back, size, resize; 2D as vector<vector<int>> g(n, vector<int>(m))
string: size, substr(pos, len), push_back, += a char, to_string, stoi and stoll; s[i] is a char
Range-for: for (auto& x : v) changes elements in place; plain auto copies each element
pair and tuple: make_pair, .first, .second, auto [a, b] = p; pairs compare by first, then second
Limits: INT_MAX, INT_MIN and LLONG_MAX from <climits>; adding to INT_MAX as infinity overflows

topics.title: STL containers
topics.summary_md: vector (dynamic array), deque, stack, queue, priority_queue (max-heap by default), set and map (balanced trees, O(log n), ordered), unordered_set and unordered_map (hash tables, O(1) average). Pick the container by the operations you need.
key_points: priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> is a min-heap.
map keeps keys sorted; unordered_map does not.
Use count or find to test membership without inserting.
learn_items: vector and deque: push_back in O(1) amortised; deque adds push_front and pop_front; both allow v[i]
stack and queue: push, pop, empty, plus top (stack) or front (queue); pop returns nothing, so read the value first
priority_queue: push, top and pop in O(log n); max-heap by default; pairs order by first, then second
set: insert, erase, find, count, lower_bound, upper_bound in O(log n); *s.begin() is the smallest, *s.rbegin() the largest
multiset: keeps duplicates; erase(x) removes every copy, erase(ms.find(x)) removes just one
map: sorted keys; insert, erase, find, count, operator[]; iterate in key order with for (auto& [k, v] : m)
unordered_map and unordered_set: insert, find, count, erase, operator[]; average O(1), worst O(n); reserve(n) helps
Pair keys: map<pair<int,int>, int> works directly; unordered_map needs a custom hash for pairs

topics.title: STL algorithms and lambdas
topics.summary_md: sort, lower_bound, upper_bound, reverse, accumulate, max_element and next_permutation cover most needs. Lambdas give custom comparators. lower_bound needs a sorted range.
key_points: sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b){ return a > b; }) sorts descending.
lower_bound returns the first element not less than the value.
accumulate with 0LL to sum into a long long.
learn_items: sort(v.begin(), v.end()) is O(n log n) and not stable; stable_sort keeps equal elements in their order
Comparator rule: return true only when a must come before b; use <, never <=, so the order stays strict
Binary search: lower_bound and upper_bound return iterators, subtract v.begin() for the index; binary_search gives a bool
Min and max: min, max, *min_element, *max_element; max({a, b, c}) for several values
Utilities: reverse, swap, fill, iota(v.begin(), v.end(), 0), and unique followed by erase to drop adjacent duplicates
Counting and maths: count(v.begin(), v.end(), x), gcd and lcm from <numeric> (C++17), accumulate in <numeric>
next_permutation: sort first, then do { … } while (next_permutation(v.begin(), v.end())) visits every ordering
Lambdas: [&] captures by reference, [=] by value; a recursive lambda needs std::function or an auto self parameter

topics.title: Common C++ pitfalls
topics.summary_md: Watch for integer overflow in products, size_t underflow when subtracting from v.size(), uninitialised variables and iterator invalidation after erasing from a container while looping.
key_points: v.size() - 1 on an empty vector wraps around (size_t is unsigned).
Erasing while iterating: use the iterator returned by erase.
Initialise every variable; local ints start with garbage values.
learn_items: Overflow: int * int overflows before it is stored in a long long; cast one operand first
Signed loops: compare with (int)v.size(), and never count down with an unsigned i >= 0, which never ends
Out of bounds: v[i] does no check; use v.at(i) while debugging or add explicit bounds checks
Iterator invalidation: push_back may reallocate and invalidate every iterator and reference into a vector
map operator[]: reading m[k] inserts a default value, which changes size() and slows loops; use find to read
Globals: global arrays start zeroed but keep values between test cases, so reset them each time
Bad comparator: <= in sort is undefined behaviour and can crash; always use a strict comparison
Recursion depth: deep DFS on 10^5 or more nodes can overflow the stack; switch to an iterative version

topics.title: Java basics for problem solving
topics.summary_md: Know primitive types and their wrappers, integer overflow, and that == on objects compares references. Use StringBuilder to build strings and long for big sums. Arrays have a fixed size; ArrayList grows.
key_points: Compare strings and Integer objects with equals, not ==.
StringBuilder.append is amortised O(1); String concatenation in a loop is O(n²).
Arrays.fill and Arrays.sort work on primitive arrays.
learn_items: Primitives: int (32-bit), long (64-bit), double, char, boolean; write 1L * a * b to multiply in long
Limits: Integer.MAX_VALUE and Long.MAX_VALUE; Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) is still negative
Arrays: new int[n] is zero-filled, new int[m][n] for a grid; length is a field, not a method
String methods: length(), charAt(i), substring(a, b) with b exclusive, toCharArray(), split, String.valueOf
StringBuilder methods: append, insert, reverse, setCharAt, deleteCharAt, toString
Char arithmetic: c - 'a' gives an int index; (char) ('a' + i) converts back
Maths: Math.max, Math.min, Math.abs; Math.pow returns a double, so avoid it for integer powers
Fast input: BufferedReader with StringTokenizer, and PrintWriter for output, beat Scanner on large input

topics.title: Collections: lists, maps, sets and queues
topics.summary_md: ArrayList, LinkedList, HashMap, TreeMap, HashSet, TreeSet, ArrayDeque and PriorityQueue cover nearly every problem. TreeMap gives floorKey and ceilingKey in O(log n). ArrayDeque is the preferred stack and queue.
key_points: map.getOrDefault(k, 0) + 1 counts frequencies.
PriorityQueue is a min-heap; pass a comparator for a max-heap.
Use ArrayDeque instead of the old Stack class.
learn_items: ArrayList: add, get, set, remove, size; contains and indexOf are O(n); Collections.reverse and Collections.swap
HashMap: put, get (null if absent), containsKey, remove, merge(k, 1, Integer::sum); loop with entrySet()
Grouping: map.computeIfAbsent(k, x -> new ArrayList<>()).add(v) creates the list only when missing
HashSet: add returns false if the value was already there; contains and remove are O(1) average
TreeMap and TreeSet: floorKey, ceilingKey, firstKey, lastKey, pollFirst, headMap, tailMap; all O(log n)
ArrayDeque: push, pop, peek as a stack; offer, poll, peek as a queue; offerFirst and pollLast at either end
PriorityQueue: offer and poll O(log n), peek O(1); new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder()) is a max-heap
Iteration order: HashMap has none, LinkedHashMap keeps insertion order, TreeMap keeps sorted order

topics.title: Sorting, comparators and generics
topics.summary_md: Arrays.sort on primitives uses a quicksort variant; on objects it is a stable merge sort. Comparators are written as lambdas. Integer.compare avoids the overflow that a - b can cause.
key_points: list.sort((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0])) sorts arrays by first value.
Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...) chains keys.
Collections.reverseOrder() gives descending order for objects.
learn_items: Comparable and Comparator: compareTo defines a class’s natural order; a Comparator is a separate rule passed in
Primitive arrays: Arrays.sort(int[]) takes no comparator; box to Integer[] or sort and reverse for descending
Key extractors: Comparator.comparingInt(a -> a[1]) avoids writing the comparison by hand
reversed(): it reverses the whole chain built so far, so place it carefully when chaining keys
Stability: List.sort, Collections.sort and Arrays.sort on objects are stable (TimSort)
Generics: List<Integer>, Map<String, List<Integer>>; primitives cannot be type arguments
Binary search: Arrays.binarySearch and Collections.binarySearch return -(insertion point) - 1 when absent
Comparator rules: consistent and transitive, and equal elements must return 0

topics.title: Common Java pitfalls
topics.summary_md: Autoboxing hides costs and the Integer cache makes == work only for small values. Modifying a collection while iterating over it throws ConcurrentModificationException. Recursion depth is limited by the thread stack.
key_points: Integer values from -128 to 127 are cached, so == may look correct in tests.
Remove during iteration with an Iterator’s remove method.
Very deep recursion can overflow the stack; convert to an explicit stack.
learn_items: equals versus ==: == compares references for objects; use equals for String, Integer and Long
Unboxing null: int x = map.get(k) throws NullPointerException when the key is missing
Silent overflow: int arithmetic wraps; use long for sums and products, Math.addExact to detect it while testing
Safe removal: use Iterator.remove() or removeIf instead of removing inside a for-each loop
List<Integer>.remove(1) removes index 1; call remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) to remove the value 1
Negative modulo: -7 / 2 is -3 and -7 % 2 is -1; use Math.floorMod for a non-negative result
Deep recursion: StackOverflowError; run the code in a Thread with a bigger stack size or make it iterative
Custom keys: override both hashCode and equals before using an object in a HashMap or HashSet

topics.title: Python basics for problem solving
topics.summary_md: Lists, dicts, sets and tuples are the core structures. Slicing copies. Integers never overflow. Use list comprehensions, enumerate and zip for short, clear loops, and "".join to build strings.
key_points: Slicing creates a copy: O(k) time and memory.
[[0] * m for _ in range(n)] builds a grid; [[0] * m] * n shares rows.
Use "".join(parts) instead of += on strings in a loop.
learn_items: Lists: append, pop, insert, len, sort, reverse; a[-1] is the last item and a[::-1] a reversed copy
Dicts: d.get(k, 0), setdefault, in, items(), keys(); a dict keeps insertion order
Sets and tuples: add, remove, discard, |, &, -; tuples are immutable and hashable, so they work as keys
Strings: split(), strip(), isalnum(), lower(), ord(c) - ord("a") and chr(i + ord("a"))
Loops: range(n), range(n - 1, -1, -1), enumerate(a), zip(a, b) and reversed(a)
Integer maths: // floors (-7 // 2 is -4), % takes the sign of the divisor, ints never overflow
Sentinels: float("inf") and float("-inf"); max(a, default=0) handles empty inputs
Fast input: sys.stdin.readline, or read every token at once with sys.stdin.read().split()

topics.title: collections: Counter, defaultdict and deque
topics.summary_md: Counter counts items, defaultdict removes "key missing" checks, and deque gives O(1) appends and pops at both ends. A plain list is a fine stack, but popping from its front is O(n).
key_points: Counter(s).most_common(k) returns the k most frequent items.
defaultdict(list) groups values by key.
Use deque for BFS queues; list.pop(0) is O(n).
learn_items: Counter: Counter(iterable), c[x] is 0 when missing, update, subtract, and c1 == c2 to compare counts
Counter arithmetic: c1 - c2 drops non-positive counts, & keeps the minimum count, | the maximum
defaultdict: defaultdict(int) for counts, defaultdict(list) for adjacency lists, defaultdict(set) for unique neighbours
deque: append, appendleft, pop, popleft, all O(1); deque(maxlen=k) drops old items automatically
deque indexing: d[0] and d[-1] are O(1), but indexing near the middle is O(n)
OrderedDict: move_to_end(key) and popitem(last=False) give a short LRU cache
Records: tuples and namedtuple sort and hash; use a dataclass for a mutable record
Stack: a plain list with append and pop; test emptiness with "if stack:"

topics.title: heapq, bisect and sorting
topics.summary_md: heapq is a min-heap on a list; push negated values for a max-heap. bisect finds insertion points in a sorted list. sorted with key= sorts by any rule, and sorting is stable.
key_points: heapq.heappush(h, -x) and -heapq.heappop(h) simulate a max-heap.
bisect_left(a, x) is the first index where x could go.
sorted(items, key=lambda t: (t[1], t[0])) sorts by two keys.
learn_items: heapq basics: heapify(list) in O(n), heappush, heappop, and heap[0] to peek; the list itself is the heap
Heap entries: (priority, counter, item) tuples so ties never compare items that cannot be compared
heapq helpers: nlargest(k, it), nsmallest(k, it), and heappushpop or heapreplace to do two steps in one
bisect: bisect_left is the first index >= x, bisect_right the first > x; insort keeps order but inserts in O(n)
Count in a range: bisect_right(a, hi) - bisect_left(a, lo) counts values in [lo, hi]
Search on answers: bisect accepts key= from Python 3.10; otherwise write the loop yourself
Sorting: list.sort() sorts in place and returns None, sorted() returns a new list; reverse=True; both are stable
Custom order: functools.cmp_to_key(cmp) when a key function cannot express the rule (largest number)

topics.title: Common Python pitfalls
topics.summary_md: Recursion depth is limited to about 1000 by default, mutable default arguments are shared between calls, and nested functions need nonlocal to reassign outer variables. Know which built-ins are O(n).
key_points: sys.setrecursionlimit raises the limit, but iterative code is safer.
Never use def f(x, seen=[]): the list is shared across calls.
"x in list" is O(n); "x in set" is O(1) on average.
learn_items: Recursion: deep DFS raises RecursionError; use an explicit stack or BFS for large inputs
Memoisation: @functools.cache or @lru_cache(None) on a function; all arguments must be hashable
Mutable defaults: defaults are created once when the function is defined; use None and create the list inside
Closures: nonlocal is needed to reassign an outer variable; mutating an outer list needs no nonlocal
Aliasing: b = a shares one list; copy with a[:] or list(a), and copy.deepcopy for nested lists
Hidden O(n): list.pop(0), list.insert(0, x), list.remove, slicing and s + t on strings
Speed: Python loops are slow; prefer built-ins (sum, sorted, max) and avoid exceptions for normal control flow
Division: / always returns a float; use // for integers and avoid floats for very large numbers

topics.title: Time and space complexity
topics.summary_md: Big-O describes how the work grows with the input size n. Count the loops: one pass is O(n), a loop inside a loop is O(n²), halving the range each step is O(log n). Space complexity counts extra memory, including the recursion stack. In interviews, state the complexity of your first idea before you optimise it.
key_points: Drop constants and lower-order terms: 3n² + 5n is O(n²).
With n up to 10^5, aim for O(n log n) or better; 10^8 simple steps is about one second.
Recursion depth counts as space: a recursive DFS on a path of n nodes uses O(n) stack.
learn_items: Big-O meaning: an upper bound on growth as n grows; order O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2^n) < O(n!)
Counting loops: sequential loops add, nested loops multiply; a loop that halves or doubles i runs O(log n) times
Space complexity: count extra arrays, maps and the recursion stack; the input itself is usually not counted
Recursion cost: number of calls × work per call; naive fib makes about 2^n calls, recursive binary search about log n
Best, average, worst case: quick sort is O(n log n) on average and O(n²) at worst; interviews mean the worst case unless stated
Amortised cost: appending to a dynamic array is O(1) amortised even though a resize copies all n items
Constraints to target: n ≤ 20 allows O(2^n), n ≤ 5000 allows O(n²), n ≤ 10^6 needs O(n) or O(n log n)
Interview drill: state the time and space of the brute force first, then of each improvement

topics.title: Number basics: digits, primes and powers
topics.summary_md: Many warm-up problems are about digits (n % 10 and n / 10), divisibility, primes and fast powers. The Sieve of Eratosthenes finds all primes below n in O(n log log n). Fast exponentiation squares the base and halves the exponent, giving O(log n) multiplications. Watch for integer overflow and negative numbers.
key_points: Extract digits with n % 10 and drop them with integer division by 10.
Sieve: mark multiples of each prime starting from p*p.
Binary exponentiation: x^n = (x^(n/2))² times x when n is odd.
learn_items: Digits: loop while n > 0 taking n % 10 and dividing by 10; handle n = 0 and negative n separately
Reversing a number: rev = rev * 10 + digit; compare rev with INT_MAX / 10 before multiplying to catch overflow
Divisors: test only up to √n (loop while i * i <= n) to check a prime or list factors in O(√n)
Sieve of Eratosthenes: boolean array of size n; for each prime p with p * p < n mark p*p, p*p + p, … as composite
Fast power: while n > 0, multiply the result by x if n is odd, square x, halve n; for n < 0 use 1/x and a 64-bit n
Modular arithmetic: (a + b) % m and (a * b) % m keep numbers small; 10^9 + 7 is the usual modulus
Integer square root: binary-search the largest k with k * k <= x, using 64-bit products
Digital root: repeatedly summing the digits of n > 0 ends at 1 + (n - 1) % 9

topics.title: Simulation and conversion problems
topics.summary_md: Simulation problems ask you to follow the rules exactly: convert numerals, walk a robot, or rebuild a string. Write the rules as a table or map first, then loop. Most bugs come from edge cases such as empty input, a single element or the last step.
key_points: Turn a rule list into a lookup table (for example Roman numeral values).
Process from the right when a later symbol changes the meaning of an earlier one.
Test the smallest and largest valid inputs by hand before submitting.
learn_items: Read the rules: rewrite the statement as numbered steps and a lookup table before writing code
Roman to integer: scan left to right; subtract a symbol’s value when the next symbol is larger, otherwise add it
Integer to Roman: greedy over 13 values from 1000 down to 1 (including 900, 400, 90, 40, 9, 4), subtracting while possible
Direction vectors: store moves as dx = [0, 1, 0, -1] and dy = [1, 0, -1, 0]; turning right is d = (d + 1) % 4
Robot bounded in a circle: after one pass of the instructions it is bounded if it is back at the start or not facing north
Clock angle: hour hand 30° per hour plus 0.5° per minute, minute hand 6° per minute; answer min(diff, 360 - diff)
Edge cases: empty input, one element, the last step and the largest value; trace each by hand
Complexity: usually O(n) over the input or O(number of steps); check the step count fits the time limit

topics.title: Traversal and in-place updates
topics.summary_md: Arrays give O(1) access by index. Many problems ask you to change the array in place: keep a write pointer for the next free slot and a read pointer that scans. Reversing parts of the array solves rotations without extra space.
key_points: Write pointer pattern: copy kept elements forward, then fill the rest.
Rotate by k: reverse all, then reverse the first k and the rest.
Merge from the back when the target array has free space at the end.
learn_items: Array costs: O(1) access by index, O(n) insert or delete in the middle because elements shift
Read and write pointers: read scans every element, write marks the next slot to keep; the new length is write
Remove duplicates from a sorted array: copy nums[read] only when it differs from nums[write - 1]
Move zeroes: shift non-zeros forward with the write pointer, then fill the tail with zeros; relative order is kept
Rotate right by k: set k %= n first, then do the three reversals; O(n) time, O(1) extra space
Merge into free space: fill from index m + n - 1 with pointers at the ends of both arrays so nothing is overwritten
Index as hash: for values in 1..n, swap each value into position value - 1 or negate to mark it (first missing positive)
Edge cases: empty array, all values equal, k larger than n, and negative numbers

topics.title: Prefix sums
topics.summary_md: A prefix sum array stores the running total, so the sum of any range [l, r] is prefix[r+1] - prefix[l] in O(1). Combined with a hash map of earlier prefix values, it counts subarrays with a target sum in one pass. Products and XORs follow the same idea.
key_points: Range sum = prefix[r+1] - prefix[l].
Count subarrays summing to k: look up prefix - k in a map of seen prefixes.
Product except self: multiply a left pass and a right pass, no division needed.
learn_items: Build: prefix[0] = 0 and prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + nums[i]; the extra slot removes the l = 0 special case
Pivot index: left sum equals total - left - nums[i]; one pass with a running sum and O(1) extra space
Subarray sum k: map prefix -> count starting with {0: 1}; at each index add count[prefix - k], then record prefix
Divisible by k: count equal prefix remainders; normalise negatives with ((p % k) + k) % k
Equal 0s and 1s: treat 0 as -1 and find the longest zero-sum subarray using the first index of each prefix
Difference array: add v at d[l] and subtract it at d[r + 1]; one prefix sum of d applies all range updates in O(n + q)
2D prefix: P[r+1][c+1] = P[r][c+1] + P[r+1][c] - P[r][c] + a[r][c]; rectangle sums by inclusion-exclusion
Recognise it: many range-sum queries or "count subarrays with sum …"; prefix sums work with negatives where windows fail

topics.title: Kadane’s algorithm and best-time problems
topics.summary_md: Kadane’s algorithm finds the maximum subarray sum in O(n): at each index either extend the current run or start a new one. The stock problems use the same running-minimum idea: track the cheapest price so far and the best profit.
key_points: cur = max(x, cur + x); best = max(best, cur).
For products, track both the max and the min (a negative flips them).
Circular arrays: answer is max(normal Kadane, total - minimum subarray).
learn_items: Idea: the best subarray ending at i is either nums[i] alone or nums[i] added to the best one ending at i - 1
Initialise with nums[0], not 0, so an all-negative array returns its largest element
Returning the subarray: note the start when the run restarts and the end whenever best improves
Buy and sell once: track the minimum price so far; profit = price - minPrice; O(n) time, O(1) space
Max product: keep curMax and curMin; when x < 0 swap them before updating, because a negative flips the order
Circular case: if every number is negative, the total minus the minimum subarray is 0, so return the normal Kadane result
Recognise it: "maximum or minimum sum of a contiguous subarray" in O(n); it is the simplest 1D dynamic programme

topics.title: Matrix traversal
topics.summary_md: Matrix problems are about index control: spiral order shrinks four boundaries, rotation is a transpose followed by a row reverse, and in-place marking reuses the first row and column as flags.
key_points: Rotate 90° clockwise: transpose, then reverse each row.
Spiral: keep top, bottom, left and right bounds and move them inward.
Use the first row and column as markers to get O(1) extra space.
learn_items: Indexing: an m × n grid has rows 0..m-1 and columns 0..n-1; cell (r, c) is index r * n + c when flattened
Bounds check: test 0 <= r < m and 0 <= c < n before each neighbour access; loop over four direction pairs
Spiral order: after walking each side, move that bound inward; stop when top > bottom or left > right
Transpose: swap a[i][j] with a[j][i] only for j > i, otherwise every pair is swapped back
Rotate anticlockwise: transpose, then reverse each column (or reverse each row first, then transpose)
Set matrix zeroes: mark in row 0 and column 0, keep one extra flag for column 0, and clear row 0 and column 0 last
Game of life in place: encode old and new state in one cell (e.g. 2 = live becoming dead) and decode in a second pass
Valid sudoku: one set per row, column and box; box index = (r / 3) * 3 + c / 3 with integer division

topics.title: Intervals
topics.summary_md: Sort intervals by start, then sweep: an interval overlaps the previous one when its start is at most the previous end. Counting rooms or overlaps uses start and end events sorted separately or a min-heap of end times.
key_points: Sort by start before merging.
To remove the fewest intervals, greedily keep the one that ends first.
Two sorted lists of intervals intersect with two pointers.
learn_items: Overlap test: [a, b] and [c, d] overlap when a <= d and c <= b; check whether touching ends count in the problem
Merge: sort by start; if cur start <= last end set last end = max(last end, cur end), else start a new interval
Insert interval: copy intervals that end before the new one, merge all that overlap it, then copy the rest; O(n)
Fewest removals: sort by end and keep an interval when its start >= the last kept end; removals = n - kept
Meeting rooms: sweep sorted starts and ends, or keep a min-heap of end times; the peak count is the answer
Interval list intersections: overlap is [max(starts), min(ends)] when valid; advance the pointer whose interval ends first
Complexity: sorting dominates at O(n log n); the sweep itself is O(n)

topics.title: Hash maps and counting
topics.summary_md: A hash map turns "have I seen this?" into an O(1) average lookup. Store value to index for pair problems, value to count for frequency problems, and a canonical key (sorted letters or a count tuple) to group equal items.
key_points: Two Sum: before inserting x, check whether target - x is already in the map.
Group anagrams by a key such as the sorted word or a 26-letter count.
Bucket sort by frequency gives top-k in O(n).
learn_items: How it works: hash the key to a bucket; average O(1) get and put, worst case O(n) when many keys collide
Value to index: for pair problems store each number’s index and check its complement before inserting
Frequency count: map value -> count in one pass; compare two maps or two 26-length arrays for anagrams
Canonical key: group by a normalised form, such as sorted letters (O(k log k)) or a tuple of 26 counts (O(k))
Top-k frequent: count, put each value in bucket[count], then read the buckets from the highest count down
Keys: use immutable keys (string, tuple, Integer); never use a mutable list as a key
Iteration order: hash maps are unordered, except Python dict and Java LinkedHashMap, which keep insertion order
Recognise it: "have I seen …", "count …" or "group …" turns an O(n²) pair loop into one O(n) pass

topics.title: Hash sets and sequences
topics.summary_md: A set answers membership in O(1). Longest consecutive sequence starts counting only from numbers whose predecessor is missing, which keeps the whole pass O(n). Sliding sets of size k detect near duplicates.
key_points: Only start a run at x when x - 1 is not in the set.
Keep a set of the last k elements for "duplicate within k".
Moore’s voting finds the majority element in O(1) space.
learn_items: Set operations: add, remove and contains in O(1) average; use a set for membership, a map when you need counts
Duplicates: return true as soon as an element is already in the set
Longest consecutive sequence: from each run start, count up while x + 1 is in the set; every number is visited once
Sliding set: when index i passes k, remove nums[i - k] before checking nums[i]
Intersection of arrays: build a set from the smaller array and test each element of the other
Boyer–Moore majority: keep a candidate and a count; count 0 takes a new candidate, equal adds 1, different subtracts 1
Cycle detection: store visited states in a set; a repeated state means a loop (happy number)
Trade-off: a set costs O(n) memory; sorting plus a scan uses O(1) extra space but O(n log n) time

topics.title: Designing with hashing
topics.summary_md: Design questions combine a map with another structure: an array plus an index map gives O(1) insert, delete and random pick; a map of sorted lists gives time-based lookups with binary search.
key_points: Delete from an array in O(1) by swapping with the last element.
Keep values sorted by timestamp and binary-search the latest one not after t.
Explain collisions and load factor when asked how a hash map works.
learn_items: Hash map internals: bucket array, hash code mod capacity, chaining or open addressing, resize past a load factor of about 0.75
Design a hash map: a fixed array of bucket lists; get, put and remove scan only one bucket
Insert, delete, getRandom in O(1): array of values plus map value -> index; update the moved value’s index on delete
Time-based store: map key -> list of (timestamp, value) in increasing time; binary-search the last entry with time <= t
Combining structures: a map for lookup plus a list, heap or linked list for order; state the cost of every operation
Interview flow: list the operations and target complexities first, then choose structures that meet each one
Edge cases: put on an existing key overwrites, removing a missing key, and removing the element that is already last

topics.title: String basics
topics.summary_md: Strings are arrays of characters, often immutable. Build results with a list or StringBuilder instead of repeated concatenation. Parsing problems (atoi, reverse words) are mostly careful index handling and edge cases: spaces, signs and overflow.
key_points: Repeated + on immutable strings is O(n²); use a builder.
Add numeric strings digit by digit from the right with a carry.
Compress in place with a read pointer and a write pointer.
learn_items: Immutability: Java and Python strings cannot change; collect pieces in a StringBuilder or list and join once at the end
Character arithmetic: ch - 'a' gives 0..25 for count arrays; know isdigit, isalnum and lower-case conversion
Reverse words: split on spaces, drop empty pieces, reverse the list and join with single spaces
String to integer: skip leading spaces, read one sign, read digits, clamp to the 32-bit range before it overflows
Add strings or binary: walk both from the right with a carry, append digits, reverse at the end
Run-length compression: count each run with two pointers, write the character then the digits of the count
Longest common prefix: compare column by column across all words; stop at the first mismatch or the shortest word
Complexity: comparing, hashing or slicing a length-k string costs O(k), so doing it inside a loop adds a factor of k

topics.title: Palindromes
topics.summary_md: Check a palindrome with two pointers from both ends. To find palindromic substrings, expand around each of the 2n - 1 centres; this is O(n²) time and O(1) space, simple enough for interviews.
key_points: Expand around centre for both odd and even lengths.
Allowing one deletion: on the first mismatch try skipping either side.
Skip non-alphanumeric characters when the problem says so.
learn_items: Check: two pointers from both ends moving inward; O(n) time, O(1) space
Cleaning input: skip characters that are not letters or digits and compare in lower case without building a new string
Expand around centre: for each i expand (i, i) for odd and (i, i + 1) for even length while both ends match
Count palindromic substrings: add one for every successful expansion step; O(n²) time
One deletion allowed: at the first mismatch check s[l+1..r] and s[l..r-1] once each with a plain palindrome check
Longest palindromic substring: keep the best (start, length) found over all expansions
Rearranging into a palindrome: possible when at most one character has an odd count
Beyond interviews: Manacher’s algorithm finds all palindromes in O(n), but expand-around-centre is usually enough

topics.title: Pattern matching
topics.summary_md: The naive search is O(n·m). KMP precomputes a failure table so the text pointer never moves back, giving O(n + m). Rolling hashes (Rabin-Karp) compare windows in O(1) with a small collision risk.
key_points: KMP failure table: the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix.
A string is a repetition of a pattern if it appears in (s + s) without the ends.
Rolling hash: remove the outgoing character, shift, add the incoming one.
learn_items: Naive search: try every start in the text and compare up to m characters; O(n·m) in the worst case
Built-ins: indexOf and find return -1 when absent; do not assume their worst case is linear
KMP table: lps[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix of it; built in O(m)
KMP search: on a mismatch set j = lps[j - 1] instead of moving the text pointer back; j == m means a match
Rabin–Karp: hash = (hash * base + c) mod p; slide in O(1) and confirm every hash match by direct comparison
Z-function: on pattern + "#" + text, every position whose Z value equals m is an occurrence
Recognise it: "find a pattern in a text" or "shortest palindrome by adding to the front" need KMP or hashing, not repeated slicing

topics.title: Two pointers
topics.summary_md: With sorted data, one pointer at each end moves inward based on a comparison, turning an O(n²) pair search into O(n). For triplets, fix one element and run two pointers on the rest; skip duplicates to avoid repeated answers.
key_points: Container with most water: always move the shorter side.
Sort first for 3Sum, then skip equal neighbours.
Dutch national flag sorts three values in one pass.
learn_items: Opposite ends on sorted data: a small sum moves left up, a large sum moves right down; each step rules out one candidate
Two Sum on a sorted array: return the indexes when the sum matches; O(n) time and O(1) space
3Sum: sort, fix i, run two pointers on i + 1..n - 1; skip equal values for i and after each match; O(n²)
Same direction: slow and fast pointers for in-place filtering and for merging two sorted arrays
Container with most water: area = min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l); the shorter side can never do better, so it moves
Trapping rain water: move the side with the lower running max; water at i = that max - height[i]
Dutch flag: low, mid, high; a 0 swaps to low and both move, a 2 swaps to high and mid stays, a 1 moves mid
Recognise it: sorted input with "pair or triplet with a target", or in-place work that must use O(1) extra space

topics.title: Fixed-size windows
topics.summary_md: A fixed window of size k slides one step at a time: add the incoming element, remove the outgoing one, and update the answer. Compare character counts in O(26) per step for anagram windows.
key_points: Initialise the first window, then slide.
Anagram in window: compare two 26-length count arrays.
Taking k cards from both ends equals leaving a middle window of n - k.
learn_items: Template: sum the first k elements, then for i = k..n-1 add a[i] and subtract a[i - k], updating the answer
Maximum average subarray: track the best window sum and divide by k once at the end
Counting windows: keep counts in a 26-length array or map and update only the entering and leaving characters
Matches counter: track how many of the 26 letters have equal counts so each step is O(1) instead of O(26)
Nearby duplicates: a set of the last k values detects a repeat within distance k
Window maximum: a monotonic deque gives the maximum of every window of size k in O(n) overall
Complexity: O(n) time and O(k) or O(alphabet) space; handle k > n and k = n
Recognise it: "every subarray or substring of length k" or "a permutation of p inside s"

topics.title: Variable-size windows
topics.summary_md: Grow the window with the right pointer and shrink it from the left while it breaks the rule. Each index enters and leaves once, so the whole scan is O(n). The rule is usually a count limit, a sum limit or a distinct-character limit.
key_points: Template: for right in range(n): add; while invalid: remove left; update answer.
Character replacement: window is valid while size - maxCount <= k.
Exactly k distinct = atMost(k) - atMost(k - 1).
learn_items: Longest valid window: expand right, shrink left while invalid, then best = max(best, r - l + 1)
Shortest valid window: expand right; while the window is valid, update best and shrink from the left
Window state: a count map, running sum or distinct count, each updated in O(1) on every add or remove
Longest substring without repeats: store each character’s last index and jump l to max(l, last + 1)
Minimum window substring: count how many required characters are satisfied; shrink while all of them are
Limits: sum-based windows need non-negative numbers; with negatives use prefix sums instead
Counting subarrays: with "at most k" allowed, each right end adds r - l + 1 valid subarrays
Recognise it: "longest/shortest subarray or substring such that …" where the condition holds as the window shrinks

topics.title: Classic binary search
topics.summary_md: Binary search halves a sorted range each step: O(log n). Pick one template and use it everywhere, for example lo = 0, hi = n - 1, while lo <= hi. Lower bound and upper bound variants find the first and last position of a value.
key_points: mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2 avoids overflow.
First position: when equal, record and keep searching left.
Check the loop with arrays of size 0, 1 and 2.
learn_items: Precondition: the range must be sorted or follow a monotonic predicate (false…false then true…true)
Exact search: lo = 0, hi = n - 1, while lo <= hi; equal returns mid, smaller sets lo = mid + 1, larger sets hi = mid - 1
Lower bound: first index with a[i] >= x; lo = 0, hi = n, while lo < hi: a[mid] >= x sets hi = mid, else lo = mid + 1
Upper bound: first index with a[i] > x; last position of x = upper - 1, count of x = upper - lower
Search insert position: it is the lower bound itself, which may be n
Sorted 2D matrix (rows chained): search 0..m·n - 1 and map mid to row mid / n and column mid % n
Infinite loops: with lo < hi and lo = mid, use the upper middle lo + (hi - lo + 1) / 2
Complexity: O(log n) time; O(1) space iteratively, O(log n) stack if recursive

topics.title: Rotated arrays and peaks
topics.summary_md: In a rotated sorted array, one half around mid is always sorted; check whether the target lies in that half. Peak finding moves towards the higher neighbour, which always leads to a peak.
key_points: Decide which half is sorted by comparing nums[lo] and nums[mid].
A peak exists in the direction of the larger neighbour.
Median of two sorted arrays partitions both so the left halves balance.
learn_items: Rotated sorted array: compare nums[mid] with nums[hi] (or nums[lo]) to find which half is sorted
Search in rotated: if the target lies within the sorted half’s range search there, otherwise search the other half
Minimum of rotated: nums[mid] > nums[hi] means the minimum is right of mid (lo = mid + 1), else hi = mid
Duplicates: when nums[mid] == nums[hi] you cannot decide, so shrink hi by one; the worst case becomes O(n)
Peak element: if nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1] set lo = mid + 1, else hi = mid; outside the array counts as minus infinity
Mountain array: find the peak first, then binary-search each side, the right side in descending order
Two sorted arrays: binary-search the cut in the smaller one so both left maxima <= both right minima; O(log min(m, n))
Recognise it: "sorted but rotated", "find a peak", or an O(log n) demand on data that is only partly sorted

topics.title: Binary search on the answer
topics.summary_md: When the answer is a number and "is x enough?" is monotonic, binary-search x and test feasibility with a greedy check. Eating speed, ship capacity and the largest subarray sum all follow this shape.
key_points: Find the smallest x where feasible(x) is true.
Bounds: low = the smallest possible answer, high = the largest useful one.
The feasibility check is usually one O(n) greedy pass.
learn_items: Monotonic predicate: if feasible(x) is true then feasible(x + 1) is too (or the reverse); that makes x searchable
Template: lo = min answer, hi = max answer; while lo < hi: feasible(mid) sets hi = mid, else lo = mid + 1; return lo
Eating speed: hours(speed) = sum of ceil(pile / speed); find the smallest speed with hours <= h
Ship within D days: lo = heaviest package, hi = total weight; fill each day greedily and count the days used
Split array largest sum: the same check as shipping; count pieces when no piece may exceed mid
Ceiling division without floats: (a + b - 1) / b for positive integers
Complexity: O(n log(range)); use 64-bit types when sums or hi can pass 2^31
Recognise it: "minimise the maximum" or "maximise the minimum", or an answer range far larger than n

topics.title: Merge sort, quick sort and counting sort
topics.summary_md: Merge sort is O(n log n) always and stable; quick sort is O(n log n) on average and in place; counting sort is O(n + k) for small value ranges. Quickselect finds the k-th element in O(n) on average.
key_points: Stable sorts keep equal items in their original order.
Quickselect partitions once and recurses into one side only.
Merge sort’s merge step also counts inversions.
learn_items: Simple sorts: bubble, selection and insertion sort are O(n²); insertion sort is fast on nearly sorted input
Merge sort: split in half, sort each half, merge with two pointers; O(n log n) always, O(n) extra space, stable
Quick sort: partition around a pivot (Lomuto or Hoare) then recurse; a random pivot avoids the O(n²) worst case
Quickselect for the k-th largest: partition, then recurse only into the side that holds index n - k
Counting sort: count each value in a range of size k, then rebuild the array; O(n + k), good for small ranges
Counting inversions: during merge, when a right element is taken first, add the number of elements left in the left half
Properties table: for each sort know its best, average and worst time, extra space, and whether it is stable
Library sorts: C++ std::sort is introsort (not stable); Java object sorts and Python use TimSort (stable)

topics.title: Sorting by a custom rule
topics.summary_md: Many problems become easy after sorting by the right key: by frequency, by distance, or by how two items compare when joined. Write the comparator carefully and keep it consistent.
key_points: Largest number: sort by comparing a + b with b + a.
Sort characters by count using a map and a bucket list.
Sort by one key, break ties by another.
learn_items: Comparator contract: return negative, zero or positive; it must be consistent and transitive or the sort may break
Key functions: sort by a computed key (length, frequency, distance) instead of a comparator when you can
Ties: sort by (primary, secondary), for example frequency descending then value ascending by negating one key
Largest number edge case: if the first string after sorting is "0", return "0" rather than "000"
K closest points: sort by x² + y² (no square root needed), or use a heap or quickselect for O(n log k) or O(n)
Keeping positions: sort (value, index) pairs when the original indexes are needed afterwards
Recognise it: when a greedy step depends on order (intervals, meetings, boxes), sort by the key the greedy uses

topics.title: Recursion basics
topics.summary_md: A recursive function needs a base case and a smaller subproblem. Trust the call: assume it solves the smaller input correctly. Draw the recursion tree to count calls and spot repeated work, which hints at memoisation.
key_points: Base case first, then the recursive step.
The recursion tree’s size is the time complexity.
Repeated subproblems mean dynamic programming will help.
learn_items: Structure: a base case that returns without recursing, then a call on a strictly smaller input
Trust the call: assume f(n - 1) is correct and only write how to build f(n) from it
Call stack: each call keeps its own locals; depth d uses O(d) stack and very deep inputs overflow it
Recursion tree: branching factor b and depth d give about b^d calls; naive fib(n) is O(2^n)
Memoisation: cache results by argument so each state is computed once; fib drops to O(n)
Warm-up drills: factorial, power, reverse a string, sum of digits, print 1..n and n..1
Divide and conquer: split, solve halves, combine; T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) gives O(n log n)
Recursion to iteration: any recursion can use an explicit stack instead when the depth is a problem

topics.title: Subsets, permutations and combinations
topics.summary_md: Backtracking builds a choice list step by step: choose, explore, un-choose. Subsets decide include or skip for each element; permutations try every unused element at each position; combination sums reuse or skip candidates.
key_points: Template: path.push(x); recurse; path.pop().
Sort and skip equal neighbours to avoid duplicate results.
Count the results to know the complexity: 2^n subsets, n! permutations.
learn_items: Backtracking skeleton: if the path is complete record a copy; for each choice add it, recurse, remove it
Subsets: at index i either take nums[i] or skip it; 2^n results, O(n·2^n) time including copies
Permutations: keep a used[] array; at each depth try every unused element; n! results
Combinations of size k: loop i from start and recurse with start = i + 1; prune when too few elements remain
Combination sum: recurse with i (reuse allowed) or i + 1 (each once); stop when the remaining target drops below 0
Duplicates in the input: sort, then skip nums[i] when i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]
Record a copy: add list(path) or new ArrayList<>(path), never path itself, which keeps changing
Recognise it: "all", "every" or "list all possible" with n up to about 15–20 means exhaustive backtracking

topics.title: Constraint search
topics.summary_md: Grid and board searches (word search, N-Queens, Sudoku) are backtracking with pruning: stop exploring as soon as a constraint fails. Mark cells as visited during the search and unmark on the way back.
key_points: Prune early: check the constraint before recursing.
Track used columns and diagonals in sets for N-Queens.
Restore the board after each attempt.
learn_items: Pattern: at each step try every legal option, recurse, undo; return early once one solution is found if one is enough
Word search: DFS from each cell matching word[0]; mark the cell (e.g. "#"), recurse on four neighbours, restore it
N-Queens: one queen per row; c, r - c and r + c identify the column and the two diagonals
Sudoku: find an empty cell, try 1–9 against row, column and box sets, recurse, undo on failure
Palindrome partitioning: from each start, try every end where s[start..end] is a palindrome, then recurse
Pruning: order choices so failures come early and stop as soon as a partial answer breaks a rule
Complexity: exponential; state it as branches^depth, e.g. 4·3^(L-1) paths per start cell in word search

topics.title: Reversal and merging
topics.summary_md: Most list problems are pointer bookkeeping. Use a dummy head to avoid special cases at the front. Reverse a list with three pointers (prev, cur, next). Merge two sorted lists by always taking the smaller head.
key_points: A dummy node removes the empty-list special case.
Reverse: next = cur.next; cur.next = prev; prev = cur; cur = next.
Draw the pointers before and after each step.
learn_items: Node model: each node holds a value and next; reaching position i means walking i steps, so access is O(n)
Dummy head: create a dummy, build after it and return dummy.next, so the first node needs no special case
Iterative reversal: O(n) time and O(1) space; when cur becomes null, prev is the new head
Recursive reversal: reverse the rest, then set head.next.next = head and head.next = null
Merge two sorted lists: attach the smaller head to the tail, advance that list, then attach whatever remains
Remove n-th from the end: move a lead pointer n steps ahead, then move both until the lead reaches the last node
Reverse a sub-list from m to n: stop at the node before m, then move each following node to the front of the segment
Edge cases: empty list, one node, two nodes, and changes at the head or the tail

topics.title: Fast and slow pointers
topics.summary_md: Move one pointer two steps and another one step. They meet if there is a cycle; the slow one is at the middle when the fast one reaches the end. Restarting one pointer from the head after they meet finds the cycle start.
key_points: Middle of a list: slow is at the middle when fast reaches the end.
Palindrome list: find the middle, reverse the second half, compare.
Cycle start: after meeting, move one pointer to head and step both by one.
learn_items: Floyd’s cycle check: slow moves one step, fast two; loop while fast and fast.next exist; meeting means a cycle
Why it works: inside the cycle the gap closes by one each step, so fast cannot jump over slow
Cycle start proof: head-to-start distance equals meeting-point-to-start distance, modulo the cycle length
Middle of an even list: the loop condition decides whether slow stops at the first or second middle node
Palindrome list: after comparing the halves, reverse the second half back if the input must stay unchanged
Reorder list: find the middle, reverse the second half, then merge the two halves alternately
Implicit lists: the same cycle check works on any sequence x -> f(x), such as find the duplicate number
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space, which beats a hash set of visited nodes

topics.title: Harder list problems and designs
topics.summary_md: Adding numbers stored as lists carries digit by digit. Copying a list with random pointers needs a map from old to new nodes or interleaving. The LRU cache pairs a hash map with a doubly linked list so get and put are O(1).
key_points: LRU: map key -> node; move a node to the front on every access; evict from the tail.
Interleave copies (A -> A' -> B) to copy random pointers in O(1) extra space.
Sort a list with merge sort: split at the middle, sort halves, merge.
learn_items: Add two numbers: walk both lists with a carry; keep looping while either list or the carry remains
Intersection of two lists: switch each pointer to the other head at its end; they meet at the join or both at null
Copy with random pointers: map old -> new in one pass, then set next and random from the map in a second pass
Reverse in k-groups: check that k nodes exist, reverse them, then link the previous group’s tail to the new head
Sort a list: split with fast and slow pointers, sort both halves, merge; O(n log n) without random access
LRU cache: doubly linked list with dummy head and tail; helpers remove(node) and addFront(node) keep get and put O(1)
Doubly linked lists: update four pointers on every insert and delete; draw them to avoid losing nodes
Flatten a multilevel list: DFS with a stack, or splice each child list in before continuing with next

topics.title: Stacks: nesting and parsing
topics.summary_md: A stack matches nested structure: brackets, function calls, or expressions. Push on open, pop and check on close. Expression evaluation keeps a stack of numbers and applies operators by precedence.
key_points: Valid brackets: push opens, pop must match each close.
Min stack: store the current minimum alongside each value.
Calculator: keep a sign and a running number; push terms; sum at the end.
learn_items: Stack operations: push, pop, peek and isEmpty in O(1); always check for empty before pop or peek
Bracket matching: map each closing bracket to its opener; the stack must also be empty at the end
Min stack variants: push (value, min so far) pairs, or keep a second stack of minimums
Reverse Polish notation: push numbers; on an operator pop b then a and push a op b; division truncates towards zero
Calculator with brackets: on "(" push the current result and sign and reset; on ")" pop them and combine
Decode string like 3[a2[c]]: on "[" push (count, partial string); on "]" pop, repeat the inner part and append
Simplify path: split on "/", push names, pop on "..", skip "." and empty parts
Recognise it: nested or most-recent-first structure such as brackets, undo or walking back up a path

topics.title: Monotonic stacks
topics.summary_md: A monotonic stack keeps elements in increasing or decreasing order. When a new element breaks the order, the popped elements have found their "next greater" or "next smaller" element. Each element is pushed and popped once: O(n).
key_points: Store indexes, not values, so you can compute distances.
Next greater: pop while the top is smaller than the current value.
Largest rectangle: each bar extends until a smaller bar on each side.
learn_items: Invariant: a decreasing stack keeps larger values below; each new value first pops every smaller one
Next greater element: the value that pops an index is that index’s answer; indexes left at the end get -1
Daily temperatures: when day i pops index j, answer[j] = i - j
Previous smaller: after popping, the stack top is the nearest smaller element to the left
Circular arrays: loop i from 0 to 2n - 1 and use i % n
Largest rectangle: when bar j is popped at i, its width runs from the new top + 1 to i - 1; append a 0 bar at the end
Sum of subarray minimums: a[i] is the minimum of (i - left) * (right - i) subarrays; use strict < on one side for ties
Complexity and cue: O(n) since each index is pushed and popped once; "nearest greater or smaller" is the signal

topics.title: Queues and deques
topics.summary_md: A queue is first in, first out; a deque allows both ends. A monotonic deque keeps the window maximum at its front, giving O(n) for sliding window maximum. Two stacks make a queue with amortised O(1) operations.
key_points: Queue from two stacks: pour the in-stack into the out-stack only when it is empty.
Window max: drop smaller elements from the back; drop expired indexes from the front.
A circular buffer needs head, tail and count.
learn_items: Queue operations: enqueue at the back and dequeue at the front, both O(1); BFS is the main use
Deque: push and pop at both ends in O(1); it can serve as a stack, a queue or both
Sliding window maximum: deque of indexes with decreasing values; its front is the maximum of the current window
Two-stack queue cost: each element moves between the stacks at most once, so every operation is amortised O(1)
Stack from one queue: after each push, rotate the queue size - 1 times so the newest element is at the front
Circular queue: array of size k plus head and count; the tail slot is (head + count) % k
Recent counter or rate limiter: queue of timestamps; drop from the front while they are older than the window
Recognise it: first-in-first-out order, level-by-level processing, or a window that expires from the front

topics.title: Traversals: DFS and BFS
topics.summary_md: Preorder, inorder and postorder are depth-first orders; level order is breadth-first with a queue. Process one level at a time by reading the queue size first. Many easy tree problems are a single traversal.
key_points: Level order: size = queue.length; process exactly size nodes.
Right side view: the last node of each level.
Iterative inorder uses an explicit stack.
learn_items: Vocabulary: root, leaf, height, depth; full, complete and perfect binary trees
Recursive orders: preorder (node, left, right), inorder (left, node, right), postorder (left, right, node)
Iterative preorder: stack; pop a node, visit it, push right then left
Iterative inorder: push left children until null, pop and visit, then move to the right child
Level order: queue; read size = queue length, process exactly that many nodes, push their children
Level variants: zigzag (reverse alternate levels), right side view, and average or maximum per level
Complexity: O(n) time; DFS uses O(h) space (h can be n when skewed), BFS uses O(width)
Choosing: BFS for anything per level or nearest; DFS for paths, heights and subtree answers

topics.title: Recursion on trees
topics.summary_md: Most tree problems return something from each subtree and combine it: height, a path sum, or whether a node was found. When the answer can pass through a node, compute it while returning a different value to the parent (diameter, maximum path sum).
key_points: Return height; update the global diameter with left + right.
Lowest common ancestor: the node where p and q are found in different subtrees.
Path sums: carry the running sum down; use a prefix-sum map for any start node.
learn_items: Template: handle null, recurse on left and right, then combine both results with the node’s value
Max depth: 1 + max(left, right); min depth must ignore a missing child, or a one-sided node returns 1 wrongly
Same and symmetric trees: compare node pairs recursively; for symmetry pair left.left with right.right
Balanced check: return the height, or -1 once a subtree is unbalanced, so the whole check is O(n), not O(n²)
Global answer pattern: return the best one-sided path to the parent, but update a global with left + right (+ node)
Max path sum: take max(0, gain) from each child so negative branches are dropped
Lowest common ancestor: return the node if it is p or q; if both sides return non-null, this node is the answer
Build from preorder and inorder: preorder gives the root, its inorder index splits the halves; a map makes it O(n)

topics.title: Distances, views and serialisation
topics.summary_md: Turning a tree into a graph (add parent links) lets you BFS outward from any node. Serialisation writes a traversal with null markers so the exact shape can be rebuilt.
key_points: Distance k: build parent pointers, then BFS from the target.
Serialise with preorder and a marker for null children.
Vertical order: BFS with (column, row) and sort within each column.
learn_items: Parent map: one DFS records parent[child], so each node has up to three neighbours (left, right, parent)
Nodes at distance k: BFS from the target over those three neighbours with a visited set; stop at level k
Time to burn a tree: the same BFS from the start node; the answer is the number of levels minus one
Vertical order: BFS with a column index (left c - 1, right c + 1); group by column, break ties by row then value
Top and bottom views: the first and the last node seen in each column during BFS
Boundary traversal: left boundary without leaves, then all leaves left to right, then the right boundary in reverse
Deserialise: read tokens with a shared index; a null marker returns null, otherwise build the node, then left, then right
Maximum width: number nodes (left 2i, right 2i + 1) per level; width = last - first + 1; subtract the first to avoid overflow

topics.title: The BST property
topics.summary_md: Every node is greater than all nodes in its left subtree and smaller than all in its right subtree. An inorder traversal visits values in sorted order. Validate by passing a (low, high) range down, not by comparing with direct children only.
key_points: Inorder of a BST is sorted.
Validate with bounds carried from ancestors.
k-th smallest: inorder and stop at the k-th node.
learn_items: Definition: for every node, all keys in the left subtree are smaller and all keys in the right subtree are larger
Search: go left or right by comparison; O(h), which is O(log n) when balanced and O(n) when skewed
Validate: pass (low, high) bounds down, or check that the inorder sequence is strictly increasing
Classic trap: checking only left < node < right misses a deeper node that breaks an ancestor’s bound
K-th smallest: iterative inorder with a counter that stops at k, so it costs O(h + k)
LCA in a BST: walk from the root; stop where p and q fall on different sides or one of them equals the node
Floor and ceiling: walk down and remember the last node that satisfies the bound
Two Sum in a BST: inorder into a sorted list and use two pointers, or use an ascending and a descending iterator

topics.title: Insert, delete and build
topics.summary_md: Insert walks down to a null child. Delete has three cases: leaf, one child, or two children (replace with the inorder successor). A balanced BST is built from sorted data by choosing the middle as the root.
key_points: Delete with two children: copy the successor’s value, then delete the successor.
Sorted list to BST: the middle element becomes the root.
Self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) keep height O(log n).
learn_items: Insert: walk down by comparison and attach the new node at the first null child; return the root
Delete a leaf or a node with one child: replace the node with its only child (or null)
Successor: the leftmost node of the right subtree, else the nearest ancestor reached by going left
Delete with two children: find the successor, copy its value, then delete it from the right subtree
Build from a sorted array: recurse on both halves around the middle; the tree height is O(log n)
Sorted linked list to BST: find each middle with fast and slow pointers, or simulate inorder with a moving pointer in O(n)
BST iterator: a stack of the left spine; next() pops a node, then pushes the left spine of its right child
Balanced trees: AVL keeps height difference ≤ 1 with rotations; in code use TreeMap or std::map (Python has none built in)

topics.title: Top-k with a heap
topics.summary_md: A min-heap of size k keeps the k largest items seen so far: push each item and pop when the size exceeds k. That is O(n log k), better than sorting when k is small.
key_points: k largest: min-heap of size k; k smallest: max-heap of size k.
Heap push and pop are O(log n); peek is O(1).
Ties: add a second key to the heap entry.
learn_items: Binary heap: a complete tree stored in an array; children of i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, the parent is (i - 1) / 2
Operations: push sifts up and pop sifts down in O(log n); building a heap from n items is O(n)
K largest: push each item into a min-heap and pop when the size passes k; the top is then the k-th largest
Kth largest in a stream: keep the size-k min-heap between calls; add() returns its top
Top-k frequent: count with a map, then keep a size-k heap of (count, value); bucket sort gives O(n)
K closest points: a max-heap of size k keyed by squared distance
Alternatives: sorting is O(n log n); quickselect is O(n) on average but reorders the array
Recognise it: "k largest, smallest, most frequent or closest" with k much smaller than n

topics.title: Merging and scheduling
topics.summary_md: Heaps merge k sorted streams (push the next item of whichever stream was popped) and schedule tasks by priority or by the earliest free time. Greedy plus a heap solves many "choose the best available" problems.
key_points: Merge k lists: heap of (value, list index).
Task scheduler: the most frequent task decides the idle slots.
Reorganise string: always place the most frequent remaining character.
learn_items: Merge k sorted lists: push each head; pop the smallest, append it, push its next; O(N log k)
Tie-breaking: store (value, index) so equal values never compare the nodes themselves
Task scheduler formula: max(tasks, (maxCount - 1) * (n + 1) + number of tasks with maxCount)
Heap simulation: pop the most frequent ready task, park it in a cooldown queue, push it back when it is ready
Meeting rooms II: sort by start; min-heap of end times; pop when the earliest end <= start; the peak size is the answer
Reorganise by pairs: pop the top two characters each round, place both, push back any with count left; one left over with count > 1 fails
Greedy plus heap: problems like IPO pick the best affordable option as you move through items sorted by cost
Kth smallest in a sorted matrix: heap of the first column; pop k times, pushing the right neighbour each time

topics.title: Two heaps
topics.summary_md: Keep the smaller half in a max-heap and the larger half in a min-heap, balanced to within one element. The median is the top of one heap or the average of both tops.
key_points: Push to the max-heap, move its top to the min-heap, rebalance.
Sliding median needs lazy deletion or a balanced tree.
Smallest range over k lists: min-heap plus the current maximum.
learn_items: Setup: max-heap low holds the smaller half, min-heap high the larger; every value in low <= every value in high
Add rule: push to low or high by comparing with low’s top, then rebalance so low has the same size or one more
Median: low’s top when the sizes differ, else the average of both tops (use a double to avoid integer division)
Complexity: add is O(log n) and finding the median is O(1)
Lazy deletion: record values to remove in a map and discard them only when they reach a heap top
Python: heapq has only a min-heap, so store -x in low and negate when reading it
Recognise it: a running median or any split into a "small half" and a "large half" that changes over time

topics.title: Greedy choices
topics.summary_md: A greedy algorithm commits to the best-looking option at each step. It works when an exchange argument shows that any optimal answer can be changed to include the greedy choice. Jump games track the furthest reachable index; gas station resets the start when the tank goes negative.
key_points: Try to break a greedy idea with a small counterexample first.
Jump game: keep the furthest reachable index.
Partition labels: extend the current part to the last occurrence of each character.
learn_items: Greedy idea: take the locally best option and never undo it; it is correct only if you can argue why
Exchange argument: show any optimal answer can swap in the greedy choice without getting worse
Jump game II: BFS by ranges; when i reaches the current end, jumps += 1 and end = furthest
Gas station: if total gas < total cost return -1; otherwise restart from i + 1 whenever the tank goes below 0
Interval greedy: sort by end to fit the most non-overlapping intervals or burst balloons with the fewest arrows
Matching greedy: assign cookies or boats by sorting both sides and pairing with two pointers
Candy: one pass left to right and one right to left; each child gets the larger of the two values
When greedy fails: coins [1, 3, 4] for amount 6; greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1, the best is 3 + 3, so use DP

topics.title: Greedy on strings and digits
topics.summary_md: Lexicographic problems often keep a stack of characters and pop when a smaller character can replace a larger one that appears again later. Digit problems swap or remove digits to make the number as large or small as possible.
key_points: Remove duplicate letters: pop larger characters that appear later.
Maximum swap: swap the first digit with the last occurrence of a larger digit.
Break a palindrome: change the first non-a character in the first half.
learn_items: Lexicographic rule: a smaller character earlier beats anything later, so fix positions from the left
Stack greedy: pop the top while it is larger than the current character and may still be removed or appear later
Remove duplicate letters: track each character’s last index and an in-stack set; skip characters already in the stack
Remove k digits: pop larger digits while k > 0, cut any remaining k from the end, strip leading zeros, empty means "0"
Maximum swap: record the last index of each digit; at each position look for a larger digit from 9 down
Break a palindrome: length 1 has no answer; if the first half is all "a", change the last character to "b"
Complexity: stack greedies are O(n) because each character is pushed and popped at most once
Check with examples: build a small counterexample before trusting any string greedy

topics.title: BFS and DFS on grids
topics.summary_md: A grid is a graph whose nodes are cells and whose edges go to the four neighbours. Count islands with DFS or BFS that marks visited cells. Multi-source BFS starts from every source at once to find the nearest distance (rotting oranges, nearest land).
key_points: Mark a cell visited when you push it, not when you pop it.
Multi-source BFS: push all sources first, then expand level by level.
BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
learn_items: Grid as a graph: each cell is a node; neighbours come from four (or eight) direction pairs with a bounds check
Counting islands: loop over all cells; on unvisited land start a DFS or BFS that marks the whole island; count the starts
Visited marking: change the grid in place (for example "1" to "0") or keep a boolean matrix
Multi-source BFS: enqueue every source with distance 0, then the level when a cell is reached is its nearest distance
Shortest path in a binary grid: BFS storing a distance per cell; return -1 when the target is never reached
Border-connected regions: start the search from border cells (surrounded regions, Pacific Atlantic) and flip the rest
Deep DFS: a 1000 × 1000 grid can overflow the recursion stack; use BFS or an explicit stack
Complexity: O(m·n) time and up to O(m·n) space for the queue or visited set

topics.title: Graph traversal and bipartite checks
topics.summary_md: Store a graph as an adjacency list. DFS finds connected components and paths; BFS finds levels. A graph is bipartite when you can two-colour it with BFS so no edge joins two nodes of the same colour.
key_points: Adjacency list: map node -> list of neighbours.
Clone a graph with a map from old node to new node.
Bipartite: colour neighbours the opposite colour; a clash means not bipartite.
learn_items: Representations: adjacency list O(V + E) space, matrix O(V²); build the list from an edge list
Directed or undirected: add both directions for every undirected edge
DFS: recursive or with a stack; mark on entry; count components by starting a search from each unvisited node
BFS: a queue with level counting gives the fewest edges from the source in an unweighted graph
Cycle checks: undirected, a visited neighbour that is not the parent; directed, use three colours
Bipartite on a disconnected graph: start a colouring BFS from every uncoloured node, not only node 0
Implicit graphs: word ladder and open the lock generate neighbours on the fly; BFS over states with a visited set
Complexity: O(V + E) for both DFS and BFS

topics.title: Topological sort
topics.summary_md: A topological order lists the nodes of a directed acyclic graph so every edge goes forward. Kahn’s algorithm repeatedly takes nodes with in-degree 0; if some nodes are never taken, there is a cycle.
key_points: Kahn: queue all in-degree-0 nodes; removing a node lowers its neighbours’ in-degree.
Fewer output nodes than total nodes means a cycle.
Course schedule is cycle detection in a directed graph.
learn_items: Requirement: only a directed acyclic graph has a topological order, and there may be several
Kahn’s algorithm: compute in-degrees, queue zeros, pop and append, decrement neighbours, queue any new zeros
DFS order: reversing the post-order (finish order) gives a topological order
DFS cycle check: states unvisited, visiting, done; reaching a visiting node means a cycle
Course schedule: edge prerequisite -> course; finishing is possible exactly when there is no cycle
Alien dictionary: the first differing letters of adjacent words give an edge; a longer word before its own prefix is invalid
Longest path in a DAG: process nodes in topological order and relax dp[next] = max(dp[next], dp[cur] + 1)
Complexity and cue: O(V + E); "prerequisites", "dependencies" or "build order" means a topological sort

topics.title: Shortest paths
topics.summary_md: Dijkstra finds shortest paths with non-negative weights using a min-heap: O((V + E) log V). Bellman-Ford handles negative weights and a limit on the number of edges. 0-1 BFS uses a deque when weights are only 0 or 1.
key_points: Dijkstra: skip a popped node if its distance is already larger than recorded.
At most k stops: Bellman-Ford for k + 1 rounds on a copy of the distances.
0-1 BFS: push 0-weight edges to the front, 1-weight edges to the back.
learn_items: Choosing: unweighted uses BFS, weights 0/1 use 0-1 BFS, non-negative use Dijkstra, negative use Bellman-Ford
Dijkstra: dist = infinity, dist[src] = 0; min-heap of (dist, node); pop, relax each edge, push improved distances
Why non-negative only: Dijkstra finalises a node when it is popped; a negative edge could lower it later
Bellman-Ford: relax every edge V - 1 times; any improvement in round V means a negative cycle; O(V·E)
Network delay: Dijkstra from the source; the answer is the largest distance, or -1 if any node is unreachable
Minimum effort path: Dijkstra where a path costs its largest edge, not the sum of its edges
Path reconstruction: store parent[v] whenever dist[v] improves, then walk back from the target
Floyd–Warshall: all pairs in O(V³); for each k set dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j])

topics.title: Union-find and spanning trees
topics.summary_md: Union-find (disjoint set union) merges groups and answers "same group?" in nearly O(1) with path compression and union by rank. Kruskal’s minimum spanning tree sorts edges and adds each edge that joins two different groups.
key_points: find with path compression; union by size or rank.
An edge whose ends are already joined is redundant (it forms a cycle).
Kruskal: sort edges by weight, union when the ends differ.
learn_items: Arrays: parent[i] = i at the start plus size or rank; find(x) returns the root of x’s group
Compression in code: parent[x] = find(parent[x]) flattens the path on every find
Union by size: attach the smaller root under the larger; with compression each operation is almost O(1)
Component count: start at n and subtract one on every union that joins two different roots
Cycle detection: union returns false when both ends already share a root, so that edge closes a cycle
Accounts merge: union account indexes that share an email, then group the emails by their root
Kruskal details: stop after V - 1 edges; if fewer are added, the graph is not connected
Prim’s algorithm: grow from one node with a min-heap of crossing edges; good for dense graphs

topics.title: 1D dynamic programming
topics.summary_md: Dynamic programming stores answers to subproblems so each is solved once. Define the state (dp[i] = best answer for the first i items), the transition from smaller states, and the base cases. Start top-down with memoisation, then convert to a bottom-up loop.
key_points: State, transition, base case, answer: write all four before coding.
House robber: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]).
Often only the last two states are needed: O(1) space.
learn_items: Recognise it: "count the ways", "minimum or maximum", and choices whose subproblems overlap
Four parts: the state in words, the transition, the base cases, and where the answer lives
Top-down: recursion plus a memo array or map; usually the easiest version to write first
Bottom-up: fill dp from the base cases in increasing order; no recursion depth limit
Climbing stairs: dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 2]; min cost climbing adds cost[i] and takes the min of the two
Decode ways: a one-digit step if s[i] is not "0", a two-digit step if the pair is 10 to 26
Word break: dp[i] is true if some j < i has dp[j] true and s[j..i) is in the dictionary set
Circular robber: run the line version on [0..n-2] and on [1..n-1] and take the larger result

topics.title: Subsets and knapsack
topics.summary_md: Knapsack DP decides for each item whether to take it, tracking a capacity or a target sum. 0/1 knapsack loops the capacity downwards so each item is used once; unbounded knapsack loops upwards.
key_points: Partition equal subset sum is 0/1 knapsack to half the total.
Target sum reduces to counting subsets with a given sum.
Coin change II counts combinations: loop coins outside, amounts inside.
learn_items: 0/1 knapsack: dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i-1][w - wt] + val) when wt <= w; O(n·W) time
One-row 0/1: loop w from W down to wt so each item is counted at most once
Unbounded knapsack: loop w upwards so an item can be reused (coin change, rod cutting)
Subset sum: boolean dp with dp[0] = true; for each x, dp[s] |= dp[s - x] going downwards
Coin change (fewest coins): dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1), dp[0] = 0; unreachable stays infinity, answer -1
Order matters: amounts in the outer loop and coins inside counts ordered sequences, not combinations
Target sum formula: the positive set sums to (total + target) / 2; no answer if that is odd or |target| > total
Recognise it: choose a subset of items under a budget or to hit an exact sum

topics.title: Grid DP
topics.summary_md: On a grid, dp[r][c] usually depends on the cell above and the cell to the left. Obstacles set a cell to zero ways. Maximal square uses the minimum of three neighbours plus one.
key_points: Paths: dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1].
Keep one row to save memory.
Dungeon game is solved from the bottom-right backwards.
learn_items: Unique paths: first row and column are 1; also equal to the binomial C(m + n - 2, m - 1)
Obstacles: an obstacle cell is 0, and a blocked cell in the first row or column blocks every cell after it
Minimum path sum: dp[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(top, left), with only one neighbour on the first row and column
Triangle: go bottom-up with one array; dp[j] = tri[i][j] + min(dp[j], dp[j + 1])
Maximal square: for a "1" cell dp[r][c] = 1 + min(top, left, top-left); the area is the best side squared
Falling path sum: dp[r][c] = a[r][c] + the minimum of the three cells above; check column bounds
Two walkers (cherry pickup): use state (step, r1, r2) because both move at the same time
Edge cases: a 1 × 1 grid, a single row or column, and a blocked start or end cell

topics.title: DP on strings
topics.summary_md: Two-string DP uses dp[i][j] for prefixes of length i and j. Longest common subsequence and edit distance are the two templates; most other string DP problems are variations of them.
key_points: LCS: equal characters extend the diagonal; else take the max of left and up.
Edit distance: 1 + min(insert, delete, replace) when characters differ.
Palindromic subsequence = LCS of the string and its reverse.
learn_items: Prefix states: dp[i][j] covers s[0..i) and t[0..j); row 0 and column 0 are the empty-string base cases
LCS details: O(m·n); rebuild the subsequence by walking back from dp[m][n] along the chosen moves
Edit distance base cases: dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j; equal characters copy dp[i-1][j-1]
Distinct subsequences: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j], plus dp[i-1][j-1] when s[i-1] == t[j-1]
Palindromic substrings: pal[i][j] = s[i] == s[j] and pal[i+1][j-1]; fill by increasing length
