topics.title: ARIA, focus management and accessibility testing
topics.summary_md: ARIA adds roles, states and names when HTML has no native element for a widget, but the first rule of ARIA is to use native HTML when you can. Dynamic interfaces must manage focus: a dialog moves focus inside, keeps it there and returns it to the trigger on close, and status messages are announced through live regions. Test with an automated checker, the keyboard and a real screen reader.
key_points: No ARIA is better than wrong ARIA: a role promises keyboard behaviour you must then build.
Put `aria-expanded` on a toggle button and update it when the panel opens or closes.
The native `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()` keeps focus inside and closes on Escape.
Automated checkers catch only some issues; manual keyboard and screen reader checks are still needed.
learn_items: Accessible name: from visible content or <label> first; aria-labelledby or aria-label only without visible text
Roles, states and properties: role="tab", aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-controls, aria-describedby
Rules of ARIA: native first, do not override native semantics, keep it operable, no aria-hidden on focusables
Dialogs: <dialog> with showModal(), focus the first control, Escape closes, focus returns to the trigger
Live regions: role="status" or aria-live="polite" for toasts and results; role="alert" for urgent errors
Accessible errors: link error text with aria-describedby, set aria-invalid="true", focus the first error
Accessibility tree: inspect role, name and state of any element in the DevTools Accessibility pane
Testing: the Lighthouse accessibility audit, then keyboard only, then the free NVDA screen reader on Windows

topics.title: Values, types, variables and operators
topics.summary_md: JavaScript has seven primitive types (string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol) plus objects. Declare with `const` by default and `let` when you must reassign; avoid `var`. Operators can **coerce** types silently, so `'5' + 1` is `'51'` while `'5' - 1` is 4. Compare with `===` and `!==` to avoid coercion.
key_points: `const` stops reassignment, not mutation: a const array can still be pushed to.
Falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined and NaN; everything else is truthy.
`typeof null` is 'object' (a historic bug); check for null with `=== null`.
Numbers are 64-bit floats: 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3, and integers are exact only up to 2^53 − 1.
learn_items: Running code: the browser console, the Node.js REPL, console.log, and <script type="module"> in a page
Variables: const, let and var, block scope, and the temporal dead zone before a let or const line
Primitives: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null and symbol; everything else is an object
typeof: its result for each type, the typeof null === 'object' quirk, and Array.isArray for arrays
Strings: template literals with ${}, length, slice, includes, split, trim; strings are immutable
Numbers: floating-point rounding, NaN and Number.isNaN, Number() vs parseInt, toFixed for display
Coercion: + concatenates when either side is a string, == coerces types, === does not; truthy and falsy
Logical operators: && and || return an operand, ?? falls back only on null or undefined, optional chaining ?.

topics.title: Functions, control flow and arrow functions
topics.summary_md: Functions are values: you can store them in variables, pass them as arguments and return them from other functions. Learn declarations, expressions and arrow functions, default and rest parameters, and the control-flow statements (if, switch, for, for...of, while) that fill function bodies. Write small functions that take input and return output without changing outside state.
key_points: Function declarations are hoisted; function expressions and arrows cannot be called before their line.
Arrow functions have no own `this` or `arguments`, which makes them good callbacks.
Use `for...of` for array values and `for...in` only for object keys.
Return early on invalid input to avoid deeply nested if blocks.
learn_items: Defining functions: declaration, function expression and arrow syntax, with implicit return in one-line arrows
Parameters: default values, rest parameters (...args), and calling with fewer or more arguments than declared
Return values: a function without return gives undefined; guard clauses that return early
Conditionals: if/else, the ternary operator, switch with break, and when a lookup object is clearer
Loops: for, while, for...of over arrays and strings, for...in over object keys, break and continue
First-class functions: passing callbacks, returning functions, and higher-order functions
Pure functions: same input gives the same output with no side effects, which makes them easy to test

topics.title: Scope, hoisting and closures
topics.summary_md: Scope decides where a variable is visible: global, module, function or block. Inner functions can read the variables of outer functions, and a **closure** is a function that keeps access to those variables even after the outer function has returned. Closures power private state, function factories, memoisation, and event handlers that remember data.
key_points: `let` in a for loop creates a new binding per iteration; `var` shares one binding across all of them.
A closure captures variables, not copies of their values.
Hoisting: var starts as undefined; let and const throw a ReferenceError before their line.
learn_items: Scope types: global, module, function and block scope, and the scope chain lookup from inner to outer
Lexical scope: what a function can see is fixed where it is written, not where it is called
Hoisting: function declarations fully hoisted, var hoisted as undefined, let and const in the temporal dead zone
Closures: a returned inner function keeps its outer variables alive; trace makeCounter() step by step
Classic loop bug: setTimeout inside for (var i …) prints the final value; fix it with let
Uses: private state (a counter), function factories (multiplier(3)), once() and memoise()
Memory: closures keep captured variables alive, so remove listeners and timers you no longer need
IIFEs: why immediately invoked functions were used for privacy before ES modules existed

topics.title: Arrays and array methods: map, filter, reduce
topics.summary_md: Arrays are ordered lists with a method for almost every job. `map` transforms each item, `filter` keeps some, `reduce` folds them into one value, and `find`, `some` and `every` search. Know which methods **mutate** the array (`push`, `splice`, `sort`, `reverse`) and which return a new one, because React and most modern code expect you not to mutate.
key_points: map, filter and slice return new arrays; push, pop, splice, sort and reverse change the original.
Default sort compares strings: [10, 9, 1].sort() gives [1, 10, 9]; pass (a, b) => a - b for numbers.
toSorted, toReversed and toSpliced return changed copies without mutating the original.
Always give reduce an initial value so it works on empty arrays.
learn_items: Basics: creating arrays, length, indexing, at(-1), push/pop, shift/unshift, includes and indexOf
Transform and select: map, filter, find, findIndex, some and every, and chaining them
reduce: accumulator and initial value; sum, maximum, count by key and grouping into an object
Mutating vs copying: splice vs slice, sort vs toSorted, reverse vs toReversed
Sorting: numeric comparators, strings with localeCompare, and sorting objects by a field
Building and flattening: flat, flatMap, Array.from({ length: n }) and Object.groupBy
Iteration choices: for...of vs forEach (you cannot break out of forEach) vs index loops

topics.title: Objects, destructuring, spread and JSON
topics.summary_md: Objects map keys to values and are passed by reference, so two variables can point to the same object. Destructuring pulls values out of objects and arrays, and spread (`...`) copies them into new ones, which is the usual way to update data immutably. JSON is the text format for sending data over the network: `JSON.stringify` and `JSON.parse` convert between objects and text.
key_points: Assigning an object to another variable copies the reference, not the object.
Spread makes a shallow copy; nested objects stay shared. Use structuredClone for a deep copy.
JSON has no functions, undefined, Date objects or comments; dates become strings.
=== on objects checks identity, not equal contents.
learn_items: Object basics: literals, dot vs bracket access, computed keys, shorthand properties and methods
References: why two equal-looking objects are not ===, and mutation through a shared reference
Iterating: Object.keys, Object.values, Object.entries, Object.fromEntries and the in operator
Destructuring: renaming, default values, nested patterns and destructuring function parameters
Spread and rest: { ...obj, key: newValue } updates, array spread, and rest to collect remaining fields
Copying: shallow copies with spread or Object.assign vs deep copies with structuredClone
JSON: stringify and parse, pretty printing with an indent argument, and what JSON cannot represent
Safe access: user?.address?.city ?? 'Unknown' for data that may be missing

topics.title: this, prototypes and classes
topics.summary_md: `this` is decided by how a function is **called**: a method call sets it to the object before the dot, a plain call leaves it undefined in strict mode, and `call`, `apply` and `bind` set it explicitly. Objects inherit through the **prototype chain**: a missing property is looked up on the prototype, then its prototype, and so on. `class` syntax is a cleaner way to write constructors and prototypes.
key_points: Arrow functions take `this` from the surrounding scope, which fixes lost-this bugs in callbacks.
Passing obj.method as a callback loses `this`; use bind or wrap it in an arrow function.
Methods declared in a class live on the prototype and are shared by all instances.
Fields named with # are private to the class and cannot be read from outside.

Lost this: passing a method as a callback, and fixing it with bind or an arrow wrapper
Arrow functions and this: lexical this, and why arrows are a poor choice for object methods
Prototype chain: Object.getPrototypeOf, property lookup, Object.hasOwn vs in, and Object.create
new in four steps: create an object, link its prototype, run the constructor with this, return the object
Classes: constructor, methods, getters and setters, static members and private #fields
Inheritance: extends and super(), overriding methods, and instanceof checks
Composition over inheritance: when plain objects and functions are simpler than class hierarchies

topics.title: Modules, Map, Set and error handling
topics.summary_md: ES modules split code into files with `export` and `import`; each module has its own scope and runs once. Map and Set are built-in collections: a Map keeps keys of any type in insertion order and a Set stores unique values. Errors are thrown with `throw new Error()` and handled with try...catch...finally, and custom error classes make different failures easy to tell apart.
key_points: A file can have many named exports but only one default export.
Use a Map for frequent additions or non-string keys, and plain objects for fixed records.
`[...new Set(array)]` removes duplicates in one line.
Throw Error objects, not strings, so you keep the message and the stack trace.
learn_items: ES modules: named exports, a default export, import { a as b }, import * as ns, <script type="module">
Module behaviour: strict mode by default, own scope, runs once, and dynamic import() returns a promise
Node modules: CommonJS require and module.exports vs ESM, and "type": "module" in package.json
Map: set, get, has, delete, size, insertion order and object keys; WeakMap for data attached to objects
Set: add, has, delete, de-duplicating arrays, and the union and intersection methods
Errors: throw, try/catch/finally, error.name, error.message, error.stack and the cause option
Custom errors: class ValidationError extends Error, and checking instanceof inside catch

topics.title: Iterators, generators and the iteration protocol
topics.summary_md: Anything with a `[Symbol.iterator]` method is **iterable**, which is why for...of, spread and destructuring work on arrays, strings, Maps and Sets alike. An iterator is an object whose `next()` returns `{ value, done }`. Generator functions (`function*`) write iterators the easy way: `yield` pauses the function and the next call resumes it, which suits lazy sequences and paged data.
key_points: Plain objects are not iterable; loop over Object.entries(obj) with for...of instead.
A generator runs only up to the next yield, so an infinite sequence is safe if you stop consuming.
Async generators with for await...of read streams and paged APIs one chunk at a time.
learn_items: Iterable protocol: [Symbol.iterator]() returns an iterator; arrays, strings, Map, Set and NodeList are iterable
Iterator protocol: next() returns { value, done }; drive one by hand to see how for...of works
Custom iterables: make a Range class iterable so for...of and spread work on it
Generators: function*, yield, the generator object, and return() to stop early
Lazy sequences: an infinite id generator, a take(n) helper, and why laziness saves work
yield*: delegate to another iterable, for example to walk a nested tree
Async iteration: async function*, for await...of, and reading paged API results
Iterator helpers: .map(), .filter(), .take() and .toArray() called directly on iterators

topics.title: DOM tree: selecting, creating and updating nodes
topics.summary_md: The DOM is the browser’s live tree of objects built from your HTML; changing it changes the page. Select nodes with `querySelector` and `querySelectorAll`, change text with `textContent`, classes with `classList`, and attributes with `setAttribute` or `dataset`. Create elements with `document.createElement` and insert them with `append`, `prepend`, `before`, `after`, and take them out with `remove`.
key_points: Prefer textContent to innerHTML for user data; innerHTML with untrusted input enables XSS.
querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList; getElementsByClassName returns a live collection.
Toggle a CSS class instead of setting many inline styles from JavaScript.
Load scripts with `defer` or `type="module"` so the DOM exists before your code runs.

Running scripts: <script defer>, type="module" and DOMContentLoaded, so elements exist when queried
Selecting: querySelector, querySelectorAll, closest() and matches(), and live vs static collections
Content: textContent vs innerHTML, and why innerHTML with user input is unsafe
Attributes and classes: getAttribute, setAttribute, dataset for data-* attributes, classList add/remove/toggle
Creating and inserting: createElement, append, prepend, before, after, replaceWith, remove, <template> clones
Performance: insert many nodes with a DocumentFragment or one append; avoid reading layout after each write

topics.title: Events, delegation, forms and browser storage
topics.summary_md: `addEventListener` runs a handler when an event fires. Events travel in three phases: **capture** down from the window, the **target**, then **bubble** back up, which enables **event delegation**: one listener on a parent handles clicks on any child via `event.target.closest()`. Forms are handled with the `submit` event, `preventDefault()` and `FormData`, and small data can be kept between visits in `localStorage`.
key_points: event.target is where the event started; event.currentTarget is the element whose listener is running.
Delegation works for children added later and needs one listener instead of hundreds.
localStorage is synchronous, per origin and stores strings only: use JSON.stringify and JSON.parse.
Never store tokens or secrets in localStorage; any script on the page can read it.
learn_items: Listening: addEventListener(type, handler, options), removeEventListener, and the once, passive and signal options
Event object: type, target, currentTarget, key for keyboard events, and preventDefault()
Propagation: capture, target and bubble phases, and stopPropagation used sparingly
Delegation: one listener on a list, event.target.closest('li') to find the item, works for new items
Common events: click, input vs change, submit, keydown, focus and blur (focusin and focusout bubble)
Forms in JavaScript: a submit handler, preventDefault, new FormData(form) and Object.fromEntries
Storage: localStorage and sessionStorage get, set and remove, JSON for objects, the storage event across tabs
Observers: IntersectionObserver for lazy loading and infinite scroll instead of scroll listeners

topics.title: Callbacks, the event loop and task queues
topics.summary_md: JavaScript runs on one thread, so slow work such as network requests and timers is handed to the browser or Node, and a callback runs later. The **event loop** takes one task at a time from the task queue, and after each task it empties the **microtask queue** (promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) before rendering or running the next task. That is why a resolved promise’s `.then` runs before a `setTimeout(fn, 0)`.
key_points: Synchronous code always finishes before any queued callback runs.
Order: the current script, then every microtask, then the next task such as a timer.
setTimeout(fn, 0) means "after at least 0 ms, when the stack is clear", never immediately.
A long synchronous loop blocks clicks, rendering and timers.
learn_items: Single thread: the call stack, and why a long loop freezes the page
Callbacks: passing a function to setTimeout, addEventListener or a Node API to run later
Callback problems: deep nesting, Node’s error-first callbacks, and errors that are easy to lose
Event loop parts: call stack, browser or Node APIs, the task (macrotask) queue and the microtask queue
Ordering: predict the output of a script mixing console.log, setTimeout and Promise.resolve().then
Rendering: the browser paints only between tasks; requestAnimationFrame runs just before the next paint
Staying responsive: split heavy work into chunks with setTimeout, or move it to a Web Worker

topics.title: Promises and async/await
topics.summary_md: A promise stands for a value that arrives later; it is pending, then fulfilled or rejected, and settles only once. Chain work with `.then`, handle failures with `.catch` and clean up with `.finally`. `async` functions always return a promise, and `await` pauses that function until a promise settles, so asynchronous code reads like synchronous code with ordinary try/catch.
key_points: Return the inner promise from a .then callback, or the chain will not wait for it.
await pauses only the current async function; the rest of the program keeps running.
An unhandled rejection is a bug: catch it, or let the caller handle it.
Awaiting inside a loop runs the steps one after another; start independent work together.
learn_items: Promise states: pending, fulfilled and rejected; a promise settles once and never changes again
Creating promises: new Promise((resolve, reject) => …), and a delay(ms) helper that wraps setTimeout
Chaining: then returns a new promise, returning values vs returning promises, catch and finally
async functions: always return a promise; a return value fulfils it and a throw rejects it
await: pauses the async function, unwraps the value, and throws on rejection, so use try/catch
Common mistakes: a missing await, a missing return in .then, and async callbacks inside forEach
Top-level await in ES modules, and turning callback APIs into promises with util.promisify in Node

topics.title: Fetch, Promise combinators and cancellation
topics.summary_md: `fetch` returns a promise for a Response; it rejects only on network failure, so check `response.ok` for HTTP errors such as 404 or 500. Run independent requests together with `Promise.all` (fails fast), `Promise.allSettled` (waits for all), `Promise.race` or `Promise.any`. Cancel slow or outdated requests with an `AbortController`, and retry temporary failures with backoff.
key_points: fetch does not reject on 404 or 500; check response.ok or response.status.
Promise.all rejects on the first failure; Promise.allSettled reports every result.
`AbortSignal.timeout(5000)` cancels a request that takes longer than 5 seconds.
Abort stale search requests so an older response cannot overwrite a newer one.
learn_items: fetch basics: a GET request, response.ok, response.status, await response.json() and headers
Sending data: method POST, a Content-Type: application/json header and body: JSON.stringify(data)
Errors: network failures reject, HTTP errors resolve, so throw your own error when !response.ok
Combinators: Promise.all, allSettled, race and any, and which one fits which job
Cancellation: AbortController, passing its signal to fetch, handling AbortError, AbortSignal.timeout(ms)
Race conditions: abort or ignore outdated responses in search-as-you-type
Retries: retry only idempotent requests, with exponential backoff and a maximum number of attempts
Concurrency limits: process 100 URLs at most 5 at a time instead of all at once

topics.title: TypeScript basics: types, inference and tsconfig
topics.summary_md: TypeScript adds a compile-time type checker to JavaScript; the types are erased when the code runs. Annotate function parameters and public boundaries, and let **inference** handle the rest. Describe object shapes with `interface` or `type`, and turn on `strict` in tsconfig.json so null checks and implicit-any errors catch real bugs.
key_points: Types do not exist at runtime: validate API and form data with code, not just a type.
Prefer `unknown` to `any` for values you have not checked yet.
Turn on strict mode from day one; adding it to a large codebase later is much harder.
Optional properties (`name?: string`) may be undefined, so handle that case.
learn_items: Setup: npm i -D typescript, npx tsc --init, tsc --noEmit to type-check, and running .ts files with tsx
Basic types: string, number, boolean, arrays (string[]), tuples, literal types, null and undefined
Inference: annotate parameters and exported return types; let TypeScript infer local variables
Object shapes: interface vs type alias, optional (?) and readonly properties, index signatures
Functions: parameter and return types, optional and default parameters, void and never
any vs unknown: any switches checking off; unknown must be narrowed before you use it
tsconfig.json: strict, target, module, moduleResolution, noUncheckedIndexedAccess and include
Reading errors: start from the last line of a long error, and hover in the editor to see inferred types

topics.title: Unions, narrowing and discriminated unions
topics.summary_md: A union type (`string | number`) says a value can be one of several types, and **narrowing** lets TypeScript work out which one inside a branch. Narrow with `typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, equality checks and custom type guards. A **discriminated union** gives each variant a literal field such as `kind` or `status`, so a switch on it is fully type-safe, and a `never` check flags any case you forgot.
key_points: Model states as a discriminated union instead of one object with many optional fields.
Exhaustive switch: assign the value to a variable of type never in the default branch.
A type guard `(x): x is User` is only as correct as the check inside it.
learn_items: Union and literal types: string | number, 'idle' | 'loading' | 'error', and why literals beat plain string
typeof and truthiness narrowing, including the typeof null === 'object' trap
instanceof and in narrowing for classes and object shapes
Discriminated unions: a shared literal field (kind, status, type) and a switch on it
Exhaustiveness: const unreachable: never = value in the default branch, so new variants fail to compile
Custom type guards: function isUser(x: unknown): x is User, and assertion functions (asserts x is User)
Intersection types: A & B to combine shapes, and when interface extends reads more clearly
Avoiding as: type assertions skip checks; prefer narrowing or a runtime validation library such as zod

tasks.title: Type a fetch state as a discriminated union (idle, loading, success with data, error with message) and handle each case in a switch

topics.title: Generics, constraints and keyof
topics.summary_md: Generics are type parameters: `function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined` works for any array and still returns the right type. Constraints (`T extends { id: string }`) say what a type parameter must have, and `keyof` with indexed access types (`T[K]`) links keys to their values. Generic types are everywhere: `Array<T>`, `Promise<T>`, `Map<K, V>` and React’s `useState<T>`.
key_points: A generic should relate input and output types; if it does not, you probably do not need one.
Let TypeScript infer type arguments, and write them only when inference cannot.
`K extends keyof T` makes `getProp(obj, key)` return the exact property type.
learn_items: Why generics: identity<T> and first<T>(items: T[]) keep types where any would lose them
Type argument inference from the call, and explicit type arguments when inference fails
Generic types and interfaces: ApiResponse<T>, Result<T, E> and Box<T>
Constraints: T extends { id: string }, and default type parameters such as <T = string>
keyof and indexed access: K extends keyof T with the return type T[K]
Built-in generics: Array<T>, Promise<T>, Record<K, V>, Map<K, V> and ReturnType<typeof fn>
Generic functions with callbacks and generic classes, such as a typed groupBy<T, K>

topics.title: Utility, mapped and conditional types
topics.summary_md: Utility types derive new types from existing ones instead of copying them: `Partial`, `Required`, `Pick`, `Omit`, `Record`, `Readonly`, `ReturnType` and `Awaited`. They are built from **mapped types** (`{ [K in keyof T]: … }`) and **conditional types** (`T extends U ? X : Y`) with `infer`. Template literal types build string patterns such as event names, and `satisfies` checks a value against a type without widening it.
key_points: Derive types from one source of truth instead of duplicating shapes.
`Omit<User, 'password'>` is the type of a user object sent to the client.
`satisfies` checks a value against a type but keeps the narrower inferred type.
Keep type-level code readable; a clear simple type beats a clever one.
learn_items: Everyday utility types: Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, Omit, Record and NonNullable
Function helpers: ReturnType, Parameters, and Awaited to unwrap a promise’s result
Types from values: keyof typeof CONFIG for a union of keys, and typeof for a value’s type
as const: freeze literals into readonly tuples, so ROLES[number] becomes a union of strings
Mapped types: { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }, the readonly and ? modifiers, and key remapping with as
Conditional types: T extends U ? X : Y, infer to extract a type, and distribution over unions
Template literal types: `on${Capitalize<Name>}` to type event handler names
satisfies: const config = { … } satisfies Config keeps literal types while checking the shape

topics.title: Components and JSX
topics.summary_md: A React app is a tree of **components**: plain functions whose names start with a capital letter and which return JSX. JSX looks like HTML but compiles to JavaScript calls, so you embed expressions with `{}`, write `className` instead of `class` and close every tag. Start a project with Vite and keep components pure: same inputs, same output, no side effects during render.
key_points: Component names start with a capital letter; lowercase tags such as <div> are HTML elements.
A component returns one root element; wrap siblings in a fragment <>…</>.
Rendering must be pure: never change outside variables or the DOM while rendering.
learn_items: Project setup: create a React + TypeScript app with npm create vite@latest and find main.tsx, where createRoot renders <App />
Function components: a function returning JSX, named in PascalCase, exported and imported like any module
JSX rules: one root element or fragment, close every tag, camelCase attributes such as className, htmlFor, onClick
Expressions in JSX: put any expression inside {}, e.g. {user.name} or {price * qty}; statements like if are not allowed
Inline styles: pass an object, style={{ marginTop: 8 }}, with camelCase property names
Component tree: split a page into small nested components; a file usually exports one main component
Purity: a component must not mutate props or outside variables while rendering; React may render it more than once
Strict Mode: in development it renders components twice to expose impure code; production renders once

topics.title: Props and component composition
topics.summary_md: **Props** are the inputs a parent passes to a child, like arguments to a function. They are read-only: a child never changes its props; it asks the parent to change data by calling a callback prop. The special `children` prop lets you build wrapper components such as Card or Layout, which is how React favours composition over inheritance.
key_points: Props flow down; events flow up through callback props such as onSelect.
Never mutate props; treat them as read-only snapshots.
`children` lets a component wrap any JSX placed between its tags.
learn_items: Passing props: <Avatar size={48} user={user} /> and reading them by destructuring, function Avatar({ size, user })
Default values: give defaults while destructuring, ({ size = 32 }), rather than a separate defaultProps object
Typing props: describe props with a TypeScript type, mark optional ones with ?, and let the editor catch misuse
Spreading props: {...props} forwards many props at once; use it sparingly so data flow stays readable
children: anything between <Card>…</Card> arrives as props.children; render it where the content belongs
Callback props: pass onDelete={(id) => remove(id)} so a child can tell its parent that something happened
Composition: build pages from small generic pieces (Card, Button, Modal) instead of one component with many flags

topics.title: State and events with useState
topics.summary_md: **State** is data a component remembers between renders; `useState` returns the current value and a setter, and calling the setter schedules a re-render. Each render sees a fixed snapshot of state, so reading state right after setting it gives the old value. Update objects and arrays immutably by creating copies, and use the updater form `setCount(c => c + 1)` when the next value depends on the previous one.
key_points: Setting state does not change the variable now; it asks React for a new render.
Copy, never mutate: [...items, item] and { ...user, name } create new values.
Use the updater form when the new state depends on the old state.
Call hooks only at the top level, never inside loops or conditions.
learn_items: useState: const [value, setValue] = useState(initial) declares state; initial is used only on the first render
Event handlers: pass a function, onClick={handleClick}, not a call, onClick={handleClick()}, which runs during render
Snapshots: state is fixed for one render, so a log right after setCount(count + 1) still prints the old count
Batching: React groups several state updates made in one event into a single re-render
Updater functions: setCount(c => c + 1) three times adds 3, while setCount(count + 1) three times adds 1
Objects and arrays in state: replace them with copies using spread, map and filter; never push or assign into them
Rules of Hooks: call hooks only at the top level of components or custom hooks, in the same order every render
Lazy initial state: useState(() => expensiveSetup()) runs the setup function only once

topics.title: Lists, keys, conditional rendering and forms
topics.summary_md: Render lists by mapping data to JSX with `items.map(...)`, giving every item a stable unique `key` so React can match items between renders. Show or hide UI with `&&`, the ternary operator or an early return. A **controlled input** takes its value from state and updates it in onChange, which makes validation and resetting simple; uncontrolled inputs are read from the form on submit.
key_points: Keys must be stable and unique among siblings; database ids are ideal, array indexes are risky.
Beware {count && <List />}: when count is 0, React renders the 0.
Controlled input = value from state + an onChange that sets that state.
learn_items: Rendering lists: {users.map(u => <UserRow key={u.id} user={u} />)} turns an array of data into elements
Keys: use a stable id from the data; index keys break when items are inserted, removed or reordered
Conditional rendering: cond && <X />, cond ? <A /> : <B />, or return null early to render nothing
The 0 trap: {items.length && <List />} prints 0 for an empty list; write items.length > 0 && … instead
Controlled inputs: <input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />; checkboxes use checked
Form submit: handle onSubmit on the <form> and call e.preventDefault() before reading state
Uncontrolled forms: read values with new FormData(e.currentTarget) on submit when you need no live updates
Derived values: compute filtered lists and validation messages during render instead of storing them in state

topics.title: useEffect: syncing with the outside world
topics.summary_md: `useEffect` runs code after React has updated the screen, to synchronise a component with something outside React: a timer, a subscription, a browser API or a network request. The dependency array tells React when to re-run it, and the cleanup function undoes the previous run. Many effects are unnecessary: derive values during render and handle user actions in event handlers.
key_points: List every reactive value the effect reads in its dependency array.
Return a cleanup function to clear timers, remove listeners and cancel requests.
You might not need an effect: derived data belongs in render, user actions in handlers.
learn_items: When effects run: after commit; [] runs once after mount, [a, b] when a or b change, no array after every render
Cleanup: the returned function runs before the next run and on unmount, e.g. clearInterval or removeEventListener
Dependencies: include every prop, state and function used inside; the react-hooks lint rule flags missing ones
Strict Mode: in development effects run, clean up and run again, to prove the cleanup works
Fetching in effects: refetch when an id changes and ignore stale responses with an AbortController in cleanup
Avoiding effects: compute fullName during render; reset a child’s state by changing its key instead of an effect
Object and function dependencies: values created during render are new each time; move them inside the effect
Data libraries: in real apps prefer a framework loader or TanStack Query over hand-written fetch effects

tasks.title: Build a user page that fetches a profile when userId changes, shows loading and error states, and aborts stale requests

topics.title: useRef, useReducer and custom hooks
topics.summary_md: `useRef` holds a mutable value that survives renders without causing one, and gives access to DOM nodes for focus, scrolling and measuring. `useReducer` moves complex state updates into a pure reducer function of state and action. **Custom hooks** (functions named `useSomething`) package stateful logic so several components can reuse it; each caller gets its own state.
key_points: Changing ref.current does not re-render; use state for anything shown on screen.
A reducer is pure: (state, action) => newState, with no side effects.
Custom hooks share logic, not state: every component calling one has its own copy.
learn_items: useRef for values: const timerId = useRef(null) keeps an interval id across renders without re-rendering
DOM refs: attach ref={inputRef} and call inputRef.current.focus() in a handler or effect, not during render
ref as a prop: in React 19 function components receive ref as a normal prop; forwardRef is no longer needed
useReducer: const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initial); then dispatch({ type: "added", item })
Writing reducers: switch on action.type, return new objects immutably, throw on unknown action types
Custom hooks: extract logic into hooks such as useOnlineStatus or useDebounce; a hook may call other hooks
Hook naming: start the name with use so the linter can check the Rules of Hooks inside it

topics.title: Re-renders, memoisation and code splitting
topics.summary_md: A component re-renders when its state changes, when its parent re-renders or when a context it reads changes. Re-renders are usually cheap, so measure with the React DevTools Profiler before optimising. `memo`, `useMemo` and `useCallback` skip work when inputs are unchanged, and the **React Compiler** can add this memoisation automatically. `lazy` with `Suspense` moves rarely used screens into separate chunks.
key_points: A parent re-render re-renders its children unless they are memoised and their props are unchanged.
Profile first: optimise only components that are measurably slow.
useCallback helps only when the function goes to a memoised child or a dependency array.
learn_items: Why components re-render: their own state, a parent re-render or a context change
React DevTools Profiler: record an interaction and find components with long or unnecessary renders
memo: wrap a component so it skips re-rendering when its props are shallowly equal to last time
useMemo: cache an expensive calculation, useMemo(() => sortJobs(jobs), [jobs]), recomputed when inputs change
useCallback: keep the same function identity between renders so memoised children do not re-render
React Compiler: a build-time plugin that memoises components and values automatically when code follows the rules
Moving state down: keep fast-changing state in the small component that uses it so less of the tree re-renders
Code splitting: const Admin = lazy(() => import("./Admin")) rendered inside <Suspense fallback={…}>

topics.title: React 19: Actions, use() and Server Components
topics.summary_md: React 19 adds **Actions**: async functions passed to a form’s `action` prop or run inside `startTransition`, with pending state, errors and optimistic updates handled for you. `useActionState`, `useFormStatus` and `useOptimistic` cover common form cases, and `use()` reads a promise or context during render. **Server Components** run only on the server and need a framework such as Next.js.
key_points: <form action={fn}> calls fn with the FormData and resets uncontrolled fields on success.
useOptimistic shows the expected result at once and reverts it if the action fails.
use(promise) suspends until the promise resolves; wrap the component in Suspense.
learn_items: Transitions: useTransition gives [isPending, startTransition]; async work inside it is a non-urgent Action
Form actions: <form action={submit}> calls submit(formData); no onSubmit or preventDefault is needed
useActionState: const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(fn, initial) tracks result and pending
useFormStatus: a component inside a form reads { pending } to disable its submit button while the action runs
useOptimistic: show a new comment immediately, then React swaps in the real result or rolls it back
use(): read a promise or a context inside render, even conditionally; the nearest Suspense shows the fallback
Context as provider: React 19 lets you render <ThemeContext value={…}> without .Provider
Server Components: async components that fetch on the server and ship no JS; interactive parts stay client

topics.title: Where state lives: local, lifted and context
topics.summary_md: Start with state **local** to the component that uses it, **lift** it to the closest common parent when siblings need it, and avoid duplicated or derivable state. **Context** passes a value deep into the tree without prop drilling; it suits values that change rarely, such as the theme, language or signed-in user. Every component reading a context re-renders when its value changes, so split contexts and memoise their values.
key_points: Keep state as low in the tree as possible; lift it only when two components need it.
Do not store what you can compute from props or other state.
Context re-renders every consumer when its value changes.
Server state (fetched data) and client state (UI choices) are different problems.
learn_items: Lifting state: move shared state to the nearest common parent and pass the value and callbacks down
Single source of truth: never keep the same data in two states; store the selected id, not a copy of the item
Prop drilling: passing props through two or three levels is fine; reach for context beyond that
Creating context: createContext(default), render <ThemeContext value={theme}>, read it with useContext
Context with a reducer: put state and dispatch from useReducer in context for a small app-wide store
Context performance: memoise the value with useMemo and split often-changing values into their own context
State categories: label each value as UI, form, URL, server cache or global client state before picking a tool
URL state: keep filters, tabs and page numbers in the query string so links and the back button work

topics.title: Stores and server state: Zustand, Redux, TanStack Query
topics.summary_md: For complex client state shared across many screens, a **store** keeps state outside the component tree and lets components subscribe to only the slice they need. **Zustand** is a minimal hook-based store; **Redux Toolkit** adds slices, Immer-powered updates and strong DevTools. Data from APIs is a cache, not app state: **TanStack Query** handles fetching, caching, refetching and invalidation.
key_points: Select the smallest slice you need so unrelated updates do not re-render you.
In Redux Toolkit slices you may write mutating code; Immer turns it into immutable updates.
Use TanStack Query for API data and invalidate queries after a mutation.
Normalise collections by id so each item is stored once.
learn_items: Zustand: const useCart = create(set => ({ items: [], add: i => set(s => ({ items: [...s.items, i] })) }))
Selectors: useCart(s => s.items.length) re-renders only when that selected value changes
Redux Toolkit: configureStore, createSlice with reducers, useSelector to read and useDispatch to send actions
Immer in slices: state.items.push(x) inside a createSlice reducer is safe because Immer produces new state
Normalising: store { byId: {…}, ids: […] } instead of nested arrays so an update touches one item
TanStack Query: useQuery({ queryKey: ["jobs", filters], queryFn }) returns data, isPending and error, cached
Mutations: useMutation for writes, then queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ["jobs"] }) to refetch
Stale time: staleTime sets how long cached data counts as fresh before a background refetch

topics.title: App Router: routes, layouts and navigation
topics.summary_md: Next.js is a React framework with file-based routing in the `app` directory: each folder is a URL segment and a `page.tsx` file makes it a route. A `layout.tsx` wraps its pages and stays mounted during navigation, while `loading.tsx`, `error.tsx` and `not-found.tsx` give each segment its own loading and error UI. Dynamic segments such as `[id]` receive the value through `params`.
key_points: Folders define routes; only page.tsx (or route.ts) makes a segment reachable.
Layouts persist across navigation and keep their state.
Use <Link> for internal navigation; it navigates on the client and prefetches.
learn_items: Create a project: npx create-next-app@latest with TypeScript, the App Router and Tailwind; run npm run dev
Routing: app/page.tsx is /, app/jobs/page.tsx is /jobs, app/jobs/[id]/page.tsx is /jobs/123
params: in current versions params is a Promise, so write const { id } = await params in an async page
Layouts: app/layout.tsx is the root layout with <html> and <body>; nested layouts wrap one section
Special files: loading.tsx while loading, error.tsx (a client component) for errors, not-found.tsx for 404s
Navigation: <Link href="/jobs"> for links, useRouter().push() in client code, redirect() on the server
Route groups and metadata: (marketing) folders group routes without a URL part; export metadata for titles

topics.title: Server Components and Client Components
topics.summary_md: In the App Router every component is a **Server Component** by default: it renders on the server, can be `async`, can read databases and secrets directly, and sends no JavaScript to the browser. Add the `"use client"` directive at the top of a file to make a **Client Component** that can use state, effects and event handlers. Keep client components small, at the leaves, and pass server data to them as serialisable props.
key_points: Server Components cannot use useState, useEffect or event handlers.
"use client" marks a boundary: that file and everything it imports also run in the browser.
Props from server to client must be serialisable: no functions or class instances.
Hydration attaches event handlers to the HTML the server sent.
learn_items: Server Components: async function Page() { const jobs = await db.job.findMany(); … } runs only on the server
Client Components: "use client" at the top of a file enables useState, useEffect, onClick and browser APIs
The boundary: a client file’s imports become client code; pass server components into client ones as children
Serialisable props: strings, numbers, plain objects, arrays, Dates and promises can cross; functions cannot
server-only: import "server-only" in modules holding secrets so an accidental client import fails the build
Environment variables: only NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables reach the browser; all others stay on the server
Hydration: React attaches handlers to server HTML; output that differs, such as Date.now(), causes mismatch errors
Streaming: wrap slow parts in <Suspense> so the rest of the page is sent and shown first

topics.title: Data fetching, caching and rendering modes
topics.summary_md: Next.js prerenders a route **statically** when it uses no request data, and renders it **dynamically** per request when it reads cookies, headers or search params. Fetch data directly in Server Components; in current versions `fetch` is not cached by default, so you opt in to caching and decide how it refreshes. **Revalidation** refreshes cached data on a timer or on demand after a change.
key_points: Static routes are fastest; reading cookies() or headers() makes a route dynamic.
Revalidate on a timer, or call revalidatePath or revalidateTag after a write.
Start independent requests together with Promise.all to avoid waterfalls.
learn_items: Static vs dynamic: routes without request data are prerendered; cookies(), headers() or searchParams make them dynamic
Fetching in Server Components: await fetch or a database query directly in the component; no useEffect needed
Caching fetch: opt in with { cache: "force-cache" }, or { next: { revalidate: 3600 } } for a timed refresh
Segment config: export const revalidate = 60 in a page refreshes it at most once a minute
On-demand revalidation: after a write call revalidatePath("/jobs") or revalidateTag("jobs")
Waterfalls: start independent requests together with Promise.all instead of awaiting them one by one
generateStaticParams: return the values of a dynamic segment, e.g. all blog slugs, to prerender them at build
use cache: newer versions add a "use cache" directive to cache a function or component output explicitly

tasks.title: Build a blog with static post pages via generateStaticParams, a dynamic dashboard reading cookies, and timed revalidation

topics.title: Server Actions, route handlers and deployment
topics.summary_md: **Server Actions** are async functions marked `"use server"` that run on the server when a form submits or a client calls them, so you can write to a database without building an API route. Treat them as public endpoints: validate input and check the user every time. **Route handlers** (`route.ts`) serve HTTP APIs for webhooks and other clients, and middleware (called proxy from Next.js 16) runs before routing.
key_points: Every Server Action is a callable endpoint: validate input and authorise inside it.
Use route handlers for webhooks, public APIs and non-React clients.
next build prints which routes are static and which are dynamic.
learn_items: Server Actions: async function createJob(formData: FormData) with "use server", used as <form action={createJob}>
Validation: parse FormData with a schema library such as zod and return field errors to useActionState
Security: check the session inside every action; never trust hidden form fields or ids sent by the client
After a write: call revalidatePath or redirect from the action so the UI shows fresh data
Route handlers: app/api/jobs/route.ts exports GET and POST functions that take a Request and return a Response
Middleware or proxy: a root file that runs before routing to redirect signed-out users or rewrite paths
Build and deploy: next build then next start, or a host that supports Next.js; read the route summary

topics.title: Utility classes, the design scale and variants
topics.summary_md: Tailwind styles elements with small **utility classes** such as `flex`, `p-4`, `text-sm` and `bg-blue-600`, each mapped to a consistent design scale. Variants apply a utility conditionally: `hover:`, `focus-visible:` and `disabled:` for states, and `sm:`, `md:`, `lg:` for breakpoints, which are mobile-first. Tailwind v4 is set up with one CSS import and generates only the classes your files use.
key_points: Breakpoints are mobile-first: md:flex means flex from the md width upward.
Spacing follows one scale: p-4 is 1rem, gap-2 is 0.5rem.
Only class names found in your source are generated, so never build them by string concatenation.
learn_items: Setup in v4: install tailwindcss and @tailwindcss/vite, add the plugin, then @import "tailwindcss"; in your CSS
Layout utilities: flex, grid, grid-cols-3, items-center, justify-between and gap-4 cover most layouts
Spacing and sizing: p-, px-, m-, mt-, w-, h- and max-w-md all follow one spacing scale
Typography and colour: text-sm to text-3xl, font-semibold, text-gray-700, bg-indigo-600, bg-black/50 for opacity
State variants: hover:, focus-visible:, active:, disabled: and group-hover: style interactive states
Responsive variants: write the mobile style first, then override, e.g. grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-3
Arbitrary values: w-[37rem] or top-[117px] for one-off values; prefer the scale when it fits
Dynamic classes: map each state to a complete class string; "bg-" + colour is never generated

topics.title: Theme tokens, dark mode and reusable components
topics.summary_md: In Tailwind v4 you customise the design system in CSS with an `@theme` block: defining `--color-brand-500` creates `bg-brand-500`, `text-brand-500` and related utilities. The `dark:` variant follows the system colour scheme by default and can be switched to a class with a custom variant. Avoid long repeated class lists by extracting components, and merge conditional classes with clsx and tailwind-merge.
key_points: Define tokens in @theme instead of scattering hard-coded values.
Reuse styles through components and props, not big @apply blocks.
tailwind-merge resolves conflicts such as p-2 and p-4 so the later class wins.
learn_items: @theme: add --color-brand-500, --font-display or --breakpoint-3xl to generate matching utilities
CSS variables: theme values are real CSS variables, usable as var(--color-brand-500) in custom CSS
Dark mode: dark:bg-gray-900 follows prefers-color-scheme; declare @custom-variant dark for a class toggle
Component extraction: build a Button whose variant and size props map to class strings
clsx and tailwind-merge: build class lists conditionally and let later utilities override conflicting ones
@apply: use it sparingly, for example on third-party markup you cannot add classes to
Container queries: @container on a parent and @md: on children style by container width, not the viewport
Accessibility: keep visible focus with focus-visible:ring-2 and check the colour contrast of your palette

topics.title: Packages, lockfiles and ES modules
topics.summary_md: `package.json` lists a project’s dependencies, devDependencies and scripts; a **lockfile** records the exact version of every installed package so every machine gets the same tree. Version ranges use semver: `^1.4.0` allows minor and patch updates, `~1.4.0` only patches. Modern code uses **ES modules** (`import`/`export`), which bundlers can analyse statically for tree-shaking.
key_points: Commit the lockfile; use npm ci in CI for a clean, exact install.
dependencies ship with the app; devDependencies are build and test tools.
Static import/export lets tools remove unused code; require() is harder to analyse.
learn_items: package.json: name, version, "type": "module", scripts, dependencies and devDependencies, and what each does
Semver: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH; ^ allows minor and patch updates, ~ only patches, an exact version none
Lockfiles: package-lock.json or pnpm-lock.yaml pin the whole tree; npm ci installs exactly from it
Scripts: npm run dev, build and test run commands from scripts; npx runs a package binary without a global install
ES modules vs CommonJS: static import/export versus require and module.exports evaluated at runtime
Package managers: npm, pnpm (shared store, strict node_modules) and Yarn do the same job differently
Workspaces: a monorepo with several packages sharing one lockfile and linking local packages together
Auditing: npm outdated and npm audit list old and vulnerable dependencies

topics.title: Vite: dev server, production builds and chunks
topics.summary_md: **Vite** serves your source as native ES modules during development, so the dev server starts quickly and **hot module replacement** swaps edited modules without a full reload. `vite build` bundles for production: it transpiles TypeScript and JSX, **tree-shakes** unused exports, minifies, splits dynamic imports into chunks and adds content hashes to filenames for long-term caching. webpack does the same job and is common in older projects.
key_points: Dynamic import() creates a separate chunk that loads on demand.
Hashed filenames let browsers cache assets for a long time; a change produces a new name.
Only VITE_-prefixed environment variables are exposed to client code.
learn_items: Dev server: Vite serves files as ES modules and pre-bundles dependencies with esbuild for a fast start
HMR: an edit replaces only the changed module; React Fast Refresh keeps component state while you edit
Production build: vite build writes dist/ with minified, hashed JS and CSS; vite preview serves it locally
Transpiling: the build strips TypeScript types without checking them; run tsc --noEmit separately
Tree-shaking: unused ES module exports are dropped; side-effectful modules and CommonJS limit it
Code splitting: import("./Chart") or React lazy creates a chunk; check chunk sizes in the build output
Environment variables: .env files and import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL; never put secrets in client variables
Config: vite.config.ts with plugins (React, Tailwind), path aliases and a dev proxy for API calls
