topics.title: Component tests with Vitest and Testing Library
topics.summary_md: Component tests render a component in a simulated DOM (jsdom) and check what a user would see. **Vitest** runs the tests with a Jest-compatible API, and **Testing Library** gives queries that find elements the way users and assistive technology do: by role, label and text. Assert on visible output and behaviour, not internal state or class names, so tests survive refactors.
key_points: Prefer getByRole with a name, e.g. getByRole("button", { name: /save/i }).
Test behaviour users see, not implementation details.
getBy throws if missing, queryBy returns null, findBy waits.
learn_items: Setup: add vitest, jsdom, @testing-library/react and @testing-library/jest-dom; set environment to jsdom
Test structure: describe, it and expect; arrange, act and assert in each test; run with npx vitest
render and screen: render(<Login />), then query through screen so tests read like a user scanning the page
Query priority: getByRole first, then getByLabelText and getByText; getByTestId only as a last resort
Query variants: getBy throws if missing, queryBy returns null for absence checks, findBy returns a promise
jest-dom matchers: toBeInTheDocument, toBeDisabled, toHaveValue and toHaveTextContent read clearly
What not to test: internal state, private functions or CSS classes; a refactor should not break good tests

tasks.title: Write Vitest and Testing Library tests for a counter and a login form: initial render, button states and error messages

topics.title: User events, async UI and mocking the network
topics.summary_md: Real interactions are asynchronous: use **user-event** to type, click and tab like a person, and await `findBy` queries or `waitFor` until the UI updates, never fixed sleeps. Mock the network rather than your own components: **Mock Service Worker (MSW)** intercepts requests and returns fake responses, so components run their real fetching code. Use `vi.fn()` for callback props and `vi.mock()` only for modules you do not control.
key_points: const user = userEvent.setup(); await user.click(button) simulates real browser events.
Wait with findBy or waitFor; fixed timeouts make tests slow and flaky.
Mock at the network boundary so your fetching code is tested too.
learn_items: user-event: userEvent.setup(), then await user.type(input, "hello"), user.click, user.keyboard("{Enter}")
findBy: await screen.findByText("Saved") waits for UI that appears after a promise resolves
waitFor: wrap an assertion in await waitFor(() => expect(…)) when no element query fits
Mock functions: const onSave = vi.fn(); then expect(onSave).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ name: "Asha" })
MSW: define http.get("/api/jobs", () => HttpResponse.json([…])) handlers and start a server in test setup
Error paths: override a handler in one test to return a 500 and assert the error message and retry button
Fake timers: vi.useFakeTimers() and vi.advanceTimersByTime(500) test a debounce without waiting
Providers: a renderWithProviders helper wraps router, query client and theme for every test

tasks.title: Test a job search component with MSW: loading state, results, empty results, a server error and a debounced input

topics.title: End-to-end tests with Playwright
topics.summary_md: End-to-end tests drive a real browser through the running app, covering routing, network and storage together. **Playwright** runs tests in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, with locators that auto-wait and web-first assertions that retry until they pass. Keep e2e tests to a few critical journeys such as sign-up, search and checkout, and leave detailed cases to faster component tests.
key_points: Locators auto-wait; expect(locator).toBeVisible() retries until it passes or times out.
Write few e2e tests, for critical paths; they are slow and costly to maintain.
Each test gets a fresh browser context, so tests do not leak state.
learn_items: Setup: npm init playwright@latest creates playwright.config.ts and an example test, and installs browsers
Locators: page.getByRole("button", { name: "Apply" }), getByLabel, getByText; avoid brittle CSS selectors
Actions: page.goto("/jobs"), then await locator.click(), locator.fill("text") and locator.press("Enter")
Web-first assertions: await expect(page.getByText("Saved")).toBeVisible() and toHaveURL(/jobs/) retry
webServer config: let Playwright start the dev or preview server before the tests and set baseURL
Auth state: sign in once in a setup project, save storageState and reuse it so tests start signed in
Network control: page.route("**/api/jobs", r => r.fulfill({ json: […] })) stubs flaky or slow APIs
Debugging: run with --ui or --debug, and open the trace viewer for failures from CI

tasks.title: Write Playwright tests for signing in, searching jobs and saving one, reusing stored auth state and running headless

topics.title: Core Web Vitals and how to measure them
topics.summary_md: Core Web Vitals measure real user experience: **LCP** (Largest Contentful Paint, loading) should be 2.5 s or less, **INP** (Interaction to Next Paint, responsiveness) 200 ms or less, and **CLS** (Cumulative Layout Shift, visual stability) 0.1 or less, judged at the 75th percentile of visits. **Lab** tools such as Lighthouse test one simulated load; **field** data from real users shows how a site actually performs.
key_points: Good thresholds: LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1, at the 75th percentile.
Lab data helps find causes; field data shows what users really experience.
INP needs real interactions, so a page-load Lighthouse run cannot measure it.
learn_items: LCP: time until the largest image or text block in the viewport renders, usually the hero image or heading
INP: the delay from a click, tap or key press until the next frame is painted, near the worst on the page
CLS: a score summing unexpected layout shifts, such as text jumping when an image or banner loads late
Thresholds: good, needs improvement and poor bands; a page passes when 75% of visits are good
Lighthouse: run it in Chrome DevTools with mobile throttling; read the diagnostics, not just the score
Performance panel: record a load and an interaction; find long tasks, layout shifts and the LCP element
Field data: the web-vitals library reports onLCP, onINP and onCLS values to your analytics
Supporting timings: TTFB (server response) and FCP (first paint) help explain a slow LCP

tasks.title: Audit a site you built with Lighthouse and the Performance panel, find its LCP element and longest task, and log web-vitals

topics.title: Faster loading: images, fonts and JavaScript
topics.summary_md: LCP improves when the browser finds and downloads the hero resource early and has less to process first. Serve images in modern formats (AVIF, WebP) at the right size with `srcset`, give the LCP image `fetchpriority="high"` and never lazy-load it, and lazy-load only below-the-fold images. Ship less JavaScript through code splitting, defer non-critical scripts, and cache static assets with hashed filenames.
key_points: Never put loading="lazy" on the LCP image; lazy-load images below the fold instead.
Every kilobyte of JavaScript must be downloaded, parsed and run on the main thread.
Fonts: use font-display: swap and preload only the one or two fonts used above the fold.
learn_items: Critical rendering path: CSS and synchronous scripts block rendering; keep critical CSS small and defer the rest
Scripts: use defer or type="module" for app code and async for independent third-party scripts
Responsive images: srcset and sizes so phones download small files; serve AVIF or WebP
LCP image: fetchpriority="high", no lazy loading, and present in the HTML rather than injected by JavaScript
Lazy loading: loading="lazy" on images and iframes below the fold; dynamic import() for heavy components
Fonts: self-host woff2 files, subset them, preload key files and use font-display: swap
Caching and CDN: long Cache-Control max-age for hashed assets, Brotli compression, serve from a CDN
Preconnect: <link rel="preconnect"> to a critical third-party origin saves connection set-up time

tasks.title: Take a slow page and improve its LCP: resize and convert the hero image, set fetchpriority, defer scripts, then re-measure

topics.title: INP and CLS: long tasks and layout shifts
topics.summary_md: INP is poor when the main thread is busy: any task over 50 ms is a **long task** that delays the response to input. Break work into smaller pieces and yield to the browser, defer non-urgent updates, and avoid rendering huge lists at once. CLS comes from content that moves after it appears; reserve space for images, embeds and ads, and animate with `transform` instead of layout properties.
key_points: Tasks over 50 ms block input; split them and yield to the main thread.
Set width and height (or aspect-ratio) on images and embeds to reserve their space.
Animate transform and opacity; animating top, width or height triggers layout work.
learn_items: Long tasks: find them in the Performance panel and see which script or event handler runs them
Yielding: split loops into chunks and await scheduler.yield() or a setTimeout(0) between chunks
Event handlers: make the visible update first and defer analytics or heavy work until after the next paint
React: startTransition or useDeferredValue keeps typing responsive while an expensive list re-renders
Large lists: virtualise long lists so only the visible rows are in the DOM
Web Workers: move heavy pure computation such as parsing or search indexing off the main thread
Layout shifts: set dimensions or aspect-ratio on media, reserve space for banners, avoid inserting content above
Fonts and CLS: fallback fonts adjusted with size-adjust reduce the shift when the web font swaps in

tasks.title: Fix a page with a slow filter and jumping images: chunk the filter work, use a transition, add image dimensions, re-measure

topics.title: Single-file components and template syntax
topics.summary_md: A Vue **single-file component** (`.vue`) holds a `<template>`, a `<script setup>` block and optional `<style scoped>`. Templates bind data with `{{ }}` for text, `:attr` (v-bind) for attributes and `@event` (v-on) for events, and use directives such as `v-if`, `v-show` and `v-for`. Create projects with `npm create vue@latest`, which uses Vite.
key_points: :href is short for v-bind:href; @click is short for v-on:click.
v-if adds and removes elements; v-show only toggles CSS display.
v-for needs a unique :key, e.g. v-for="job in jobs" :key="job.id".
learn_items: Project setup: npm create vue@latest with TypeScript, then npm run dev; main.ts mounts createApp(App)
SFC structure: <template>, <script setup lang="ts"> and <style scoped>, which styles only this component
Interpolation: {{ user.name }} renders escaped text; only expressions are allowed, not statements
v-bind and v-on: :src="url", :class="{ active: isActive }", @click="save", @submit.prevent="send"
Conditionals: v-if, v-else-if and v-else remove elements; v-show keeps them and toggles display
Lists: v-for="(job, index) in jobs" :key="job.id"; never put v-if and v-for on the same element
Event modifiers: .prevent, .stop and .once, plus key modifiers such as @keyup.enter
Vue DevTools: inspect the component tree, props and state in the browser

tasks.title: Build a Vue job list page with v-for cards, a v-if empty state, a class binding for saved jobs and a click handler

topics.title: Reactivity: ref, reactive, computed and watch
topics.summary_md: Vue 3 tracks which reactive values a template or computation reads, using JavaScript Proxies, and updates exactly those parts when the values change. `ref()` wraps any value (read and write `.value` in script; templates unwrap it), and `reactive()` makes an object deeply reactive. `computed()` caches derived values, while `watch` and `watchEffect` run side effects when their sources change.
key_points: ref needs .value in script but not in the template.
Destructuring a reactive() object loses reactivity; use toRefs or separate refs.
computed is cached and recalculates only when its dependencies change.
learn_items: ref: const count = ref(0); count.value++ in script; {{ count }} in the template unwraps it automatically
reactive: const form = reactive({ name: "", email: "" }) for objects; it cannot be replaced as a whole
Pitfalls: destructuring reactive() breaks reactivity; use toRefs(form) or keep separate refs
computed: const total = computed(() => …) caches until its sources change; keep it free of side effects
Writable computed: give get and set functions when a derived value must also be editable
watch: watch(query, (q) => fetchResults(q)) for side effects on a specific source; deep and immediate options
watchEffect: runs at once and re-runs whenever any reactive value it reads changes
nextTick: await nextTick() when you need the updated DOM after a state change

tasks.title: Build a shopping cart with ref items, a computed total and item count, and a watch that saves the cart to localStorage

topics.title: Props, emits, v-model and slots
topics.summary_md: Parent components pass data to children with **props**, declared in `<script setup>` with `defineProps`, and children report back by emitting events declared with `defineEmits`. `v-model` on a component is two-way binding built from a prop and an update event, and `defineModel()` sets it up in one line. **Slots** let a parent pass template content into a child, much like children in React.
key_points: Props are read-only in the child; emit an event to ask for a change.
v-model on a component = modelValue prop + update:modelValue event.
Scoped slots let the child pass data back into the parent’s slot content.
learn_items: defineProps: const props = defineProps<{ title: string; count?: number }>() with TypeScript types
Defaults: destructure with defaults, const { count = 0 } = defineProps<…>(), which stays reactive in Vue 3.5+
defineEmits: const emit = defineEmits<{ save: [id: number] }>(); emit("save", id); the parent uses @save
v-model on inputs: v-model="name" binds form fields; .trim and .number modifiers clean the value
defineModel: const model = defineModel<string>() lets a child component support v-model
Default slot: <slot /> renders content placed between the component tags; put fallback content inside it
Named and scoped slots: <template #header>, and <slot :item="item"> to expose data to the parent template
provide/inject: share a value with deep descendants without passing props through every level

tasks.title: Build a reusable Modal with header, body and footer slots, and a SearchInput that supports v-model through defineModel

topics.title: Composables, lifecycle hooks and Vue Router
topics.summary_md: **Composables** are functions named `useX` that use the Composition API to package reusable stateful logic, such as fetching data or tracking the mouse; each call gets its own state. Lifecycle hooks like `onMounted` and `onUnmounted` run code when a component appears or is removed. **Vue Router** maps URLs to components and supports dynamic params, nested routes, lazy-loaded pages and navigation guards.
key_points: A composable returns refs so callers keep reactivity when they destructure.
Remove listeners and timers in onUnmounted.
Lazy-load route components with () => import("./views/Admin.vue").
learn_items: Lifecycle: onMounted for DOM access and set-up, onUnmounted for cleanup; onUpdated is rarely needed
Composables: function useFetch(url) { const data = ref(null); const error = ref(null); …; return { data, error } }
Reactive arguments: accept refs or getters and read them with toValue() inside watchEffect so changes refetch
Router set-up: createRouter({ history: createWebHistory(), routes }), app.use(router), render <RouterView />
Links and params: <RouterLink to="/jobs/42">, a path "/jobs/:id", and useRoute().params.id in the page
Programmatic navigation: useRouter().push({ name: "job", params: { id } })
Navigation guards: router.beforeEach((to) => …) redirects signed-out users away from protected routes
Lazy routes: component: () => import("./views/Admin.vue") puts each page in its own chunk

tasks.title: Build a Vue Router app with a job list and a job detail page loaded by a useFetch composable, plus a guarded /saved route

topics.title: Pinia stores and server rendering with Nuxt
topics.summary_md: **Pinia** is the official Vue store for state shared across many components. A setup store looks like a composable: refs become state, computed values become getters and functions become actions. **Nuxt** is the full-stack Vue framework: file-based routing in `pages/`, server rendering, auto-imports and data fetching with `useFetch`, which avoids fetching twice during hydration.
key_points: Use storeToRefs() to destructure store state without losing reactivity.
Keep API data in fetching utilities; use Pinia for shared client state.
Nuxt useFetch runs on the server during SSR and passes the result to the client.
learn_items: Installing Pinia: app.use(createPinia()), then defineStore("cart", () => { … }) as a setup store
Using a store: const cart = useCartStore(); call cart.add(item); read cart.total in templates
storeToRefs: const { items, total } = storeToRefs(cart) keeps reactivity; call actions on the store itself
Pinia in DevTools: inspect state, follow actions and step back through changes
Nuxt basics: npm create nuxt@latest; pages/ for routes; components/ and composables/ are auto-imported
Nuxt data: const { data, status, error } = await useFetch("/api/jobs") fetches on the server during SSR
Server routes: files in server/api/ become endpoints, e.g. server/api/jobs.get.ts handles GET /api/jobs
Rendering modes: SSR by default; route rules can make pages prerendered, client-only or cached

tasks.title: Move the cart from the reactivity exercise into a Pinia setup store used by a header badge and a cart page

topics.title: Standalone components, templates and the CLI
topics.summary_md: Angular is a full framework built on TypeScript. Create projects with the **Angular CLI** (`ng new`, `ng serve`, `ng generate component`). Components are **standalone** classes decorated with `@Component` that list what they use in `imports`. Templates bind data with `{{ }}`, `[property]` and `(event)`, and use built-in control flow blocks `@if`, `@for` (with a required `track`) and `@switch`.
key_points: [prop] binds data in, (event) listens for events, [(ngModel)] is two-way.
@for requires a track expression, e.g. track job.id.
Standalone components import what they use directly; NgModules are optional.
learn_items: CLI: npm install -g @angular/cli, then ng new, ng serve, ng generate component job-card and ng build
Component anatomy: @Component({ selector, imports, templateUrl, styleUrl }) on an exported class
Bootstrapping: main.ts calls bootstrapApplication(App, appConfig), with providers in app.config.ts
Bindings: {{ title }} for text, [src]="logoUrl" for properties, (click)="save()" for events, [class.active]
Control flow: @if (user) { … } @else { … } and @for (job of jobs; track job.id) { … } @empty { … }
Pipes: transform values in templates with | date, | currency: "INR" and | uppercase; write your own with @Pipe
Component styles: styles apply only to the component by default through view encapsulation

tasks.title: Generate an Angular app with a JobCard component; render jobs with @for and track, an @if empty state and pipes

topics.title: Signals, inputs and outputs
topics.summary_md: **Signals** are Angular’s reactive primitive: `signal()` holds a value you read by calling it, `computed()` derives values lazily and caches them, and `effect()` runs side effects when signals it reads change. Components receive data through `input()` and send events through `output()`. Because Angular knows exactly which signals a template reads, it can update only the views that changed.
key_points: Read a signal by calling it: count(); write with set() or update().
computed() is read-only and recalculates only when its dependencies change.
Use effect() sparingly, for syncing with things outside Angular.
learn_items: signal: count = signal(0); read count() in code and templates; count.set(5) or count.update(c => c + 1)
computed: total = computed(() => this.items().reduce(…)) is cached and read-only
effect: effect(() => localStorage.setItem("cart", JSON.stringify(this.items()))) for side effects only
Immutability: update arrays with update(list => [...list, item]) so the signal sees a new value
input(): job = input.required<Job>() in the child, bound by the parent with [job]="selectedJob"
output(): saved = output<number>(); this.saved.emit(id); the parent listens with (saved)="onSaved($event)"
model(): a two-way bindable input for custom controls, used by the parent with [(value)]
linkedSignal: a writable signal that resets when its source changes, e.g. a selection when the list changes

tasks.title: Build a cart with signal state, a computed total, an effect that saves it, and a child component using input() and output()

topics.title: Services and dependency injection
topics.summary_md: Angular creates and supplies objects for you through **dependency injection** (DI). A **service** is a class marked `@Injectable` that holds shared logic or state, such as an API client or the signed-in user. Components ask for it with `inject(JobService)` and Angular provides the instance from an injector, which keeps code testable: in tests you provide a fake instead.
key_points: providedIn: "root" gives one shared, tree-shakable instance for the whole app.
Providing a service in a component gives that component subtree its own instance.
inject() works in field initialisers, constructors and factory functions.
learn_items: Services: @Injectable({ providedIn: "root" }) export class JobService { … }, created with ng generate service
inject(): private jobs = inject(JobService) as a class field; constructor parameters are the older equivalent
Injector hierarchy: root providers are app-wide singletons; providers: [X] on a component scopes a new instance
Shared state: keep signals in a service so several components read and update the same data
Injection tokens: new InjectionToken<string>("API_URL") with { provide: API_URL, useValue: … } for config
Provider kinds: useClass, useValue, useFactory and useExisting, and when each one fits
Testing with DI: TestBed.configureTestingModule({ providers: [{ provide: JobService, useValue: fake }] })

tasks.title: Create a SavedJobsService with signal state, inject it into a list and a header badge, and provide a fake in a test

topics.title: Routing, guards and reactive forms
topics.summary_md: The Angular **router** maps paths to components with `provideRouter(routes)`, renders them in `<router-outlet>`, and can lazy-load pages with `loadComponent`. Functional **guards** such as `canActivate` decide whether navigation may continue. **Reactive forms** build a typed form model in TypeScript with `FormGroup`, `FormControl` and validators, which keeps validation logic testable.
key_points: Lazy-load pages with loadComponent: () => import(…).then(m => m.AdminPage).
Guards are plain functions that return true, false or a UrlTree redirect.
Reactive forms keep the model in TypeScript; template-driven forms keep it in the template.
learn_items: Routes: [{ path: "jobs/:id", component: JobDetail }, { path: "**", component: NotFound }] in app.routes.ts
Navigation: routerLink="/jobs" with routerLinkActive, and inject(Router).navigate(["/jobs", id]) in code
Route params: withComponentInputBinding() binds :id to a matching input() of the page; or use ActivatedRoute
Lazy loading: loadComponent and loadChildren split routes into separate chunks
Guards: canActivate: [() => inject(Auth).isSignedIn() || inject(Router).parseUrl("/login")]
Reactive forms: new FormGroup({ email: new FormControl("", [Validators.required, Validators.email]) })
Template binding: [formGroup]="form" and formControlName="email"; show errors when touched and invalid
Typed forms and submit: form.getRawValue() is typed; disable the submit button while form.invalid

tasks.title: Add routing with a lazy-loaded admin page and an auth guard, plus a reactive sign-up form with validators and errors

topics.title: RxJS observables and HttpClient
topics.summary_md: Angular’s `HttpClient` returns **RxJS observables**: lazy streams that do nothing until subscribed and can be cancelled. Operators such as `map`, `switchMap`, `debounceTime` and `catchError` transform streams, for example a search box that cancels stale requests. Subscribe in templates with the `async` pipe or convert to signals with `toSignal()`, and add auth headers in one place with an interceptor.
key_points: Observables are lazy: no subscription, no HTTP request.
switchMap cancels the previous inner request when a new value arrives.
Avoid leaks: use the async pipe, toSignal or takeUntilDestroyed rather than bare subscribe.
learn_items: Set-up: provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([authInterceptor])) in app.config.ts; inject(HttpClient) in a service
Requests: this.http.get<Job[]>("/api/jobs") returns an Observable; post, put and delete work the same way
Observables vs promises: lazy, can emit many values, and cancellable by unsubscribing
Operators: pipe(map(…), filter(…), catchError(() => of([]))) to transform values and recover from errors
Search pattern: valueChanges.pipe(debounceTime(300), distinctUntilChanged(), switchMap(q => api.search(q)))
Subscribing safely: async pipe in templates, toSignal(obs$) in components, takeUntilDestroyed() otherwise
Interceptors: (req, next) => next(req.clone({ setHeaders: { Authorization: … } })) runs for every request
Subjects: a BehaviorSubject holds a current value; prefer signals for new component state

tasks.title: Build a job search box: debounced input, switchMap to the API, a loading signal, error handling and an auth interceptor

topics.title: Change detection, zoneless apps and @defer
topics.summary_md: Angular historically used **zone.js** to notice async events and then checked the component tree for changes. With signals, Angular can run **zoneless**, refreshing views only when signals, inputs or events mark them dirty, and recent versions create zoneless apps by default. `OnPush` components skip checks unless an input changes or they are marked dirty, and `@defer` blocks lazy-load parts of a template.
key_points: OnPush plus signals keeps change detection cheap and predictable.
In zoneless apps, change state through signals so the view refreshes.
@defer (on viewport) loads a block’s code only when it scrolls into view.
learn_items: zone.js: patches async APIs such as setTimeout and fetch to trigger a check of the whole component tree
OnPush: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush re-checks on input changes, template events or signal updates
Zoneless: provideZonelessChangeDetection() drops zone.js; signals, events and the async pipe schedule updates
Pitfall: in zoneless or OnPush code, changing a plain field in setTimeout does not refresh the view; use a signal
@defer: @defer (on viewport) { <app-chart /> } @placeholder { … } @loading { … } lazy-loads template parts
Defer triggers: on idle, on viewport, on interaction, on hover, on timer, and prefetch on idle
SSR and hydration: ng add @angular/ssr; incremental hydration with @defer (hydrate on viewport)
Profiling: the Angular DevTools profiler shows change detection cycles and slow components

tasks.title: Convert a dashboard to OnPush components with signals, defer a heavy chart with @defer (on viewport), compare in DevTools

topics.title: Git basics: commits, history and undoing changes
topics.summary_md: **Git** records snapshots of your project as **commits**, each with an author, a message and a parent. Files move from the working tree to the **staging area** (`git add`) and then into a commit (`git commit`). Learn to read history with `git log` and `git diff`, and to undo safely with `git restore` and `git revert` before you ever touch `git reset --hard`.
key_points: Three places: working tree, staging area (index) and the repository of commits.
git status tells you what is staged, unstaged and untracked; run it often.
git revert makes a new commit that undoes an old one, so it is safe on shared branches.
Write small commits with messages that say what changed and why.
learn_items: Setup: git config --global user.name and user.email, git init, and what the hidden .git folder holds
Three areas: working tree, staging area and commits; move a file through them with git add and git commit
Reading state: git status, git diff (unstaged) and git diff --staged (what the next commit will contain)
History: git log --oneline --graph, git show <commit> and what a commit hash identifies
.gitignore: ignore node_modules, build output and .env files; git rm --cached to stop tracking a file
Undo locally: git restore <file> discards edits, git restore --staged unstages, git commit --amend fixes the last commit
Undo shared work: git revert <commit> vs git reset --soft/--hard, and why reset rewrites history

tasks.title: Create a repo, make five small commits with clear messages, then inspect them with git log --oneline and git show
Break a file on purpose three ways and undo each: restore an edit, unstage a file, revert a bad commit

topics.title: Branches, merges, rebase and pull requests
topics.summary_md: A **branch** is a movable pointer to a commit, so creating one is cheap. Team work follows a pattern: branch from `main`, commit, push to a **remote** such as GitHub, open a **pull request**, get a review, then merge. Learn how merges create a merge commit or fast-forward, how to resolve a **merge conflict** by hand, and when `git rebase` gives a cleaner history.
key_points: git switch -c feature/login creates a branch and moves you onto it.
A conflict is Git asking you to choose; edit the markers, then add and commit.
Never rebase commits that others have already pulled.
git fetch downloads; git pull is fetch plus merge (or rebase if configured).
learn_items: Branches: git branch, git switch -c <name>, and HEAD as a pointer to the current branch
Merging: fast-forward vs a merge commit, and git merge --no-ff to keep a feature visible in history
Conflicts: read the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers, edit the file, then git add and git commit
Remotes: git remote -v, git clone, git push -u origin <branch>, git fetch vs git pull
Rebase: git rebase main replays your commits on top of main; resolve, then git rebase --continue
Pull request flow: branch, push, open a PR, respond to review comments, squash or merge
Recovery: git stash for unfinished work and git reflog to find a commit you thought was lost

tasks.title: Create two branches that edit the same line, merge them, and resolve the conflict by hand
Push a feature branch to GitHub, open a pull request with a clear description, and merge it after self-review

topics.title: Command line basics: navigating and managing files
topics.summary_md: The command line is how developers run tools, servers and scripts. Learn to move around the file system, create, copy, move and delete files, and read files without an editor. The commands below are for a Unix shell (bash or zsh, also Git Bash and WSL on Windows); PowerShell has similar commands with different names.
key_points: Absolute paths start at the root (/); relative paths start from the current directory.
rm -r deletes without a recycle bin; check the path before you press Enter.
Tab completes names and the up arrow recalls earlier commands.
man <command> or <command> --help shows every option.
learn_items: Where am I: pwd, ls -la (hidden files, sizes, permissions) and cd with ., .., ~ and -
Paths: absolute vs relative paths, and why spaces in names need quotes
Files and folders: mkdir -p, touch, cp -r, mv for move and rename, rm and rm -r
Reading files: cat, less (search with /, quit with q), head -n 20 and tail -f for live logs
Wildcards: * and ? globs, e.g. ls *.js, and how the shell expands them before the command runs
Help and history: man, --help, Tab completion, the up arrow and Ctrl+R to search history
Windows equivalents: Get-ChildItem (ls), Set-Location (cd), Remove-Item (rm) in PowerShell

tasks.title: Using only the terminal, create a project folder with src, tests and docs, add files, then rename and tidy them

topics.title: Pipes, grep, environment variables and processes
topics.summary_md: The shell becomes powerful when you combine small tools: a **pipe** (`|`) sends one command's output into the next, and **redirection** writes output to files. Learn to search with `grep` and `find`, use **environment variables** and `PATH`, and manage running processes. These skills make debugging servers and build scripts much faster.
key_points: > overwrites a file, >> appends, and 2> redirects error output.
grep -rn "text" . searches every file below the current folder with line numbers.
A command is found by searching the folders listed in PATH, left to right.
Ctrl+C stops a foreground process; kill <pid> stops one by its process id.
learn_items: Pipes and redirection: |, >, >>, 2> and 2>&1, e.g. npm test > out.txt 2>&1
Searching text: grep -rn, -i for case-insensitive, -v to invert, and grep with a pipe, e.g. ps aux | grep node
Finding files: find . -name "*.log" and find . -type f -mtime -1 for files changed in the last day
Counting and sorting: wc -l, sort, uniq -c and cut to summarise a log file
Environment variables: export NAME=value, echo $NAME, and reading them in code via process.env
PATH: what it is, which <command> to see what runs, and adding a folder to PATH in ~/.bashrc
Processes: ps, top, Ctrl+C, Ctrl+Z, bg, kill <pid>, and finding what holds a port with lsof -i :3000

tasks.title: Given a web server log, use grep, cut, sort and uniq -c in one pipeline to list the ten most requested paths
Write a tiny script, put its folder on PATH, and make it print an environment variable you set with export

topics.title: HTTP requests, methods and status codes
topics.summary_md: **HTTP** is the request-response protocol behind every website and API. A request has a **method**, a path, **headers** and an optional body; a response has a **status code**, headers and a body. Learn what each common method means, the status code families, and how to read a raw exchange with `curl -v` or the browser Network tab.
key_points: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH updates part, DELETE removes.
2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
GET, PUT and DELETE should be idempotent: repeating them has the same effect.
HTTP is stateless; cookies or tokens carry identity between requests.
learn_items: URL parts: scheme, host, port, path, query string and fragment, e.g. localhost:3000/api/users?page=2
Request anatomy: method, path, headers (Host, Content-Type, Authorization, Accept) and body
Methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE; which are safe and which are idempotent
Content types: application/json vs form data, and why the Content-Type header must match the body
Tools: curl -v, curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{...}', and the browser Network tab
Statelessness: how cookies (Set-Cookie, Cookie) and bearer tokens carry identity across requests

tasks.title: Call a public JSON API with curl -v using GET and POST, and note the method, status code and three headers each time

topics.title: HTTPS, DNS, caching headers and CORS
topics.summary_md: Before a request is sent, the browser resolves the domain with **DNS** and opens a TCP connection, then a **TLS** handshake for HTTPS. Responses can be cached using headers such as `Cache-Control` and `ETag`. Browsers block cross-origin reads unless the server sends **CORS** headers, which is the source of many beginner bugs. Know what happens end to end when you type a site name and press Enter.
key_points: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS: encrypted, tamper-proof and the server proves its identity with a certificate.
An origin is scheme + host + port; any difference makes a request cross-origin.
CORS is enforced by browsers, not by curl or servers.
HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 keep the same methods and status codes but change how bytes travel.
learn_items: DNS: domain to IP via resolvers, A and CNAME records, TTL, and checking with nslookup or dig
Connection: TCP handshake, then TLS handshake and certificate check for HTTPS on port 443
Typing a site name and pressing Enter: DNS, TCP, TLS, request, response, HTML parse, more requests
Caching headers: Cache-Control max-age, no-cache vs no-store, ETag with If-None-Match and 304 Not Modified
Same-origin policy: what an origin is and why localhost:5173 calling localhost:3000 is cross-origin
CORS: Access-Control-Allow-Origin, preflight OPTIONS requests, and allowing credentials safely
HTTP versions: HTTP/1.1 keep-alive, HTTP/2 multiplexing over one connection, HTTP/3 over QUIC

tasks.title: Run a frontend and an API on different ports, reproduce the CORS error, then fix it with the right response headers
Use nslookup and curl -v on a site you use daily and write down each step from DNS to the first byte of HTML

topics.title: Unit tests: structure, assertions and test runners
topics.summary_md: A **unit test** runs a small piece of code with known inputs and checks the output automatically, so you can change code without fear. Structure each test as **Arrange, Act, Assert**, give it a name that states the expected behaviour, and keep it fast and independent. Use a test runner such as **Vitest** or **Jest** (JavaScript) or **pytest** (Python).
key_points: One behaviour per test, and the test name says what that behaviour is.
Tests must not depend on each other or on the order they run in.
Test edge cases: empty input, zero, negative numbers, very long strings.
A test that never fails is useless; see it fail first, then make it pass.
learn_items: Why test: catching regressions, safer refactoring, and tests as living documentation of behaviour
Test runner basics: describe, it/test and expect in Vitest or Jest; def test_ and assert in pytest
Arrange, Act, Assert: set up inputs, call the function once, then check the result
Matchers: toBe vs toEqual, toThrow, toContain, and toBeCloseTo for floating-point numbers
Edge cases: empty arrays, null or undefined, boundaries such as 0 and the maximum, invalid input
Setup and teardown: beforeEach and afterEach to keep tests independent of each other
Running tests: watch mode, running one file or one test, and reading a failure message and stack trace

tasks.title: Write eight unit tests for a slugify(text) function, including empty input, extra spaces and symbols, and make them pass

topics.title: Mocks, test doubles and testing async code
topics.summary_md: Real code calls databases, APIs and clocks, which make tests slow and flaky. **Test doubles** (stubs, mocks, spies, fakes) replace those dependencies so a unit test checks only your logic. Learn to test async functions properly, inject dependencies so they can be swapped, and avoid over-mocking, which makes tests pass while the real code is broken.
key_points: A stub returns canned data; a mock or spy also records how it was called.
Pass dependencies in (parameters or constructor) so tests can swap them.
Always await async code in tests, or the test can finish before the assertion runs.
Mock the boundary (HTTP, database, time), not your own small helper functions.
learn_items: Test doubles: stub, mock, spy and fake, with one example of when to use each
Dependency injection: pass a fetch function or repository into code instead of importing it directly
Mocking in practice: vi.fn() or jest.fn(), mockResolvedValue, and toHaveBeenCalledWith
Async tests: return or await promises, test rejected promises with await expect(...).rejects.toThrow()
Time and randomness: fake timers (vi.useFakeTimers) and seeding or injecting random values
Over-mocking: why tests that mock everything prove little, and keeping mocks at system boundaries
Flaky tests: common causes (time, order, network, shared state) and how to make them deterministic

tasks.title: Test a getWeather(city) function that calls an API: mock fetch for success, a 404 and a network error
Test a debounce helper with fake timers so the test runs instantly and checks the function fires once

topics.title: Integration tests, the test pyramid, TDD and CI
topics.summary_md: Unit tests alone do not prove the parts work together. **Integration tests** call a real API route or a real test database; **end-to-end tests** drive the app like a user with tools such as **Playwright**. The **test pyramid** suggests many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and a few E2E tests. **TDD** writes the test first, and **CI** runs every test on each push.
key_points: Pyramid: many unit tests, some integration tests, few slow end-to-end tests.
Use a separate test database and reset it between tests.
Coverage shows which lines ran, not whether behaviour was checked.
CI should block a merge when any test fails.
learn_items: Test levels: unit, integration and end-to-end; what each catches and how fast each runs
API integration tests: start the app in tests and call routes with supertest (Node) or a test client (FastAPI, Django)
Test database: a separate database or container, migrations before the run, and cleanup between tests
End-to-end basics: Playwright opens a browser, clicks, types and asserts on visible text
TDD cycle: red (failing test), green (simplest code that passes), refactor with tests still green
Coverage: line vs branch coverage, reading a coverage report, and why 100% is not the goal
CI: a GitHub Actions workflow that installs dependencies and runs npm test on every push and pull request

tasks.title: Write integration tests for a small REST API covering create, read, a 404 and a validation error, using a test database
Add a GitHub Actions workflow that runs your tests on every push and show a red, then green, run

topics.title: Deploying an app: builds, hosting and environment variables
topics.summary_md: Deployment turns code on your laptop into an app anyone can open. A static site (HTML, CSS, JS) can go on a static host such as **Vercel**, **Netlify** or GitHub Pages; an API needs a server or platform such as **Render** or **Railway**. Learn the **build step**, how the platform picks a port, and how to keep secrets in **environment variables**, never in the repository.
key_points: Static hosting serves files; a backend needs a process that keeps running.
Read the port from process.env.PORT; platforms assign it at run time.
Secrets go in the platform's environment settings, never in Git.
Most platforms redeploy automatically when you push to the main branch.
learn_items: What deploying means: build artefacts, a host, a public address, and logs you can read
Build step: npm run build creates a dist or build folder; only that output is served for static sites
Static vs server hosting: static hosts for frontends, platform hosts for Node or Python APIs
Ports and start commands: listen on process.env.PORT and set the start command, e.g. node server.js
Environment variables: .env locally (ignored by Git), platform settings in production, a .env.example file
Git-based deploys: connect the repo, choose the branch, build command and output folder
First debugging: read build logs and runtime logs, and check a failed deploy before changing code

tasks.title: Deploy a small frontend from a GitHub repo to a static host and confirm a push to main triggers a new deploy

topics.title: Domains, HTTPS, logs and rolling back a deploy
topics.summary_md: Once an app is live, you need a **custom domain**, **HTTPS**, and a way to see what goes wrong. Point a domain at the host with DNS records, let the platform issue a free TLS certificate, and watch **logs** and a **health check** endpoint. Keep deploys reversible: know how to **roll back** to the previous version and how staging differs from production.
key_points: A CNAME or A record points your domain at the host; DNS changes can take time to spread.
Most hosts issue and renew HTTPS certificates automatically.
A /health endpoint lets the platform and you check the app is up.
Rolling back to the last good deploy is faster than fixing forward under pressure.
learn_items: Custom domains: buy a domain, add an A or CNAME record, and verify it on the host
Certificates: automatic TLS certificates, redirecting HTTP to HTTPS, and mixed-content errors
Environments: development, staging and production with separate databases and variables
Logs: structured log lines, reading runtime logs on the platform, and never logging secrets
Health checks: a /health route that returns 200, and how platforms use it to restart a failed app
Rollback: redeploy the previous build or revert the commit, and when to choose each
Preview deploys: a temporary address per pull request to test changes before merging

tasks.title: Add a /health route to a deployed API, deploy a deliberate bug, then roll back to the previous deploy

topics.title: Node.js runtime, ES modules and npm
topics.summary_md: Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser on the V8 engine, with built-in modules for files, networking and processes instead of the DOM. Modern projects use **ES modules** (`"type": "module"` in `package.json`, `import`/`export`) and manage dependencies with npm. Learn to start a project, run scripts and read command-line input before touching a framework.
key_points: Set "type": "module" in package.json so .js files use import/export; .cjs files stay CommonJS.
Built-in modules use the node: prefix, e.g. import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises'.
Commit package-lock.json and install with npm ci in CI for repeatable installs.
learn_items: Install and versions: install an LTS release (22 or later), check with node -v and npm -v, run a file with node app.js
Globals: process.argv, process.env, process.exit(code), and that window and document do not exist in Node
ES modules: named vs default exports, import.meta.dirname, top-level await, and file extensions required in import paths
npm init: package.json fields name, version, type, scripts, dependencies vs devDependencies
npm commands: npm install, npm install -D, npm ci, npm run <script>, npx, and what package-lock.json pins
Semver ranges: ^1.4.0 allows 1.x minor and patch updates, ~1.4.0 allows patches only
Dev loop: node --watch app.js restarts on save; node --env-file=.env loads environment variables
CLI input: util.parseArgs for flags, process.stdout.write, and non-zero exit codes on failure

tasks.title: Build a word-count CLI that reads a file path from process.argv and prints lines, words and the 5 most common words

topics.title: Event loop, async file I/O and streams
topics.summary_md: Node handles many connections on one JavaScript thread: slow work such as disk and network is handed to the operating system or the libuv thread pool, and callbacks run when results are ready. Learn the event loop order, use `async`/`await` with `node:fs/promises`, and process large data with **streams** so memory stays flat.
key_points: CPU-heavy code (big loops, sync hashing) blocks every request; move it to worker_threads or a job queue.
process.nextTick and promise callbacks run before timers and I/O callbacks of the next phase.
Use pipeline from node:stream/promises: it forwards errors and handles backpressure.
learn_items: Event loop phases: timers, poll (I/O callbacks), check (setImmediate), close; microtasks run between each callback
Order puzzle: predict the output of console.log, setTimeout 0, setImmediate, Promise.resolve().then and process.nextTick
libuv thread pool: fs, dns.lookup, crypto.pbkdf2 and zlib run there (4 threads by default, UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE)
fs/promises: readFile, writeFile, readdir, stat, mkdir with recursive: true; avoid the Sync versions in servers
Parallel work: Promise.all for independent awaits, Promise.allSettled when some may fail
Streams: Readable, Writable, Transform; fs.createReadStream for large files; readline for line-by-line reads
Backpressure: write() returns false when the buffer is full; pipeline waits for drain for you
Events: EventEmitter on/once/emit, and why an unhandled error event crashes the process

tasks.title: Write 8 snippets mixing timers, setImmediate, nextTick and promises; predict each output, then run them to check
Stream a large log file through a Transform that keeps only ERROR lines and gzip the result with pipeline

topics.title: HTTP servers, Express 5 routing and middleware
topics.summary_md: The `node:http` module shows what every framework does underneath: parse a request, write status, headers and a body. **Express 5** adds routing, JSON body parsing and **middleware**, functions that run in order and either call `next()` or end the response. Build CRUD routes for one resource with an in-memory array before adding a database.
key_points: Middleware runs in the order you register it; one that neither responds nor calls next() leaves the request hanging.
Express 5 sends rejected promises from async handlers to the error middleware automatically.
req.body is undefined unless a body parser such as express.json() is registered first.
learn_items: node:http: createServer((req, res) => ...), req.method, req.url, res.writeHead(status, headers), res.end(body)
Express app: express(), app.get/post/put/patch/delete, app.listen(port), and res.status(201).json(obj)
Request data: req.params for /items/:id, req.query for ?page=2, req.body after app.use(express.json())
Middleware signature (req, res, next); logging, auth and parsing are all middleware; order matters
Routers: express.Router() per resource, mounted with app.use('/api/items', itemsRouter)
Error middleware: four arguments (err, req, res, next), registered last, maps errors to status and JSON
Express 5 changes: async errors forwarded, wildcards must be named (/*splat), optional parts written {/:id}
Static files and CORS: express.static for a folder; the cors package only when a browser on another origin calls you

topics.title: Python setup, types and control flow
topics.summary_md: Python is a readable, dynamically typed language used for scripts, backends, data and ML. Start by installing Python 3.12 or later, running files and the REPL, and learning the built-in types and control flow. Indentation is syntax: a block is defined by its indentation, not braces.
key_points: Use // for integer division and / for true division; 7 // 2 is 3 but 7 / 2 is 3.5.
Empty strings, 0, None and empty collections are falsy; everything else is truthy.
Compare values with ==; use is only for None checks, as in if x is None.
learn_items: Setup: install Python 3.12+, run python --version, start the REPL, run a file with python main.py
Built-in types: int (no overflow), float, bool, str, None; check with type() and isinstance()
Operators: + - * / // % **, comparison chains like 0 < x < 10, and, or, not
Strings: f-strings f'{name} is {age}', slicing s[1:4] and s[::-1], split, join, strip, lower, in
Control flow: if/elif/else, for over range(n) and over sequences, while, break, continue
match statement: match a value against literal, sequence and dict patterns with case _ as the default
Input and output: input() returns a str, convert with int(); print with sep and end arguments
Style: four-space indentation, snake_case names, and a formatter such as black or ruff format

topics.title: Lists, dicts, sets, tuples and comprehensions
topics.summary_md: Most Python code is built from four collections: **list** (ordered, mutable), **tuple** (ordered, immutable), **dict** (key to value, insertion ordered) and **set** (unique items, fast membership). Comprehensions build them in one readable line. Know the cost of common operations, because it matters in interviews and in loops over real data.
key_points: x in a set or dict is O(1) on average; x in a list is O(n).
b = a copies the reference, not the list; use a.copy() or list(a) for a shallow copy.
Only immutable (hashable) values such as str, int and tuple can be dict keys or set items.
learn_items: Lists: append, extend, insert, pop, remove, sort vs sorted, indexing a[-1], slicing and list(range(5))
Tuples: packing and unpacking a, b = b, a; star unpacking first, *rest = items; tuples as dict keys
Dicts: d[k] vs d.get(k, default), setdefault, items(), keys(), values(), update, del, the | merge operator
Sets: add, discard, union |, intersection &, difference -, and using a set to remove duplicates
Comprehensions: [x*x for x in nums if x > 0], {k: v for k, v in pairs}, {w.lower() for w in words}
collections: Counter.most_common(k), defaultdict(list) for grouping, deque for O(1) pops from the left
Sorting: sorted(items, key=lambda p: (p.age, p.name), reverse=True); sort is stable
Copies: shallow copy vs copy.deepcopy for nested lists; the [[0]*3]*3 shared-row trap

topics.title: Functions, modules and virtual environments
topics.summary_md: Functions in Python take positional, keyword and default arguments and are first-class values you can pass around. Group code into **modules** and **packages**, and give each project its own **virtual environment** so its dependencies do not clash with other projects. These habits are what make a script grow into an application.
key_points: Default values are evaluated once: def f(x, items=[]) shares one list across calls; use None and create it inside.
Code under if __name__ == "__main__": runs only when the file is executed, not when imported.
Create a venv per project and record dependencies in requirements.txt or pyproject.toml.
learn_items: def basics: parameters, return values, returning several values as a tuple, docstrings
Arguments: positional, keyword, defaults, *args, **kwargs, keyword-only after *, positional-only before /
Mutable default trap: why def add(x, acc=[]) leaks state and the acc=None fix
Scope: local, enclosing, global, built-in (LEGB); global and nonlocal; closures that capture variables
Functions as values: lambda, passing key functions, map and filter vs comprehensions
Modules and packages: import x, from x import y, a folder with __init__.py, relative imports in a package
Virtual env: python -m venv .venv, activate (.venv\Scripts\activate on Windows), pip install, pip freeze
Entry point: the if __name__ == "__main__": guard and a main() function

topics.title: Classes, dataclasses and dunder methods
topics.summary_md: Classes bundle data with behaviour. Learn `__init__` and `self`, instance vs class attributes, inheritance with `super()`, and the **dunder methods** that make objects print, compare and behave like built-ins. For plain data holders, `@dataclass` writes the boilerplate for you and is what most modern code uses.

Prefer composition (an object holds another) over deep inheritance chains.
Use @property to add validation or computed values without changing how callers access the attribute.
learn_items: Class basics: class, __init__, self, instance attributes, methods, creating objects
Class vs instance attributes: a list defined on the class is shared by all instances
Inheritance: subclassing, overriding methods, super().__init__(...), isinstance and issubclass
Dunder methods: __repr__ and __str__, __eq__ and __hash__, __lt__ for sorting, __len__ and __iter__
Decorated methods: @property with a setter, @classmethod as an alternative constructor, @staticmethod
Dataclasses: @dataclass, field(default_factory=list), frozen=True, order=True
Abstract interfaces: abc.ABC with @abstractmethod, and duck typing as the Pythonic default

topics.title: Exceptions, files, JSON and type hints
topics.summary_md: Robust programs expect failure: catch specific exceptions, clean up with context managers and raise clear errors of your own. Read and write text, CSV and JSON files safely with `pathlib`. Add **type hints** so editors and a checker such as mypy catch mistakes before you run the code; they are also how FastAPI and Pydantic read your intent.
key_points: Catch the narrowest exception you can handle; a bare except: also swallows bugs and Ctrl+C.
with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f closes the file even when an exception is raised.
Type hints are not checked at run time by Python itself; run a type checker to enforce them.
learn_items: try/except/else/finally: what runs when, catching several types, except ValueError as e
Raising: raise ValueError("..."), custom exception classes, raise NewError(...) from err to keep the cause
Context managers: with for files and locks; write one with contextlib.contextmanager
pathlib: Path("data") / "file.txt", exists, read_text, write_text, glob, mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
Formats: json.load/json.dump with indent, csv.DictReader and DictWriter, always encoding="utf-8"
Type hints: list[int], dict[str, float], str | None, Callable, function return types, type aliases
Checking: run mypy or pyright on a small module and fix the reported errors
Logging: logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) and logger.exception inside except blocks

topics.title: Generators, decorators and asyncio
topics.summary_md: Three features power most Python frameworks. **Generators** produce values lazily with `yield`, so you can stream large data. **Decorators** wrap functions to add behaviour such as timing, caching or routing. **asyncio** runs many I/O-bound tasks concurrently on one thread with `async` and `await`, which is how async web frameworks serve many requests.
key_points: A generator keeps its state between yields and is consumed once.
Use functools.wraps in decorators so the wrapped function keeps its name and docstring.
Inside async code never call blocking functions such as time.sleep; use await asyncio.sleep.
learn_items: Iterator protocol: iter() and next(), StopIteration, and why a for loop works on any iterable
Generators: yield, generator expressions (x for x in ...), reading a large file line by line lazily
itertools: islice, chain, groupby (needs sorted input), product, and accumulate
Decorators: a function returning a wrapper, *args/**kwargs pass-through, functools.wraps, decorators with arguments
Built-in caching: functools.cache and lru_cache(maxsize=...) for pure functions
asyncio basics: async def, await, asyncio.run(main()), asyncio.gather for concurrent awaits
Concurrency choice: asyncio or threads for I/O-bound work, multiprocessing for CPU-bound work (the GIL)

topics.title: First API with FastAPI: routes and parameters
topics.summary_md: **FastAPI** builds APIs from ordinary Python functions with type hints: it reads path and query parameters from the signature, validates and converts them, and generates interactive OpenAPI docs. Function parameters not in the path become query parameters; give them defaults to make them optional.

topics.title: Pydantic models, validation and dependencies
topics.summary_md: Request and response bodies are described with **Pydantic** models: FastAPI parses JSON into them, validates every field and documents them. Use separate models for input and output so clients cannot set server fields and you never leak secrets. **Dependencies** with `Depends` share things like the current user or a database session across routes.
key_points: Have separate models such as ItemCreate (input) and ItemOut (output); never return a model holding a password hash.
response_model filters the output to the declared fields, even if you return extra data.
A dependency that uses yield runs its cleanup code after the response is sent.
learn_items: BaseModel: fields with types and defaults, Field(min_length=1, max_length=200), Field(gt=0) for prices
Body parsing: a parameter typed as a model is read from the JSON body; invalid input returns 422 with field errors
Model methods: model_dump(), model_dump(exclude_unset=True) for PATCH, model_validate(data)
Output models: response_model=ItemOut or a return type annotation; list[ItemOut] for collections
Custom validation: @field_validator for one field, @model_validator for checks across fields
Dependencies: def get_settings(), Annotated[Settings, Depends(get_settings)], dependencies calling dependencies
Yield dependencies: def get_db(): open session, yield it, close in finally
Routers: APIRouter(prefix="/items", tags=["items"]) and app.include_router to split files

Test endpoints with `TestClient` and pytest, swapping the real database for a test one through `dependency_overrides`.

Change the schema only through migrations so every environment ends up with the same tables.
A plain def endpoint runs in a thread pool; an async def endpoint must use async drivers only.

topics.title: Java 21 basics: JDK, types and control flow
topics.summary_md: Java is a statically typed language compiled to bytecode that runs on the JVM, and it is the most common backend language in Indian service and product companies. Install JDK 21, compile and run a class, and learn primitive types, strings, arrays and modern control flow such as switch expressions.
key_points: Compare strings with equals(), not ==; == checks whether two references point to the same object.
int overflows silently past about 2.1 billion; use long for large counts and sums.
Arrays have a fixed length; use ArrayList when the size changes.

Arrays: new int[n], int[] a = {1, 2}, a.length, Arrays.sort, Arrays.toString, 2D arrays

topics.title: Java OOP: classes, interfaces, records, enums
topics.summary_md: Java code is organised into classes. Learn encapsulation with private fields, constructors, inheritance and **interfaces**, and the modern features that cut boilerplate: **records** for immutable data, **enums** for fixed sets, and sealed types with pattern matching in Java 21. The equals/hashCode contract matters as soon as objects go into a HashMap.

Program to interfaces (List, Repository) so implementations can be swapped and mocked.
Records give immutable data classes with constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString.

Inheritance: extends, super(...), @Override, polymorphism through a parent-type reference
Abstract classes vs interfaces: implements, default methods, when to use which
Object contract: equals, hashCode and toString; why equal objects must have equal hash codes
Records: record Point(int x, int y), compact constructors for validation, records as DTOs
Enums: values(), fields and methods on enums, switch over an enum
Java 21 patterns: sealed interfaces with permits, switch pattern matching and record patterns

topics.title: Collections, generics, lambdas and streams
topics.summary_md: The Collections Framework (List, Set, Map, Deque) is used in every Java program and every coding interview. **Generics** make collections type-safe. **Lambdas** and the **Stream API** let you filter, transform and group data declaratively, which is how most modern Spring code processes lists.

Ordered variants: LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, ArrayDeque as stack and queue, PriorityQueue

Streams: filter, map, sorted, distinct, limit, reduce, anyMatch, toList()

Optional: findFirst returns Optional; orElse, orElseThrow, map; never call get() without a check

topics.title: Go toolchain, syntax and basic types
topics.summary_md: Go is a small, compiled, statically typed language built for network services and tools. Go has one loop keyword, for, which also covers while-style and infinite loops.
learn_items: Toolchain: install Go 1.22+, go version, go mod init example.com/app, go run ., go build
Program shape: package main, import blocks, func main(), and that unused imports and variables are errors
Variables: var x int, x := 5, const, multiple assignment, zero values for every type
Basic types: int, int64, float64, string, bool, byte, rune; explicit conversions like float64(n)
Functions: parameters, multiple return values, named results, variadic ...int
Control flow: for i := 0; i < n; i++, for cond, for range, if with an init statement, switch without fallthrough
Range over int (Go 1.22): for i := range 10, and per-iteration loop variables
Tools: go fmt, go vet, and reading errors from the compiler

tasks.title: Solve in Go: FizzBuzz, reverse a string by runes, sum digits, and a function returning both min and max of a list

topics.title: Slices, maps, structs and methods
topics.summary_md: Slices and maps are Go's everyday collections, and structs with methods replace classes. A slice is a view over an array with a length and capacity, so `append` and sharing behave in ways you must understand. Methods can have value or pointer receivers, which decides whether they can change the struct.
key_points: append may return a new backing array; always write s = append(s, x).
Reading a missing map key returns the zero value; use v, ok := m[k] to tell absent from zero.
Use a pointer receiver when a method changes the struct or the struct is large.
learn_items: Arrays vs slices: [3]int is fixed, []int is a slice; len, cap, make([]int, 0, 10)
Slicing: s[1:3] shares the backing array; copy(dst, src) for an independent copy
append: growth and reallocation, and why two slices can unexpectedly share data
Maps: make(map[string]int), m[k]++, v, ok := m[k], delete(m, k), random iteration order
Packages slices and maps: slices.Sort, slices.Contains, slices.Index, maps.Keys
Structs: type User struct { Name string; Age int }, literals, embedding, struct tags `json:"name"`
Methods: func (u User) Greet() vs func (u *User) Rename(n string); automatic & and * on calls
Pointers: &x, *p, new; nil pointers; no pointer arithmetic

tasks.title: Build a gradebook with a Student struct, a map from roll number to student and methods to add marks and rank students

topics.title: Interfaces, errors and packages
topics.summary_md: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly: any type with the right methods fits, which keeps code decoupled and easy to test. Errors are ordinary values returned as the last result and checked with `if err != nil`; wrap them with context and inspect them with `errors.Is` and `errors.As`. Organise code into packages where capitalised names are exported.
key_points: Keep interfaces small and define them where they are used, not where they are implemented.
Wrap with fmt.Errorf("load user %d: %w", id, err) so callers can still match the cause.
panic is for programmer bugs; expected failures such as bad input or a missing row return an error.
learn_items: Interfaces: type Store interface { Get(id int) (Item, error) }, implicit satisfaction, io.Reader and io.Writer
any and type assertions: v, ok := x.(string), and type switches with switch v := x.(type)
Error basics: errors.New, return nil on success, the if err != nil pattern
Wrapping: fmt.Errorf with %w, errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound), errors.As(err, &target)
Sentinel and custom errors: var ErrNotFound = errors.New(...), a struct type with an Error() method
Packages: one folder per package, exported names start with a capital letter, internal/ for private code
Generics: func Map[T, U any](s []T, f func(T) U) []U, and constraints such as cmp.Ordered

tasks.title: Define a Store interface with an in-memory implementation that returns a wrapped ErrNotFound, and check it with errors.Is

topics.title: REST API with net/http and JSON
topics.summary_md: Go's standard library is enough for a production REST API. Since Go 1.22, `http.ServeMux` supports method and wildcard patterns such as `GET /items/{id}`, so you rarely need a router library. Decode and encode JSON with struct tags, write correct status codes, and add middleware by wrapping handlers.
key_points: Each request runs in its own goroutine; protect shared in-memory data with a sync.Mutex.
Set the Content-Type header and call WriteHeader before writing the body; later header changes are ignored.
Always configure server timeouts such as ReadHeaderTimeout instead of a bare http.ListenAndServe in production.
learn_items: Handlers: func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request), http.HandlerFunc, mux := http.NewServeMux()
Go 1.22 patterns: mux.HandleFunc("GET /items/{id}", h), r.PathValue("id"), automatic 405 on wrong method
JSON in: json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&req), DisallowUnknownFields, 400 on decode errors
JSON out: w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json"), w.WriteHeader(201), json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v)
Struct tags: `json:"title"`, omitempty, and the json:"-" tag to hide a field
Shared state: a store struct with a sync.Mutex (or RWMutex) guarding a map of items
Middleware: func(next http.Handler) http.Handler for logging and recovery; log/slog for structured logs
Server: &http.Server{Addr, Handler, ReadHeaderTimeout}, srv.ListenAndServe(), strconv.Atoi for ids

tasks.title: Build a todo REST API with net/http 1.22 patterns: list, get, create, update and delete, with a mutex-guarded map

topics.title: Goroutines, channels, select and context
topics.summary_md: Concurrency is Go's signature feature. **Goroutines** are cheap functions running concurrently and **channels** pass values between them safely. `select` waits on several channels, `sync.WaitGroup` waits for a group, and `context.Context` carries cancellation and deadlines through a request so no goroutine is left running forever.
key_points: Every goroutine you start needs a clear way to stop; a goroutine blocked forever is a leak.
Only the sender closes a channel; sending on a closed channel panics.
Pass ctx as the first parameter and stop work when ctx.Done() is closed.
learn_items: Goroutines: go f(), why main exiting kills them, and sync.WaitGroup Add/Done/Wait
Channels: make(chan int), unbuffered vs buffered, send and receive block, close and range over a channel
select: waiting on several channels, a default case, and time.After for timeouts
Patterns: worker pool with a jobs channel, fan-out and fan-in, a semaphore with a buffered channel
Shared memory: sync.Mutex, sync.RWMutex, sync.Once, and atomic counters
context: context.WithTimeout, WithCancel, defer cancel(), checking ctx.Done() and ctx.Err()
Request contexts: r.Context() in handlers, passed to database and outgoing HTTP calls
Race detector: go test -race and go run -race to find data races

tasks.title: Build a worker pool that checks 50 URLs from a slice with 5 workers, a 2-second timeout per call via context, and collects results

topics.title: Go tests, database/sql and graceful shutdown
topics.summary_md: Finish the Go API: test handlers with `httptest`, write table-driven tests, store data in PostgreSQL or SQLite through `database/sql`, and shut down cleanly so in-flight requests finish. These are the habits interviewers look for when you say you built a Go service.
key_points: Table-driven tests with t.Run give one named sub-test per case and are idiomatic Go.
Always close rows with defer rows.Close() and check rows.Err() after the loop.
srv.Shutdown(ctx) stops new connections and waits for running requests to finish.
learn_items: Testing basics: files ending _test.go, func TestX(t *testing.T), t.Errorf vs t.Fatalf, go test ./...
Table-driven tests: a slice of cases with name, input and want, looped with t.Run(tc.name, ...)
HTTP tests: httptest.NewRecorder with handler.ServeHTTP, or httptest.NewServer for a real client
database/sql: sql.Open with a driver (pgx or a SQLite driver), db.PingContext, connection pool settings
Queries: QueryRowContext(...).Scan(&a, &b), QueryContext with rows.Next, ExecContext, $1 placeholders
Not found: errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) mapped to a 404 response
Graceful shutdown: signal.NotifyContext(ctx, os.Interrupt), then srv.Shutdown with a timeout context

tasks.title: Move the todo API to database/sql with SQLite or PostgreSQL, map sql.ErrNoRows to 404 and add graceful shutdown
Write table-driven httptest tests for the todo API covering 201, 400, 404 and 405 responses

topics.title: Resources, HTTP methods and status codes
topics.summary_md: A REST API exposes **resources** as nouns in URLs and uses HTTP methods as the verbs. Learn which methods are safe and idempotent, how to name and nest resources, and which status code to return in each common case. Getting these basics right makes an API predictable for every client and is a frequent interview topic.
key_points: Plural nouns, no verbs in paths: POST /orders, not /createOrder.
GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not, and PATCH is not guaranteed to be.
401 means not authenticated; 403 means authenticated but not allowed.
learn_items: Resources: collections /users and items /users/42, nesting one level for ownership /users/42/orders
Methods: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH updates part, DELETE removes
Safe and idempotent: safe = no state change (GET, HEAD); idempotent = repeating has the same effect (PUT, DELETE)
Success codes: 200 OK with body, 201 Created with a Location header, 204 No Content
Client errors: 400 malformed, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 422 failed validation
Server errors: 500 for unexpected failures, 503 when temporarily unavailable; never 200 with an error inside
Representations: JSON bodies, Content-Type and Accept headers, consistent camelCase or snake_case field names

tasks.title: Design the endpoints, methods and status codes for a college library API with books, members and loans, in a table

topics.title: Pagination, filtering, errors and versioning
topics.summary_md: Real APIs return lists that grow without limit, receive bad input and change over time. Paginate every list, support filtering and sorting through query parameters, return errors in one documented format, and plan how to version without breaking existing clients. Prefer additive changes; a new version is for breaking ones.
key_points: Never return an unbounded list; set a default page size and a maximum.
Cursor pagination stays correct when rows are inserted; offset pagination can skip or repeat items.
Adding an optional field is non-breaking; renaming or removing one is breaking.
learn_items: Offset pagination: ?limit=20&offset=40, simple but slow for deep pages and unstable under inserts
Cursor pagination: ?limit=20&after=<cursor>, an opaque cursor encoding the last sort key, and a next cursor in the response
Filtering and sorting: ?status=open&sort=-created_at, allow-listing sortable fields
Error format: problem details (RFC 9457) with type, title, status, detail and per-field errors
Validation: validate types, ranges and required fields at the boundary, and report all field errors at once
Versioning: /v1 in the path or a header; deprecate old versions with notice instead of breaking them
Compatibility: additive changes, tolerant clients that ignore unknown fields, never reuse a field name

tasks.title: Add cursor pagination, a status filter and problem-details errors to the API you built in your server language

topics.title: Idempotency keys, caching, rate limits, OpenAPI
topics.summary_md: Networks fail, so clients retry; your API must make retries safe. **Idempotency keys** stop a retried POST from charging twice, **ETags** enable caching and safe concurrent updates, and **rate limits** protect the service. Describe the whole contract in an **OpenAPI** document so clients, docs and tests share one source of truth.
key_points: Store the result of a POST against its Idempotency-Key and replay it for repeated requests with the same key.
If-Match with an ETag rejects stale updates with 412 instead of silently overwriting.
Return 429 with a Retry-After header when a client exceeds its rate limit.
learn_items: Idempotency keys: client sends an Idempotency-Key header on POST; the server stores key, request hash and response
Retries: retry only idempotent requests or those with a key, with exponential backoff and jitter
Caching: Cache-Control max-age and no-store, ETag with If-None-Match returning 304 Not Modified
Optimistic concurrency: ETag or version field, If-Match on PUT/PATCH, 412 Precondition Failed on mismatch
Rate limiting: per-user or per-key limits, token bucket idea, 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After
Long operations: 202 Accepted with a status resource the client polls
OpenAPI 3.1: paths, operations, schemas, responses and security schemes; generate docs and clients from it

tasks.title: Add Idempotency-Key support to a POST /payments endpoint so that a repeated key returns the first response unchanged
Write an OpenAPI 3.1 file for your library API with two paths, request schemas and error responses

topics.title: Passwords, sessions and JWTs
topics.summary_md: **Authentication** proves who a user is; **authorisation** decides what they may do. Store passwords only as slow salted hashes, then keep users signed in with either a **server-side session** (a random ID in a secure cookie) or a signed **JWT**. Know the trade-offs: sessions are easy to revoke, JWTs avoid a lookup but are hard to revoke before they expire.
key_points: Hash passwords with argon2id or bcrypt; never store plain text or a fast hash such as SHA-256.
A JWT is signed, not encrypted: anyone holding it can read the payload.
Session cookies should be HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite=Lax or Strict.
learn_items: AuthN vs AuthZ: identity first, then permission checks on every request, on the server only
Password storage: argon2id or bcrypt with a per-user salt and a work factor; verify with the library compare function
Login hygiene: generic "invalid email or password" errors, rate limiting and lockout against guessing
Sessions: random session ID in a cookie, data in a server store, delete on logout, new ID after login
Cookie flags: HttpOnly (no JavaScript access), Secure (HTTPS only), SameSite against CSRF, Max-Age
JWT structure: header.payload.signature in base64url, claims sub, exp, iat, iss and aud
JWT checks: verify signature with a pinned algorithm, check exp, iss and aud; reject alg none
Access and refresh tokens: short-lived access token (minutes), rotating refresh token, revocation list on logout

tasks.title: Add register and login to your API with bcrypt or argon2 hashing, issue a 15-minute JWT, and protect one route with it

topics.title: OAuth 2.0 with PKCE, OpenID Connect and RBAC
topics.summary_md: "Sign in with Google" uses **OAuth 2.0** with **OpenID Connect**: the user signs in at the identity provider, your app receives a short-lived code and exchanges it for tokens. Public clients (mobile, desktop, single-page apps) must use **PKCE**. Once you know who the user is, enforce permissions with roles and object-level ownership checks.
key_points: Use the Authorization Code flow with PKCE; the implicit flow is deprecated.
OAuth access tokens grant API access; the OIDC ID token says who signed in. Do not use one for the other.
Check ownership on every object: being signed in does not mean /orders/42 belongs to this user.
learn_items: OAuth roles: resource owner (user), client (your app), authorisation server, resource server (the API)
Code flow: redirect to the provider with client_id, redirect_uri, scope and state; receive a code; exchange it for tokens
PKCE: random code_verifier, code_challenge = base64url(SHA-256(verifier)), method S256, verifier sent at exchange
Safety checks: exact redirect URI match, state against CSRF, nonce in OIDC, tokens never in URLs or logs
OpenID Connect: openid scope, ID token claims sub, email, aud and exp; userinfo endpoint
Machine-to-machine: client credentials flow for service calls without a user
RBAC: roles map to permissions (admin can delete, user can read); checked in middleware or service code
Object-level authorisation: query by id and owner, return 404 or 403 for other users' records (IDOR)

tasks.title: Generate a PKCE code_verifier and S256 code_challenge in your server language and verify the pair matches
Add roles to your API: users edit only their own records, admins edit any, with tests for each 403 case

topics.title: GraphQL schemas, queries, mutations, resolvers
