Cluster DNS: web.shop.svc.cluster.local, or just web from pods in the same namespace
EndpointSlices: kubectl get endpointslices shows which pod IPs a Service sends to; empty means a selector mismatch
kubectl port-forward svc/web 8080:80: reach a ClusterIP Service from your laptop while debugging
Ingress: host and path rules to backend Services, served by an ingress controller you install
Gateway API: newer, role-oriented successor to Ingress with Gateway and HTTPRoute objects

tasks.title: Expose a Deployment with a ClusterIP Service, curl it by DNS name from a temporary pod, then break the selector and debug it
Install an ingress or Gateway API controller in kind and route /api and / to two different Services

topics.title: ConfigMaps, Secrets and persistent storage
topics.summary_md: Keep configuration out of images so the same image runs in every environment. **ConfigMaps** hold plain settings and **Secrets** hold sensitive values; both reach containers as environment variables or mounted files. For data that must survive pod restarts, a pod claims storage through a **PersistentVolumeClaim**, and **StatefulSets** give databases stable names and their own volumes.
key_points: Secrets are only base64-encoded by default: restrict access with RBAC and enable encryption at rest.
Env vars from a ConfigMap are read at start-up; mounted files update, but the app must re-read them.
A PVC asks for storage; a StorageClass provisions the actual volume automatically.
learn_items: ConfigMap: key-value settings created from literals or files (kubectl create configmap --from-literal)
Secret: same shape for sensitive data; values are base64 in YAML, which is encoding, not encryption
Consuming config: env with valueFrom, envFrom for all keys, or a volume that mounts keys as files
Restart to pick up env changes: kubectl rollout restart deployment/web
emptyDir: scratch space that lives as long as the pod; lost when the pod is deleted
PersistentVolume, PersistentVolumeClaim and StorageClass: request size and access mode, provisioned dynamically
StatefulSet: stable pod names (db-0, db-1) and one PVC per replica via volumeClaimTemplates

tasks.title: Move an app’s settings into a ConfigMap and its password into a Secret, then change a value and roll the Deployment
Run PostgreSQL with a PVC, insert a row, delete the pod and confirm the row is still there

topics.title: Health probes, resource limits and autoscaling
topics.summary_md: Production pods tell Kubernetes when they are healthy and how much they need. **Readiness probes** keep traffic away from pods that are not ready, **liveness probes** restart stuck ones, and **startup probes** protect slow starters. **Requests** drive scheduling and **limits** cap usage, and the **Horizontal Pod Autoscaler** adds or removes replicas based on load.
key_points: Readiness failing removes the pod from Service endpoints; liveness failing restarts the container.
Over the CPU limit a container is throttled; over the memory limit it is OOMKilled.
The HPA measures CPU utilisation as a percentage of the request, so pods need requests set.
A liveness probe that checks the database can restart every pod when only the database is down.
learn_items: Probe kinds: httpGet, tcpSocket, exec, grpc; settings initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds, failureThreshold
Readiness vs liveness vs startup: gate traffic, restart a hung process, delay checks for slow start-up
Requests vs limits: requests reserve capacity for scheduling; limits are the hard ceiling at runtime
Units: CPU in millicores (250m = a quarter core), memory in Mi and Gi
QoS classes: Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort; BestEffort pods are evicted first under memory pressure
Debugging: CrashLoopBackOff (check logs --previous), OOMKilled (raise memory), Pending (no node fits)
HPA: needs metrics-server; autoscaling/v2 with min, max replicas and a target such as 70% CPU

tasks.title: Add readiness and liveness probes plus requests and limits to a Deployment, then trigger an OOMKilled pod on purpose
Install metrics-server in kind, create an HPA at 50% CPU and watch it scale under a busybox load loop

topics.title: Namespaces, RBAC, Helm and Kustomize
topics.summary_md: Shared clusters need boundaries and repeatable packaging. **Namespaces** group resources per team or environment, and **RBAC** controls who (users and service accounts) can do what. **Helm** packages an app as a versioned chart with configurable values, while **Kustomize** patches plain YAML per environment without templates.
key_points: RBAC = Role (what) + RoleBinding (who); ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding apply cluster-wide.
kubectl auth can-i lets you test permissions before a pipeline fails on them.
Helm keeps release history, so helm rollback returns to an earlier revision.
learn_items: Namespaces: kubectl create namespace, -n flag, and setting a default namespace in your context
ResourceQuota and LimitRange: cap total and default per-pod CPU and memory in a namespace
RBAC: Role and ClusterRole list verbs on resources; RoleBinding attaches them to users or service accounts
ServiceAccount: the identity pods use to call the API; grant it only the verbs it needs
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as system:serviceaccount:dev:app: check a permission
Helm: chart (templates + values.yaml), release; helm install, upgrade --install, rollback, uninstall
Kustomize: a base plus overlays per environment; kubectl apply -k overlays/prod

tasks.title: Create a service account that can only read pods in one namespace and prove it with kubectl auth can-i
Package your app as a Helm chart with replicas and image tag in values.yaml; upgrade it, then roll back

topics.title: Continuous integration with GitHub Actions
topics.summary_md: **Continuous integration** builds and tests every push and pull request so broken code never reaches main unnoticed. In GitHub Actions a **workflow** file defines triggers, **jobs** that run on fresh runners, and **steps** that run commands or reuse actions. Keep pipelines fast with dependency caching and parallel jobs, and make the checks required before merging.
key_points: Workflows live in .github/workflows/*.yml and run on events such as push and pull_request.
Jobs run in parallel on separate runners unless needs: makes one wait for another.
Secrets come from the repository secret store as ${{ secrets.NAME }}, never from the code.
Required status checks on a protected main branch turn CI from advice into a gate.
learn_items: CI vs continuous delivery vs continuous deployment: test every change; always releasable; release automatically
Workflow anatomy: name, on (push, pull_request, workflow_dispatch), jobs, runs-on, steps
Steps: uses runs an action (actions/checkout, actions/setup-node); run executes shell commands
Typical CI job: checkout, set up the language, install with a lockfile, lint, test, build
Caching: setup-node cache: npm or actions/cache keyed on the lockfile hash
Matrix builds: strategy.matrix runs one job across several versions or operating systems
Secrets and variables: repository secrets, ${{ secrets.X }}, and masked output in logs
Branch protection: require pull requests and passing status checks before merging into main

tasks.title: Add a GitHub Actions workflow that lints, tests and builds your project on every pull request, with dependency caching
Make the CI job a required check on main, open a PR with a failing test and confirm merging is blocked

topics.title: Build once, deploy many: artifacts and releases
topics.summary_md: Delivery pipelines build an artefact (usually a container image) once, tag it with the commit SHA, and promote that exact artefact through staging and production. **Environments** add approvals and their own secrets, and **OIDC** lets a workflow get short-lived cloud credentials without storing keys. Release strategies such as rolling, blue-green and canary limit how many users a bad release can hurt.
key_points: Never rebuild per environment: what you tested in staging must be the bytes you ship.
Tag images with the commit SHA; tags like latest cannot tell you what is running.
OIDC federation replaces long-lived cloud keys in CI with tokens that expire in minutes.
learn_items: Artefacts: build output stored by the pipeline (actions/upload-artifact) or pushed to a container registry
Image tags: tag with the git SHA (and a semver release tag); push to a registry from the workflow
Promotion: deploy the same image digest to staging, run checks, then to production
GitHub environments: protection rules, required reviewers and environment-specific secrets
OIDC: permissions id-token: write plus a cloud role that trusts your repository; no stored access keys
Strategies: rolling (gradual), blue-green (switch traffic between two stacks), canary (small share first)
Rollback: redeploy the previous known-good artefact; keep database migrations backwards compatible

tasks.title: Extend your workflow to build a Docker image tagged with the commit SHA and push it to GitHub Container Registry on merge to main
Add a production environment with a required reviewer and a deploy job that waits for approval

topics.title: GitOps principles and Argo CD basics
topics.summary_md: In GitOps the desired state of a cluster lives in a git repository, and an agent inside the cluster continuously pulls it and reconciles the cluster to match. Deployments become pull requests, rollbacks become reverts, and manual changes are detected as **drift**. **Argo CD** models each deployed app as an `Application` that points at a repo path and a destination cluster and namespace.
key_points: Four principles: declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, continuously reconciled.
Pull model: CI never needs cluster credentials; the in-cluster agent fetches from git.
Synced means the cluster matches git; Healthy means the resources are actually working.
learn_items: Push vs pull deployment: CI running kubectl apply vs an in-cluster agent pulling from git
OpenGitOps principles: declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, continuously reconciled
Argo CD install: its own namespace, the official manifests or Helm chart, then the UI via port-forward
Application resource: source (repoURL, path, targetRevision) and destination (server, namespace)
Sync status (Synced, OutOfSync) vs health status (Healthy, Progressing, Degraded)
Sync policy: manual sync, or automated with prune (delete removed objects) and selfHeal (undo drift)
Rollback: git revert the commit and let the agent sync, rather than editing the cluster
Flux CD: the other main GitOps tool, built from GitRepository and Kustomization controllers

tasks.title: Install Argo CD in kind, point an Application at a folder of manifests in your GitHub repo and enable automated sync
Scale the app by hand with kubectl, watch Argo CD report OutOfSync, then turn on selfHeal and watch it revert

topics.title: Repo layout, promotion and secrets in GitOps
topics.summary_md: A working GitOps setup separates application code from deployment config and promotes releases between environments with commits. CI builds the image, then updates the image tag in the config repo; Argo CD deploys it. Environments are usually folders (Kustomize overlays or Helm values files), not long-lived branches, and secrets never sit in git in plain form.
key_points: App repo builds images; config repo describes what runs where.
Promote by changing the image tag in the next environment’s folder through a pull request.
Encrypt or reference secrets (Sealed Secrets, SOPS, External Secrets) instead of committing them.
learn_items: Two repos (or two folders): application code with CI, and deployment config watched by Argo CD
Environment folders: base plus overlays/dev, overlays/staging, overlays/prod using Kustomize
Image update flow: CI pushes an image, then commits the new tag to the config repo (by PR for prod)
Why not branch per environment: merges drift and differences between environments become hard to see
App of apps and ApplicationSet: one Argo CD Application or generator that creates many Applications
Secrets options: Sealed Secrets (encrypted in git), SOPS, or External Secrets Operator reading a vault

tasks.title: Restructure your manifests into a Kustomize base with dev and prod overlays and create one Argo CD Application per overlay

topics.title: Cloud basics: regions, service models and billing
topics.summary_md: AWS, Google Cloud and Azure rent you the same building blocks: compute, storage, networking, databases and identity, billed by use. Resources live in **regions**, each split into isolated **availability zones**, and under the **shared responsibility model** the provider secures the hardware while you secure your configuration and data. Before creating anything, lock down the root account and set a budget alert.
key_points: Spread production across at least two availability zones; one zone can fail on its own.
Pick a region near your users and with the services you need; India has regions such as Mumbai.
Turn on MFA for the root account, never use it day to day, and set a budget alert on day one.
learn_items: Service models: IaaS (VMs), PaaS (managed runtimes and databases), SaaS (finished software)
Region and availability zone: a region holds several isolated zones linked by low-latency networks
Shared responsibility: provider secures facilities and hypervisors; you own IAM, data, patching guests, config
Equivalents: EC2 / Compute Engine / Azure VMs; S3 / Cloud Storage / Blob Storage; IAM / IAM / Entra ID
Pricing: on-demand, committed use (reserved instances, savings plans), and cheap interruptible spot capacity
Hidden costs: data transfer out, NAT gateways, idle public IPv4 addresses, forgotten snapshots
Account safety: root MFA, an admin user or SSO for daily work, a budget with email alerts
Interfaces: the web console for exploring, the CLI (aws, gcloud, az) and SDKs for anything repeatable

tasks.title: On a free-tier or credit account, enable root MFA, create an admin identity for daily use and set a small monthly budget alert

topics.title: Identity and access management
topics.summary_md: IAM decides **who** (a principal) can do **what** (actions) on **which resources**, under which conditions. Humans should sign in through single sign-on with short-lived sessions, and workloads should use **roles** that hand out temporary credentials instead of stored access keys. Everything is denied by default, an explicit deny always wins, and the goal is least privilege.
key_points: Default deny; an explicit Deny in any applicable policy overrides every Allow.
Give VMs, functions and CI pipelines roles, not long-lived access keys.
Start from narrow permissions and widen on evidence, not from admin access narrowed later.
learn_items: Principals: users, groups, roles (AWS); users, groups, service accounts (GCP); users and managed identities (Azure)
Policy JSON: Effect, Action (s3:GetObject), Resource (an ARN) and optional Condition
Evaluation: implicit deny, explicit allow, explicit deny always wins
Roles and STS: assume a role to get temporary credentials; instance profiles give them to EC2
Human access: SSO or IAM Identity Center with MFA instead of IAM users with access keys
Least privilege: scope actions and resources tightly; use access analysis tools to remove unused permissions
Resource policies: bucket policies and similar grant access from the resource side, including cross-account

tasks.title: Write a policy allowing read-only access to one bucket prefix, attach it to a role, and test allowed and denied calls with the CLI

topics.title: Compute: VMs, managed containers and serverless
topics.summary_md: The cloud offers three main ways to run code. **Virtual machines** give full control and full responsibility for patching; **managed containers** (ECS on Fargate, Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps, managed Kubernetes) run your images without managing servers; and **functions** (Lambda, Cloud Run functions, Azure Functions) run code per event and bill per invocation. Choose by how much control you need versus how much you want to operate.
key_points: VMs: most control, most work (patching, scaling, OS hardening).
Serverless functions scale to zero but have time limits and cold starts.
Auto Scaling groups replace unhealthy VMs and add capacity based on metrics.
Managed container services are often the simplest home for a Dockerised web API.
learn_items: VM basics: image (AMI), instance type (vCPU, memory, burstable families), key pair, security group
User data: a start-up script that installs and starts your app on first boot
Connecting: SSH with a key pair, or a browser session manager that needs no open port 22
Auto Scaling group: launch template, min/desired/max size, health checks and scaling policies
Managed containers: ECS with Fargate, Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps run an image behind an HTTPS endpoint
Managed Kubernetes: EKS, GKE, AKS run the control plane for you; you still manage workloads
Functions: event triggers (HTTP, queue, file upload), maximum run time, cold starts, pay per request

tasks.title: Launch a small Linux VM with a user-data script that starts a web server, reach it in a browser, then terminate it
Deploy your Docker image to a managed container service or a function behind an HTTP endpoint on the free tier

topics.title: Object, block storage and managed databases
topics.summary_md: Pick storage by access pattern. **Object storage** (S3, Cloud Storage, Blob Storage) holds files of any size behind an API and is the default for uploads, backups and static sites. **Block storage** (EBS, persistent disks) is a virtual disk attached to one VM in one zone. **Managed databases** (RDS, Cloud SQL, Azure Database) handle backups, patching and failover so you can focus on schema and queries.
key_points: Keep buckets private (Block Public Access on); share single files with time-limited presigned URLs.
Lifecycle rules move old objects to cheaper storage classes or delete them automatically.
Multi-AZ gives a database a standby for failover; read replicas add read capacity.
learn_items: Object storage: buckets, keys (paths), objects, metadata; strong read-after-write consistency in S3
Storage classes: standard, infrequent access, archive; cheaper storage costs more to retrieve
Bucket safety: Block Public Access, bucket policies, versioning, default encryption
Presigned URLs: grant temporary upload or download of one object without making the bucket public
Block storage: volume types, attach to one VM in the same zone, snapshots for backup
Managed relational DB: engine choice, automated backups, point-in-time restore, Multi-AZ standby
Managed NoSQL: DynamoDB, Firestore, Cosmos DB for key-value or document access at scale

tasks.title: Create a private bucket with versioning, upload a file with the CLI and share it through a presigned URL that expires in 10 minutes

topics.title: VPCs, subnets, security groups and load balancers
topics.summary_md: A **VPC** is your private network in the cloud, divided into **subnets** in each availability zone. Public subnets route to an internet gateway; private subnets reach the internet only through a NAT gateway, so databases and app servers stay unreachable from outside. **Security groups** act as stateful firewalls on each resource, and a **load balancer** in the public subnets spreads traffic across healthy targets.
key_points: Put the load balancer in public subnets and app servers and databases in private ones.
Security groups are stateful and allow-only; reference other security groups instead of IP ranges.
NAT gateways are billed per hour and per GB: a common surprise on student bills.
learn_items: VPC CIDR: an address range such as 10.0.0.0/16, split into /24 subnets, one or more per zone
Route tables: a public subnet has a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway; private routes to a NAT gateway
Security groups: stateful, allow rules only, attached to instances, load balancers and databases
Network ACLs: stateless subnet-level rules with allow and deny; return traffic needs its own rule
Load balancers: application (layer 7, HTTP paths and hosts) vs network (layer 4, TCP/UDP)
Target groups and health checks: the load balancer only sends traffic to targets that pass
DNS and TLS: a managed DNS record pointing at the load balancer, plus a free managed certificate
Private endpoints: reach S3 or other services from private subnets without going through NAT

tasks.title: Draw and then build a VPC with public and private subnets in two zones, a load balancer in front and the app in private subnets

topics.title: Designing for availability, scale and cost
topics.summary_md: Good cloud designs assume parts will fail and costs will creep. Keep app servers **stateless** behind a load balancer so any instance can be replaced, put state in managed services, and spread across zones. Define recovery targets (RTO, RPO) and back them with tested backups. Track spend with tags and cost reports, right-size idle resources and delete what nobody uses.
key_points: Stateless servers + managed state + multiple zones is the default highly available web pattern.
RTO is how long recovery may take; RPO is how much recent data you can afford to lose.
A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a backup.
learn_items: Stateless app tier: sessions in a cache or database, files in object storage, so instances are disposable
Scaling: vertical (bigger machine) vs horizontal (more machines); horizontal needs statelessness
Caching layers: a CDN for static files and a managed cache in front of the database for hot reads
RTO and RPO: recovery time and data-loss targets that decide backup frequency and failover design
Well-Architected pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance, cost, sustainability
Cost control: tags per project, cost explorer reports, right-sizing, schedules to stop dev resources
Clean-up habit: delete idle load balancers, NAT gateways, unattached volumes and old snapshots

tasks.title: Draw a highly available design for a student marketplace app and annotate each part with its failure mode and monthly cost driver

topics.title: Terraform basics: providers, resources, plan, apply
topics.summary_md: Infrastructure as code describes infrastructure in versioned files so it can be reviewed, repeated and rebuilt. Terraform (and its open-source fork OpenTofu, with the same language) reads HCL files, builds a dependency graph, and shows a **plan** of what it will create, change or destroy before you **apply** it. You can practise for free on a laptop with the Docker or local providers before touching a cloud account.
key_points: Read every plan: the + ~ - markers show create, update in place and destroy.
References between resources (aws_subnet.main.id) create dependencies automatically.
terraform destroy removes everything the configuration manages, so use it on practice stacks.
learn_items: IaC benefits: repeatable environments, code review for infrastructure, history in git, no click-ops drift
HCL blocks: terraform { required_providers }, provider, resource "type" "name", data sources
Workflow: terraform init (download providers), fmt, validate, plan, apply, destroy
Plan symbols: + create, ~ update in place, -/+ replace, - destroy; replacement can mean downtime
Dependency graph: attribute references order creation; depends_on only for hidden dependencies
Provider version pinning: version constraints plus the committed .terraform.lock.hcl file
OpenTofu: community fork of Terraform with the same HCL; tofu replaces terraform in commands

tasks.title: Use the Docker provider to create an nginx image and container with Terraform, change the port, read the plan, then destroy

topics.title: State, variables, outputs and remote backends
topics.summary_md: Terraform remembers what it manages in a **state** file that maps resources in your code to real IDs. Teams keep state in a **remote backend** with locking so two applies cannot collide, and never commit it to git because it can hold secrets. **Variables** make a configuration reusable across environments, and **outputs** expose values such as an IP address to people or other configurations.
key_points: State maps code to real resources; lose it and Terraform no longer knows what it created.
Remote state with locking (for example S3 with a lock file) is a must for teams and CI.
Changes made by hand in the console show up as drift in the next plan.
learn_items: State file: resource addresses mapped to real IDs and attributes; may contain secrets in plain text
Remote backend: S3, Cloud Storage or Azure Blob with state locking; configure in the backend block
Never edit state by hand: use terraform state list, show, mv and rm, or moved and import blocks
Variables: variable blocks with type, default, description, validation and sensitive = true
Setting values: terraform.tfvars, -var-file=prod.tfvars, or TF_VAR_name environment variables
Outputs and locals: output blocks expose values; locals name repeated expressions
Drift: terraform plan -refresh-only shows changes made outside Terraform
Importing: an import block brings an existing resource under management without recreating it

tasks.title: Parameterise your Docker stack with variables for port and image tag, add outputs, and apply it with two different tfvars files
Change a managed container by hand to cause drift, find it with a refresh-only plan, then import an unmanaged one

topics.title: Modules, environments and Terraform in CI
topics.summary_md: As configurations grow, **modules** package a group of resources behind input variables and outputs so you can reuse them, for example one network module used by dev and prod. **count** and **for_each** create many similar resources from one block. In a team, Terraform runs in a pipeline: format and validate on every pull request, post the plan for review, and apply only after merge.
key_points: Prefer for_each over count when items have names; removing one item then does not shift the rest.
Pin module versions so an upstream change cannot alter your infrastructure unexpectedly.
Plan on the pull request, apply on merge: reviewers approve the exact change.
learn_items: Module structure: main.tf, variables.tf, outputs.tf in a folder; call it with a module block and source
Module sources: local paths, git references, or a registry with a pinned version
count vs for_each: index-based copies vs keyed copies from a map or set of strings
Environments: separate folders or state per environment (dev, prod) sharing the same modules
Workspaces: several states for one configuration; handy for experiments, weaker isolation than folders
CI pipeline: fmt -check, validate, a linter such as tflint, plan on PR, apply on main with OIDC credentials
Policy and security checks: scan configurations for open security groups or public buckets before apply

tasks.title: Extract your container setup into a module, call it twice with for_each for two apps, and run fmt, validate and plan in GitHub Actions

topics.title: Metrics, logs and traces: the three signals
topics.summary_md: Monitoring tells you that something is wrong; observability lets you ask why, using three signals. **Metrics** are cheap numeric time series for dashboards and alerts, **logs** are detailed records of individual events, and **traces** follow one request across services. Start from the **golden signals** (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) for each service.
key_points: Golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. RED for services, USE for resources.
Look at latency percentiles (p95, p99), not averages, which hide slow requests.
Use structured JSON logs with a request ID so you can search and join them across services.
learn_items: Monitoring vs observability: known failure checks vs exploring unknown problems from rich signals
Metrics: numbers over time with labels; cheap to store, ideal for dashboards and alerts
Logs: timestamped events; structured JSON with level, message, request ID beats free text
Traces: a trace is a tree of spans (timed operations) sharing a trace ID across services
Golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation for every user-facing service
RED (rate, errors, duration) for request-driven services; USE (utilisation, saturation, errors) for resources
Percentiles: p50, p95, p99 latency; averages hide the slow tail that users notice

tasks.title: Switch an API to structured JSON logs with a request ID per request, and log status code and duration for every call

topics.title: Prometheus, PromQL, Grafana and alerting
topics.summary_md: **Prometheus** scrapes `/metrics` endpoints on a schedule and stores time series identified by a metric name and labels. You query them with **PromQL**, chart them in **Grafana**, and define alert rules that **Alertmanager** groups and routes to people. Good alerts fire on user-facing symptoms that need a human, last long enough to be real, and link to a runbook.
key_points: Counters only go up: always wrap them in rate() before charting or alerting.
Every unique label combination is a new series; never put user IDs or URLs with IDs in labels.
An alert should be actionable: if nobody needs to act, make it a dashboard panel instead.
learn_items: Pull model: Prometheus scrapes targets listed in scrape configs or found by service discovery
Metric types: counter (only increases), gauge (up and down), histogram (buckets for latency)
Instrumenting: a client library exposes /metrics, e.g. http_requests_total with method and status labels
PromQL basics: rate(http_requests_total[5m]) and sum by (status) (…) for per-status request rates
Latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(…_bucket[5m]))) gives p95
Cardinality: unbounded label values explode the number of series and memory use
Grafana: add Prometheus as a data source, build panels per golden signal, use variables per service
Alerting: rules with expr and for:, labels for severity; Alertmanager groups, routes and silences

tasks.title: Run Prometheus and Grafana with Docker Compose, instrument your API, and build a request rate, error rate and p95 latency dashboard
Write an alert rule for error rate above 5% for 5 minutes and trigger it with a failing endpoint

topics.title: Distributed tracing and logs with OpenTelemetry
topics.summary_md: **OpenTelemetry** is the vendor-neutral standard for producing traces, metrics and logs: SDKs instrument your code, and the **Collector** receives, processes and exports the data to back ends such as Jaeger, Grafana Tempo or Loki. Trace context travels between services in the W3C `traceparent` header, so spans from different services join into one trace. Sampling keeps tracing affordable.
key_points: Instrument once with OpenTelemetry and switch back ends without changing application code.
Context propagation through headers is what links spans from different services.
Put the trace ID in every log line so you can jump from a slow trace to its logs.
learn_items: Spans: name, start and end time, attributes, status, and a parent span ID
Context propagation: the W3C traceparent header carries trace ID and parent span to the next service
Instrumentation: auto-instrumentation for common frameworks plus manual spans around key operations
OTLP and the Collector: receivers, processors (batching, filtering), exporters to tracing and log back ends
Back ends: Jaeger or Grafana Tempo for traces, Loki or an ELK/OpenSearch stack for logs
Sampling: head sampling decides at the start; tail sampling keeps errors and slow traces after the fact
Correlation: add trace_id to structured logs and use exemplars to link metrics to traces

tasks.title: Add OpenTelemetry to two small services that call each other, send traces through a Collector to Jaeger, and find a slow span

topics.title: SLIs, SLOs and error budgets
topics.summary_md: Site reliability engineering turns "is it reliable enough?" into numbers. An **SLI** measures what users feel, usually good events divided by valid events; an **SLO** sets a target for it over a window, such as 99.9% over 30 days; and the **error budget** is the remaining 0.1% you are allowed to fail. When the budget is spent, the team slows releases and fixes reliability.
key_points: SLI = measurement, SLO = internal target, SLA = contract with consequences, set looser than the SLO.
99.9% over 30 days allows about 43 minutes of full downtime; 99.99% allows about 4.3 minutes.
100% is the wrong target: it blocks all change and users cannot tell 99.99% from 100%.
learn_items: SLI: good events ÷ valid events, e.g. requests under 300 ms and not 5xx ÷ all requests
Choosing SLIs: availability, latency, correctness or freshness, measured as close to the user as possible
SLO: SLI target over a rolling window, e.g. 99.9% over 30 days; SLA: a contract with penalties
Error budget: 1 − SLO; 99.9% over 30 days = 43.2 minutes of total failure or the same share of requests
Error budget policy: what happens when it runs out (freeze features, focus on reliability work)
Burn rate: how fast the budget is spent; alert on fast burn (page) and slow burn (ticket)

tasks.title: Write two SLIs and SLOs for a food-delivery checkout API and calculate the monthly error budget in minutes and in requests

topics.title: On-call and incident response
topics.summary_md: An incident is any event that hurts users or puts an SLO at risk, and a good response is calm, structured and fast. Declare it early, assign an **incident commander** who coordinates rather than debugs, and **mitigate first** (roll back, fail over, shed load) before looking for the root cause. Sustainable on-call needs actionable pages, clear runbooks and a fair rotation.
key_points: Stop the bleeding before finding the cause: a rollback is often the fastest mitigation.
The incident commander coordinates, delegates and communicates; others investigate.
Every page should be urgent, actionable and tied to user impact, or it should not page.
learn_items: Severity levels: define SEV1 to SEV3 by user impact, with matching response times and who is paged
Roles: incident commander, operations lead, communications lead, scribe keeping the timeline
Response loop: detect, declare, triage, mitigate, resolve, then review
Mitigation options: roll back the last deploy, toggle a feature flag, fail over, scale up, rate-limit
Communication: one incident channel, regular status updates, a public status page for users
Runbooks: step-by-step checks and fixes linked from each alert
Healthy on-call: rotations with handover notes, escalation paths, follow-up time after heavy shifts

tasks.title: Run a tabletop drill with friends: break your demo app, take the commander role, mitigate and keep a timestamped timeline
Write a runbook for your high error rate alert: dashboards to open, checks to run and safe mitigations

topics.title: Blameless postmortems, toil and chaos testing
topics.summary_md: After an incident, a **blameless postmortem** records what happened, why the system allowed it and what will change, assuming people acted sensibly with what they knew. Reliability also improves by cutting **toil**, the manual, repetitive operational work that grows with the service, and by testing failure on purpose with **chaos experiments** and game days.
key_points: Blameless does not mean no accountability: it means fixing the system that let a mistake through.
Action items need an owner and a due date, or the same incident will happen again.
Start chaos experiments small, with a hypothesis, a limited blast radius and a stop button.
learn_items: Postmortem sections: summary, impact, timeline, root cause and contributing factors, what went well, actions
Blameless language: describe decisions and system gaps, not individual fault
Causes: look for several contributing factors; a single root cause and five whys can oversimplify
Action items: prevent, detect faster, mitigate faster; each with an owner, priority and due date
Toil: manual, repetitive, automatable work with no lasting value that grows with traffic; automate it
Chaos engineering: define steady state, hypothesise, inject a failure (kill a pod, add latency), observe
Game days: planned team exercises that rehearse failures and test runbooks and alerts

tasks.title: Write a blameless postmortem for your drill or a past outage of your own project, with a timeline and three owned action items
With a load loop running, delete random pods of your kind Deployment and check whether error rate and latency stay within SLO

topics.title: Shift-left security scanning in CI
topics.summary_md: DevSecOps builds security checks into the same pipeline that tests code, so problems are found minutes after they are written rather than after release. Scan source code (**SAST**), dependencies (**SCA**), container images, infrastructure code and commits for leaked secrets, and test the running app (**DAST**). Fail the build on serious, fixable findings and triage the rest so the pipeline is trusted, not ignored.
key_points: Most vulnerabilities you ship come from dependencies and base images, not your own code.
Block on critical and high findings that have a fix; track the rest with an owner and expiry.
Secret scanning must run before push: a key pushed to a public repo should be treated as leaked.
learn_items: SAST: scans source for risky patterns (SQL injection, unsafe deserialisation), e.g. Semgrep or CodeQL
SCA: checks dependencies against known CVEs; npm audit, pip-audit, Dependabot or Renovate updates
Image scanning: Trivy or Grype list OS and library CVEs in an image; smaller base images mean fewer
IaC scanning: Trivy config or Checkov flag public buckets, open security groups and privileged pods
Secret scanning: gitleaks or push protection; if a secret leaks, revoke and rotate it, then clean history
DAST: probes a running app from outside, e.g. a ZAP baseline scan against a staging URL
CVSS severity and triage: fix, upgrade, or suppress with a reason and an expiry date

tasks.title: Add Trivy image and config scans plus a secret scan to your GitHub Actions workflow, failing on critical and high findings

topics.title: Secrets, least privilege and supply chain security
topics.summary_md: Attackers increasingly target the build itself: compromised dependencies, CI actions and stolen pipeline credentials. Protect the chain by pinning third-party actions, using short-lived **OIDC** credentials and a **secrets manager**, publishing an **SBOM** and **signing** images so clusters run only what your pipeline built. At runtime, run containers with least privilege and enforce it with policy.
key_points: Pin third-party CI actions to a full commit SHA; tags can be moved by an attacker.
Sign images in CI and verify signatures at deploy time so only your builds run.
Containers: non-root, read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities, no privileged mode.
learn_items: Secrets managers: AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault or Vault; fetch at runtime, rotate
Pipeline credentials: OIDC to the cloud, minimal workflow permissions, no long-lived keys in CI secrets
Pinning: lockfiles, base image digests, and third-party actions pinned to a commit SHA
SBOM: a list of every component in an artefact in SPDX or CycloneDX format, generated with Syft or Trivy
Signing: cosign signs images, keyless through the CI identity; verify before deploy
Provenance: SLSA levels describe how trustworthy the record of how an artefact was built is
Runtime hardening: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, drop ALL capabilities, Pod Security restricted
Network and detection: NetworkPolicies limit pod traffic; Falco alerts on suspicious runtime behaviour

tasks.title: In CI, generate an SBOM for your image and sign the image with cosign keyless signing, then verify it locally
Harden a Deployment with a restrictive securityContext and label its namespace with Pod Security restricted enforcement

topics.title: Spreadsheet basics: formulas, references and SUMIFS
topics.summary_md: Every spreadsheet model rests on formulas that copy correctly. Learn when a reference should move as you fill (`A2`) and when it must stay put (`$B$1`), then summarise with conditional functions such as `SUMIFS` and `COUNTIFS`. Store raw data as a formatted table so formulas grow with new rows.
key_points: A $ locks what follows it: $A$1 locks both, A$1 only the row, $A1 only the column.
SUMIFS takes the sum range first, then pairs of criteria range and criterion.
Keep raw data, calculations and outputs on separate sheets.
Dates are numbers underneath, so you can subtract them and group them.
learn_items: Relative, absolute and mixed references: predict how A1, $A$1, A$1 and $A1 change when a formula is filled down or across
Arithmetic and order of operations: write formulas with +, -, *, /, ^ and brackets, and read #DIV/0!, #VALUE! and #REF! errors
IF and IFS: return a label from a condition, e.g. "Pass" when marks are 40 or more, and combine tests with AND and OR
SUMIFS, COUNTIFS and AVERAGEIFS: total, count and average rows that meet one or more conditions, including date ranges
Text functions: clean and combine text with TRIM, UPPER, PROPER, LEFT, RIGHT, MID, LEN and TEXTJOIN
Date functions: TODAY, YEAR, MONTH, EOMONTH and DATEDIF, and formatting a date without changing its value
Excel tables (Ctrl+T): structured references like Sales[Amount] that expand automatically as rows are added

tasks.title: Build a monthly sales sheet for a small kirana store with region-wise totals using SUMIFS and COUNTIFS
Grade a class marks table with IFS, flag students below 40 in any subject and count them per section

topics.title: Lookups and pivot tables
topics.summary_md: Lookups join two tables by a shared key, the spreadsheet version of a SQL join. `XLOOKUP` is the modern default; `INDEX`/`MATCH` and exact-match `VLOOKUP` still appear in older files and interviews. Pivot tables then summarise thousands of rows by any category in seconds, without writing a formula.
key_points: XLOOKUP(lookup, lookup_array, return_array, if_not_found) matches exactly by default.
VLOOKUP needs FALSE as its last argument for an exact match and can only look to the right.
A pivot table needs clean headers and one row per record with no blank rows.
Refresh a pivot table after the source data changes; it does not update by itself.
learn_items: XLOOKUP: find a value in one column and return the matching value from another, with a not-found message
VLOOKUP: the exact-match form with FALSE, why inserting a column breaks its column index, and why it cannot look left
INDEX and MATCH: combine them for a lookup in any direction, with 0 as the match type for exact matches
Lookup errors: why #N/A appears (extra spaces, numbers stored as text) and how to fix the data rather than hide it
Pivot table layout: place fields in Rows, Columns, Values and Filters, and switch Sum to Count or Average
Pivot options: Show Values As % of grand total, sort by value, and group dates into months, quarters and years
Slicers and pivot charts: add a slicer to filter one or more pivot tables and build a chart from a pivot

tasks.title: Join an e-commerce orders sheet to a product price list with XLOOKUP and compute revenue per order
Pivot an IPL match results table to show wins per team per season, with a slicer for venue

topics.title: Dynamic arrays, charts and Power Query
topics.summary_md: Modern Excel and Google Sheets formulas can return a whole range that **spills** into neighbouring cells. `FILTER`, `UNIQUE` and `SORT` replace many manual steps and pivot tables for small reports. Power Query records repeatable import and cleaning steps, so next month’s file is cleaned with one refresh.
key_points: A #SPILL! error means cells in the spill range are not empty.
FILTER(range, condition) returns every matching row and updates when the data changes.
Power Query steps are recorded and replayed on refresh; the raw file is never edited.
Use conditional formatting to point at exceptions, not to colour every cell.
learn_items: Spill ranges: how a dynamic array formula fills cells below it, the # reference (A2#) and the #SPILL! error
FILTER, UNIQUE and SORT: list distinct customers, filter rows by a condition and sort the result in one formula
LET: name intermediate results inside a long formula so it is easier to read and calculates once
Data validation: drop-down lists and number limits that stop bad entries at the source
Conditional formatting: highlight values above a threshold, duplicates and top 10 items with formula-based rules
Charts: build column and line charts from a table, add a clear title and axis labels, and remove gridline clutter
Power Query: import a CSV, change types, split columns, remove duplicates, unpivot and load back as a table

tasks.title: Build a one-sheet report on a state-wise rainfall table using UNIQUE, FILTER and SORT driven by a drop-down
Use Power Query to combine three monthly bank statement CSVs into one cleaned, typed table that refreshes

topics.title: Descriptive statistics: centre, spread and shape
topics.summary_md: Before any test or model, describe the data. Measure the **centre** (mean, median, mode), the **spread** (range, variance, standard deviation, IQR) and the **shape** (skew, outliers). Choosing the median and IQR for skewed data such as salaries or delivery times is the most common practical decision.
key_points: The median resists outliers; the mean is pulled towards them.
Sample variance divides by n − 1, not n, to avoid underestimating spread.
A value is often flagged as an outlier if it lies more than 1.5 × IQR beyond Q1 or Q3.
In right-skewed data the mean is usually larger than the median.
learn_items: Mean, median and mode: compute each by hand for a small list and say which suits skewed data
Range and IQR: find Q1, Q3 and IQR = Q3 − Q1, and use percentiles such as the 90th to describe tails
Variance and standard deviation: compute them, and know why a sample uses n − 1 in the denominator
Z-score: (x − mean) / SD tells how many standard deviations a value is from the mean
Skewness: recognise left and right skew from a histogram and from the order of mean and median
Box plots: read median, quartiles, whiskers and outlier points, and the 1.5 × IQR rule
Types of data: categorical (nominal, ordinal) and numerical (discrete, continuous) and which summaries fit each

tasks.title: Summarise a table of fresher job offers in ₹ LPA: mean, median, SD, IQR and outliers, then explain which to report

topics.title: Probability rules and common distributions
topics.summary_md: Probability is the language behind every test and model. Learn the addition and multiplication rules, conditional probability and **Bayes’ theorem**, then the distributions that appear most: **binomial** for counts of successes, **Poisson** for events per interval and **normal** for many measurements and averages.
key_points: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) only when A and B are independent.
P(A | B) is not the same as P(B | A); Bayes’ theorem converts one into the other.
In a normal distribution about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values lie within 1, 2 and 3 SDs.
Binomial: fixed n independent trials, each with the same success probability p.
learn_items: Basic rules: sample space, complement P(not A) = 1 − P(A) and the addition rule for overlapping events
Independence: multiply probabilities only for independent events, and spot when events are dependent
Conditional probability: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B), worked from a two-way table
Bayes’ theorem: update a prior with evidence, e.g. the chance of a disease given a positive test result
Expected value: the probability-weighted average outcome, e.g. of a game or a lottery ticket
Binomial distribution: mean np and variance np(1 − p) for counting successes in n trials
Poisson distribution: counts of events in a fixed interval with a known average rate λ
Normal distribution: shape, the 68–95–99.7 rule and using z-scores to find a probability

tasks.title: Work out the chance a flagged UPI transaction is really fraud from a hypothetical base rate and detector accuracy
Simulate 10,000 rounds of 10 coin tosses in Python or a sheet and compare the histogram with the binomial formula

topics.title: Sampling, the central limit theorem and confidence intervals
topics.summary_md: We almost never see the whole population, so we estimate from a sample. The **central limit theorem** says that sample means are roughly normal for large enough samples, whatever the shape of the data. That lets us attach a **standard error** and a **confidence interval** to an estimate instead of reporting a bare number.
key_points: Standard error of the mean = SD / √n: quadrupling the sample halves it.
A 95% interval is roughly estimate ± 1.96 standard errors for large samples.
A biased sample stays biased however large it is.
95% describes the method: about 95 of 100 such intervals would contain the true value.
learn_items: Population and sample: parameter versus statistic, and why we estimate parameters from samples
Sampling methods: simple random, stratified, cluster and convenience sampling, and the bias each can bring
Sampling distribution: the spread of a statistic such as the mean across many repeated samples
Central limit theorem: sample means are approximately normal for large n, even when the data is skewed
Standard error: SD / √n for a mean and √(p(1 − p) / n) for a proportion
Confidence interval for a mean: estimate ± critical value × SE, using the t distribution for small samples
Interpreting intervals: what 95% confidence does and does not mean, and how width depends on n and spread

tasks.title: Draw repeated samples from a skewed list of auto-rickshaw fares and plot how the sample means become normal as n grows
Compute a 95% confidence interval for the share of students in a campus survey who prefer remote internships

topics.title: Hypothesis tests, p-values and errors
topics.summary_md: A hypothesis test asks whether the data is surprising if nothing is really going on. State a **null** and an **alternative**, choose a significance level (often 0.05), compute a test statistic and its **p-value**, and decide. Know which test fits which data: t-tests for means, z-tests or chi-square for proportions and counts.
key_points: A p-value is P(data at least this extreme | the null is true), not P(null is true).
Type I error: rejecting a true null (false positive); Type II: missing a real effect.
Statistically significant is not the same as large or important.
Running many tests at 0.05 makes some false positives likely; correct for it.
learn_items: Null and alternative hypotheses: write them for a real question, and one-sided versus two-sided tests
Test statistic and p-value: what the p-value measures and how it is compared with alpha
Type I and Type II errors: alpha, beta and power = 1 − beta, and how sample size changes power
One-sample and two-sample t-tests: compare means, and why Welch’s t-test is the safe default for unequal variances
Paired t-test: before-and-after measurements on the same people
Chi-square test of independence: test whether two categorical variables are related, from a contingency table
Two-proportion z-test: compare conversion rates between two groups
Multiple testing: why 20 tests at 0.05 expect about one false positive, and the Bonferroni correction

tasks.title: Test whether two sections of a class have different mean exam marks with Welch’s t-test and report the p-value and interval
Use a chi-square test on a branch × placed/not placed table to see if placement depends on branch

topics.title: Correlation and simple linear regression
topics.summary_md: Correlation measures how strongly two numeric variables move together; regression fits a line to predict one from the other. Learn to read a **slope**, **intercept** and **R²**, to check **residuals**, and to say clearly why a correlation alone never proves cause, because confounders and reverse causation are always possible.
key_points: Pearson r runs from −1 to 1 and measures only linear association.
The slope is the expected change in y for a one-unit increase in x.
R² is the share of variance in y explained by the model.
Correlation is not causation: look for confounders and reverse causation.
learn_items: Scatter plots: read direction, strength, form and outliers before computing anything
Pearson and Spearman correlation: linear versus rank-based, and when outliers or curves call for Spearman
Causation traps: confounding variables, reverse causation and spurious correlations in time series
Least squares line: y = a + bx, and how the line minimises the sum of squared residuals
Interpreting coefficients: slope, intercept and their units in a real example
R² and residuals: what R² means, and residual plots that reveal curves or uneven spread
Multiple regression: holding other variables constant, and the danger of extrapolating beyond the data

tasks.title: Fit a line predicting flat rent from carpet area on a city rentals table, then interpret slope, R² and residuals

topics.title: Profiling data and fixing types, formats and duplicates
topics.summary_md: Cleaning starts with **profiling**: count rows, check types, nulls and distinct values, and look at the extremes. Then fix what profiling found: numbers stored as text, mixed date formats, inconsistent spellings and duplicate records. Write each fix as a rule in code or a query so it can be rerun on the next file.
key_points: Profile before you clean: row count, types, nulls, distinct values, min and max.
Indian dates are usually day-first; parse them explicitly instead of letting a tool guess.
Deduplicate on a clear business key, and decide which copy to keep.
Never overwrite the raw file; clean into a new table.
learn_items: Profiling: row and column counts, data types, null counts, distinct counts and min/max per column
Type fixes: turn "₹1,20,000" or "12 LPA" into numbers by stripping symbols and commas before converting
Dates: parse DD-MM-YYYY versus MM-DD-YYYY explicitly, and store dates in ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD)
Text standardisation: trim spaces, fix case and map variants such as "Bangalore" and "Bengaluru" to one value
Categorical checks: list distinct values to find typos and unexpected categories
Duplicates: exact duplicates versus duplicates on a key such as email, and keeping the latest record
Validation rules: ranges, allowed values and unique keys checked after every cleaning step

tasks.title: Profile and clean a messy restaurant listings table: costs as text, city spellings, duplicate outlets and mixed dates

topics.title: Missing values, outliers and reproducible cleaning
topics.summary_md: Missing values and outliers need a decision, not a reflex. Find out **why** a value is missing, then drop, impute or flag it, and check whether an extreme value is an error or a real event before you cap or remove it. Record every rule in a cleaning log so others can reproduce and question your choices.
key_points: Hidden nulls such as 0, −1, 999, "NA" or "-" must be turned into real nulls first.
Imputing the median keeps the row but shrinks variance; add a flag column when you impute.
Remove an outlier only when it is an error, not because it is inconvenient.
A cleaning log lists each rule, why it exists and how many rows it changed.
learn_items: Hidden missing values: find placeholders such as 0, −1, 999, blank strings and "NA" and convert them to nulls
Why data is missing: completely at random, related to other columns, or related to the missing value itself
Drop, impute or flag: when each is right, and imputing with the median or a group median
Time series gaps: forward fill and interpolation, and when they would invent data
Outlier detection: the IQR rule, z-scores above about 3, and domain rules such as an age above 120
Outlier handling: fix errors, cap (winsorise) heavy tails or keep real extremes and report them
Reproducibility: a scripted pipeline, assertions after each step and a cleaning log with row counts

tasks.title: Clean a daily city weather table with gaps and 999 placeholders: decide per column to drop, impute or flag
Write a rerunnable cleaning script for a hostel fee payments file with assertions and a cleaning log

topics.title: NumPy arrays: creation, indexing and vectorised maths
topics.summary_md: A NumPy `ndarray` holds values of one type in contiguous memory, so maths on whole arrays runs in fast compiled loops. Learn to create arrays, read `.shape` and `.dtype`, slice and filter with boolean masks, and aggregate along an axis. Replacing Python loops with vectorised expressions is the core habit.
key_points: Check .shape and .dtype whenever a result looks wrong.
Basic slices are views: changing them changes the original array; use .copy() when needed.
Combine boolean conditions with & and |, with brackets around each condition.
axis=0 aggregates down the rows (one result per column).
learn_items: Creating arrays: np.array, np.arange, np.linspace, np.zeros, np.ones and np.full
Attributes: shape, ndim, dtype and size, and how dtype affects memory and precision
Indexing and slicing: a[i], a[i, j], a[1:4], a[:, 0] and negative indices on 1-D and 2-D arrays
Views versus copies: slices share memory, fancy indexing returns a copy, and .copy() makes one explicitly
Vectorised operations: element-wise +, *, ** and universal functions such as np.sqrt, np.exp and np.log
Boolean masks: a[a > 0], combining conditions with & and |, and counting matches with .sum()
Aggregations: sum, mean, std, min, max, argmax along axis=0 and axis=1
Reshaping: reshape, ravel, transpose (.T) and adding an axis with np.newaxis

tasks.title: Load a 2-D array of marks (students × subjects) and compute subject averages, toppers and students below 40 without loops

topics.title: Broadcasting, np.where and random numbers
topics.summary_md: **Broadcasting** lets NumPy combine arrays of different shapes without copying data, for example subtracting each column’s mean from a whole matrix. Add conditional logic with `np.where`, handle NaN with the `nan`-aware functions, and use a seeded random generator for simulations you can reproduce.
key_points: Broadcasting compares shapes from the right; sizes must match or one must be 1.
np.where(cond, x, y) is the vectorised if-else.
NaN spreads through sum and mean; use np.nansum and np.nanmean.
Create random numbers with rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) for reproducible results.
learn_items: Broadcasting rules: align shapes from the right; each dimension must be equal or 1, e.g. (4, 3) with (3,)
Common broadcasts: centring columns with X − X.mean(axis=0) and scaling rows with keepdims=True
np.where: vectorised if-else to build a new array from a condition
Missing values: np.nan, np.isnan, np.nanmean and np.nansum
Sorting and ranking: np.sort, np.argsort and np.unique with return_counts=True
Combining arrays: np.concatenate, np.vstack, np.hstack and np.stack
Random numbers: np.random.default_rng(seed), rng.integers, rng.normal and rng.choice
Matrix maths: the @ operator for matrix multiplication versus * for element-wise multiplication

tasks.title: Standardise every column of a city air-quality readings array to z-scores with broadcasting and np.nanmean
Simulate one million dice rolls with a seeded generator and compare the frequencies with the expected 1/6

topics.title: pandas DataFrames: loading, inspecting and selecting
topics.summary_md: A pandas **DataFrame** is a table of typed columns with a row index. Load data with `read_csv`, inspect it with `info()` and `describe()`, and select rows and columns with `.loc` (labels) and `.iloc` (positions). Boolean filtering and `sort_values` cover most first questions you will ask of a dataset.
key_points: .loc selects by label and includes the end of a slice; .iloc selects by position and excludes it.
Combine filter conditions with & and |, with brackets around each one.
Assign with df.loc[mask, "col"] = value, not chained indexing like df[mask]["col"] = value.
df.info() shows types and non-null counts: run it first on every new file.
learn_items: Series and DataFrame: columns as Series, the index, and df.shape, df.columns and df.dtypes
Loading: pd.read_csv with sep, usecols, dtype and parse_dates, plus pd.read_excel
Inspecting: head, tail, sample, info, describe and value_counts on a new dataset
Selecting columns: df["col"] versus df[["a", "b"]], and renaming with df.rename(columns=...)
.loc and .iloc: select rows and columns by label or position, and how slice ends differ
Boolean filtering: df[(df.city == "Pune") & (df.price > 500)], isin, between and df.query
Sorting and new columns: sort_values by several columns and creating columns from vectorised expressions
Assignment rules: why chained assignment fails under pandas copy-on-write and how .loc fixes it

topics.title: pandas: grouping, aggregating and text columns
topics.summary_md: `groupby` is pandas’ version of SQL `GROUP BY`: split rows into groups, apply an aggregation and combine the results. Use named aggregations for readable output, `transform` to add a group-level value back to every row, and the `.str` and `.dt` accessors to derive grouping keys from text and dates.
key_points: groupby + agg = SQL GROUP BY; named aggregations give clear column names.
transform returns a result the same length as the original, so it can become a new column.
Use as_index=False or reset_index() to get a flat table back.
value_counts(normalize=True) gives shares instead of counts.
learn_items: groupby basics: df.groupby("team")["runs"].sum() and grouping by several columns
Named aggregations: .agg(total=("runs", "sum"), matches=("match_id", "nunique")) for readable output
Flat output: as_index=False versus reset_index(), and sorting groups by the aggregated value
transform: add each row’s group mean or share of group total as a new column
filter on groups: keep only groups that meet a condition, such as teams with at least 10 matches
String accessor: .str.lower, .str.strip, .str.contains and .str.extract to tidy and parse text columns
Date accessor: pd.to_datetime then .dt.year, .dt.month and .dt.day_name for grouping by time
Category counts: value_counts with normalize=True and pd.crosstab for two-way counts

Add a column giving each product’s share of its category’s revenue using groupby and transform

topics.title: pandas joins, reshaping and time series
topics.summary_md: Real analysis combines tables and changes their shape. `merge` joins DataFrames like SQL joins, `concat` stacks them, and `pivot_table` and `melt` switch between long and wide formats. For time-indexed data, `resample` and `rolling` give weekly totals and moving averages in one line.
key_points: merge = SQL JOIN; check row counts before and after to catch duplicate keys.
validate="many_to_one" makes merge fail loudly if the right-hand keys are not unique.
Long format (one row per observation) is easier to group and plot; wide suits reports.
resample needs a DatetimeIndex (or the on= argument) and a frequency such as "W" or "MS".
learn_items: merge: inner, left, right and outer joins with on, left_on and right_on, and suffixes for clashing names
Join checks: validate="one_to_one" or "many_to_one", and indicator=True to find unmatched rows
concat: stacking monthly files vertically and resetting the index with ignore_index=True
pivot_table: index, columns, values, aggfunc and fill_value to build a wide summary
melt: turn wide columns such as month names back into long rows for grouping
Time index: set a datetime index, slice by date strings and resample("W").sum() for weekly totals
Rolling windows: rolling(7).mean() for a 7-period moving average, and pct_change for growth

tasks.title: Merge an orders table with a customers table, find orders without a customer, and pivot revenue by state and month
Reshape a wide table of monthly UPI transaction counts by bank into long format and plot a 3-month rolling average

topics.title: Choosing the right chart for the question
topics.summary_md: A chart answers a question, so pick it from the question: **bar** to compare categories, **line** for change over time, **histogram** or box plot for a distribution, **scatter** for a relationship. Then design for honesty and clarity: zero baselines for bars, direct labels, and colour used to highlight the one thing that matters.
key_points: Bar = compare, line = trend, histogram = distribution, scatter = relationship.
Bar charts must start at zero; line charts may zoom in if the axis is clearly labelled.
Grey out the context and colour only the series you want the reader to notice.
Avoid 3D effects, dual y-axes and pie charts with many slices.
learn_items: Comparison: sorted horizontal bar charts for categories with long names, and grouped versus stacked bars
Change over time: line charts, consistent time intervals and when a column chart suits few periods
Distribution: histograms (bin width matters), box plots and when to show individual points
Relationship: scatter plots, a trend line and using size or colour for a third variable sparingly
Part-to-whole: 100% stacked bars or a pie with at most a few slices, and why angles are hard to compare
Honest axes: zero baseline for bars, no truncated axes that exaggerate, and no dual y-axes
Clutter and focus: remove heavy gridlines, borders and legends where direct labels work; highlight with colour
Accessibility: colour-blind-safe palettes, enough contrast and never colour as the only cue

topics.title: Plotting in Python with Matplotlib and seaborn
topics.summary_md: Matplotlib is the base plotting library in Python and seaborn builds statistical charts on top of it. Use the object-oriented API (`fig, ax = plt.subplots()`) so every chart is controllable, plot from a tidy pandas DataFrame, and finish each chart with a title that states the finding, labelled axes and a highlight colour.
key_points: Use fig, ax = plt.subplots() and call methods on ax rather than relying on plt state.
seaborn works best with long-format DataFrames and the hue argument for groups.
A title that states the finding beats a title that names the chart.
Small multiples (subplots) beat one chart with many overlapping lines.
learn_items: Figure and Axes: fig, ax = plt.subplots(), ax.bar, ax.plot, ax.scatter and ax.hist
Labelling: ax.set_title, ax.set_xlabel, ax.set_ylabel, tick formatting and rotating long labels
Highlighting: grey for context, one accent colour, and ax.annotate to label the key point
seaborn basics: histplot, boxplot, barplot, lineplot and scatterplot with x, y, hue and data
Small multiples: plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, sharey=True) and seaborn relplot or catplot with col=
Plotting from pandas: df.plot(kind=...) for quick looks and when to switch to Matplotlib for control
Exporting: fig.tight_layout, savefig with dpi and a format (PNG for slides, SVG for the web)

topics.title: BI basics: connecting data and building a first report
topics.summary_md: BI tools such as **Power BI**, **Tableau** and **Looker Studio** connect to data, shape it and turn it into interactive reports that others open in a browser. The workflow is the same in each: connect, clean and type the data, build visuals, add filters and slicers, then publish and share with the right people.
key_points: Clean and type data before building visuals; a wrong type breaks every chart that uses it.
Filters can apply to one visual, one page or the whole report.
Cards show one key number; tables and matrices show detail.
Publishing makes the report a shared, refreshable web page, not a file sent by email.
learn_items: Tool landscape: Power BI, Tableau and Looker Studio, what each is commonly used for and their free options
Connecting data: import an Excel or CSV file and connect to a database or Google Sheet
Shaping data: Power Query in Power BI (or the data source pane in Tableau) to set types and remove columns
Core visuals: card, bar, line, table and matrix, and dragging fields to axes and values
Default aggregation: why a numeric field is summed automatically and how to change it to average or count
Filters and slicers: visual-level, page-level and report-level filters, and slicers for users
Publishing: publish to the web service, share with specific people and set a scheduled refresh

topics.title: Data models, relationships and DAX measures
topics.summary_md: Good dashboards rest on a clean **data model**: one fact table of events joined to dimension tables that describe them, a **star schema**. Define metrics once as **measures** (DAX in Power BI, calculated fields in Tableau) so every visual uses the same logic. Understanding filter context is what makes DAX click.
key_points: Star schema: fact tables hold events and numbers; dimensions hold descriptions to filter by.
Relationships should be one-to-many from dimension to fact, filtering in one direction.
A measure is computed at query time in the current filter context; a calculated column is stored per row.
Use DIVIDE(a, b) in DAX instead of a / b to handle division by zero safely.
learn_items: Star schema: identify fact tables (orders, sales) and dimensions (date, product, customer) in a dataset
Relationships: one-to-many, cardinality, single versus both-direction filtering, and why single is safer
Date table: create a continuous calendar table and mark it as the date table for time calculations
Measures versus calculated columns: when each is right, and why measures are preferred for totals and ratios
Basic DAX: SUM, COUNTROWS, DISTINCTCOUNT, AVERAGE and DIVIDE in measures
CALCULATE: change the filter context, e.g. sales for one region or with a filter removed via ALL
Tableau equivalents: calculated fields and a first LOD expression such as {FIXED [Customer] : SUM([Sales])}

tasks.title: Model a sales dataset as a star schema with a date table and write measures for revenue, orders and average order value
Write a CALCULATE measure for each region’s share of all-India revenue and show it in a matrix

topics.title: Dashboard design, drill-downs and sharing
topics.summary_md: A dashboard should help a named person make a recurring decision. Put the key numbers first, give each visual one job, and let users explore with cross-filtering, drill-down and tooltips instead of extra pages. Before sharing, add time comparisons, check performance and restrict rows with **row-level security** where needed.
key_points: Start from the decision and the user, then choose the five or six visuals that support it.
Place headline KPIs top left; people scan from there.
Compare against something: last period, target or last year.
Row-level security limits which rows each viewer can see in the same report.
learn_items: Requirements: write the user, the decision and the three questions a dashboard must answer before building
Layout: KPI cards at the top, trends next, detail tables last, aligned to a grid with consistent colours
Interactivity: cross-filtering between visuals, drill-down through a hierarchy and drill-through pages
Comparisons: time intelligence such as SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR and TOTALYTD, and variance against target
Tooltips and bookmarks: add context on hover and save views for common questions
Performance: reduce visuals per page, remove unused columns and prefer measures to heavy calculated columns
Governance: row-level security roles, scheduled refresh and naming measures clearly for other authors
