topics.title: Structuring an insight: answer first
topics.summary_md: Analysis matters only if it changes a decision. Start from the audience and the decision they face, write the **big idea** in one sentence, and lead with the answer and recommendation before the evidence. Quantify the impact and state the caveats plainly so the reader can trust the conclusion.
key_points: Lead with the answer and recommendation, then give the supporting evidence.
The big idea is one complete sentence with a point of view and what is at stake.
Quantify impact in the reader’s terms: rupees, users, hours or risk.
State assumptions and limitations openly; hidden caveats destroy trust later.
learn_items: Audience and decision: who will read it, what they already know and what they must decide
The big idea: one sentence that states your point and why it matters now
Pyramid principle: answer at the top, three supporting points, evidence under each
Situation, complication, resolution: a short narrative frame for opening a presentation or memo
So what: turn every finding into an implication or action, not a description of a chart
Quantifying impact: size the opportunity or risk with transparent, simple arithmetic
Caveats: sample limits, data gaps and correlation versus causation, stated once and clearly

tasks.title: Write a one-sentence big idea and a three-point pyramid for an analysis of why cart abandonment rose on mobile

topics.title: Action titles, annotated charts and decision memos
topics.summary_md: Turn the structure into slides or a memo that a busy reader can follow in two minutes. Give each slide an **action title** that states its takeaway, keep one message per chart, annotate the key point on the chart itself, and move methods into an appendix. Tailor depth: leaders want the so-what, analysts want the method.
key_points: An action title is a full sentence takeaway, e.g. "Repeat orders fell after the fee change".
One chart, one message: if a chart needs two titles, split it.
Reading only the slide titles in order should tell the whole story.
Put methods and extra cuts in an appendix, ready for questions.
learn_items: Action titles: rewrite topic titles like "Revenue by month" into takeaways that state what changed and why
Storyboarding: sketch the slide titles in order on paper before making any chart
Annotation: mark the key point on the chart with a label or callout instead of explaining it aloud
Decluttering: remove decoration and use grey for context and one colour for the message
Executive summary memo: answer, three supporting points, impact, risks and the ask, on one page
Audience depth: what to show leaders versus technical reviewers, and using an appendix for the rest
Handling questions: prepare for "how sure are we?", "compared with what?" and "what would change your mind?"

tasks.title: Turn an analysis of a college canteen’s sales data into a five-slide deck with action titles and annotated charts

topics.title: Warehouses, ELT and dimensional modelling
topics.summary_md: Analytics engineers turn raw data in a cloud **warehouse** (BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift, Databricks) into clean, trusted tables. Modern teams load raw data first and transform it inside the warehouse (**ELT**). Dimensional modelling organises the results into **facts** and **dimensions** at a clearly stated **grain**.
key_points: OLTP databases serve the app; OLAP warehouses serve analysis with columnar storage.
ELT loads raw data first, then transforms it in the warehouse with SQL.
State the grain of every fact table: what exactly one row represents.
Facts hold measurable events; dimensions hold the who, what, where and when.
learn_items: OLTP versus OLAP: transactional databases versus analytical warehouses, and why columnar storage suits analysis
ETL versus ELT: where transformation happens, and why cheap warehouse compute made ELT the default
The modern data stack: ingestion tools, a warehouse, a transformation layer such as dbt, and BI on top
Grain: declare what one row of a table means, e.g. one row per order line
Fact tables: additive, semi-additive and non-additive measures, and foreign keys to dimensions
Dimension tables: descriptive attributes, surrogate keys and a conformed date dimension
Slowly changing dimensions: Type 1 overwrites, Type 2 keeps history with valid_from and valid_to columns

tasks.title: Design a star schema for a food delivery app: state the grain, list facts and dimensions, and sketch the keys

topics.title: dbt models, sources, ref() and layers
topics.summary_md: **dbt** turns SQL `SELECT` statements into tables and views in your warehouse, in dependency order. Declare raw tables as **sources**, build models that reference each other with `ref()`, and organise them in layers from staging to marts. dbt works out the DAG from those references, so you never hard-code table names.
key_points: A dbt model is one .sql file containing one SELECT; dbt writes the DDL.
Use {{ ref("model") }} and {{ source("src", "table") }}, never hard-coded table names.
Staging models clean and rename one source each; marts serve business users.
Materialisations: view, table, incremental and ephemeral.
learn_items: Project layout: dbt_project.yml, the models folder, profiles for the warehouse connection and dbt Core versus Cloud
Sources: declare raw tables in YAML and select from them with {{ source("app", "orders") }}
Models and ref(): one SELECT per file, {{ ref("stg_orders") }} and how dbt builds the DAG from refs
Layers and naming: stg_ staging, int_ intermediate, and fct_ and dim_ marts, with a clear job for each layer
Staging rules: one model per source table, rename columns, cast types and no joins
Materialisations: view, table, incremental and ephemeral, set in config() or dbt_project.yml
Commands: dbt run, dbt build, dbt compile and selecting models with --select and the + graph operator
Jinja basics: variables, simple macros and reading the compiled SQL in the target folder

tasks.title: Set up a dbt project on DuckDB with an e-commerce dataset: two sources, three staging models and a fct_orders mart

topics.title: dbt tests, documentation and incremental models
topics.summary_md: Trusted data needs tests and documentation that live next to the code. Add generic tests such as `unique` and `not_null` in YAML, write singular tests for business rules, check source freshness, and generate docs with lineage. Large event tables use **incremental** models, and **snapshots** record history for changing source rows.
key_points: Every primary key gets unique and not_null tests.
dbt build runs models and their tests in DAG order, stopping downstream models when a test fails.
Incremental models process only new rows; is_incremental() guards the filter.
Snapshots implement Type 2 history for source tables that change in place.
learn_items: Generic data tests: unique, not_null, accepted_values and relationships, declared under data_tests in YAML
Singular tests: a SQL file that returns failing rows, e.g. orders with a negative amount
Unit tests: check a model’s logic on small mocked inputs before it touches real data
Source freshness: loaded_at_field with warn_after and error_after thresholds
Documentation: model and column descriptions in YAML, dbt docs generate and the lineage graph
Incremental models: materialized="incremental", is_incremental(), unique_key and full refreshes
Snapshots: capture changes to a source table over time with the timestamp or check strategy
CI habits: run changed models and their children on each pull request before merging

tasks.title: Add unique, not_null, relationships and a singular test to your dbt e-commerce project, then make one fail on purpose
Convert an app events model into an incremental model keyed on event ID and check it on a second load

topics.title: Designing an A/B test: hypothesis, metrics and sample size
topics.summary_md: An A/B test randomly splits users between versions to measure a change’s causal effect. Write the hypothesis, choose the randomisation unit, one **primary metric** and a few **guardrails** before launch, then size the test from the baseline rate and the **minimum detectable effect**. Run it for whole weeks to cover weekday and weekend behaviour.
key_points: Randomise at the unit you analyse, usually the user, not the page view.
Pick the primary metric and the stopping rule before launch, never after.
Halving the minimum detectable effect needs roughly four times the sample.
Common defaults: alpha 0.05 and 80% power.
learn_items: Hypothesis: write "if we change X for users Y, metric Z will rise because…" before building anything
Randomisation unit: user, session or device, and why splitting by page view leaks users between groups
Metrics: one primary metric, secondary metrics and guardrails such as latency, refunds or unsubscribes
Minimum detectable effect: the smallest change worth detecting, chosen from business value
Sample size: how baseline rate, MDE, alpha and power set users per group, using a standard calculator formula
Duration: users per day sets the run time; run whole weeks and avoid festival-sale weeks unless intended
A/A tests and sample ratio mismatch: check that the split works and groups receive the planned shares

tasks.title: Write a one-page test plan for a new checkout button on a ticket booking site: hypothesis, metrics, MDE, sample size, duration

topics.title: Reading A/B results and avoiding common pitfalls
topics.summary_md: Reading a test means comparing the groups with the right test, reporting the **lift with a confidence interval**, and asking whether it is big enough to matter. Most wrong decisions come from pitfalls: **peeking** and stopping early, testing many metrics or segments without correction, sample ratio mismatch and novelty effects.
key_points: Report the effect size with a confidence interval, not just "significant".
Peeking and stopping at the first p < 0.05 inflates false positives; use a fixed horizon or a sequential method.
A sample ratio mismatch means the split is broken; do not trust the result.
Segment results found after the fact are hypotheses for the next test, not conclusions.
learn_items: Comparing conversion rates: a two-proportion z-test or chi-square test, and absolute versus relative lift
Confidence interval for the difference: read whether it excludes zero and how wide it is
Practical significance: compare the interval with the smallest effect worth shipping
Peeking: why repeated looks inflate false positives, and sequential testing as the fix
Multiple comparisons: many metrics, variants or segments, and corrections such as Bonferroni
Sample ratio mismatch: test the observed split with a chi-square test before reading any metric
Novelty and primacy effects: watch the effect over time, and why some changes need longer tests
Variance reduction: CUPED uses pre-experiment data to narrow intervals with the same sample

tasks.title: Analyse a hypothetical test of 50,000 users per group: compute the lift, z-test, interval and an SRM check
Simulate A/A tests checked every day and count how often peeking finds a false winner

topics.title: Product metrics, event tracking and funnels
topics.summary_md: Product analytics explains how users move through a product. It starts with a **tracking plan**: consistently named events with properties and a user ID. On top of those events you define metrics such as active users and a **North Star metric**, and build **funnels** that show where users drop off between steps.
key_points: A tracking plan names each event, its properties and when it fires, before engineers build it.
North Star = the value users get, supported by a few input metrics teams can move.
Funnel conversion depends on the step order and the time window you choose.
DAU/MAU (stickiness) shows how often monthly users return.
learn_items: Event tracking: object_action names such as order_placed, event properties and user properties
User identity: anonymous IDs, merging them with a user ID at sign-up, and why it matters for counts
Activity metrics: DAU, WAU, MAU and stickiness (DAU/MAU), and defining what "active" means
North Star metric: a single measure of delivered value with three or four input metrics beneath it
Funnels: step-to-step and overall conversion, conversion windows and strict versus any-order steps
Diagnosing drop-off: segment a funnel by platform, source or city to find where users leave
Frameworks: AARRR (acquisition, activation, retention, referral, revenue) and vanity versus actionable metrics

tasks.title: Write a tracking plan of 10 events for a college events app, with names, properties and the funnel they feed
From an events table, compute a 4-step sign-up funnel in SQL or pandas with step and overall conversion

topics.title: Cohorts, retention curves and engagement analysis
topics.summary_md: Retention shows whether users keep getting value. Group users into **cohorts** by sign-up week, track what share return in later periods, and read the **retention curve**: a curve that flattens means a group of users has found lasting value. Segment cohorts and track feature adoption to find what drives the users who stay.
key_points: A healthy retention curve flattens; one that keeps falling towards zero signals no product fit.
Compare cohorts over time: newer cohorts retaining better means the product is improving.
State the retention definition: N-day, unbounded or bracketed.
Behaviour linked to retention is a hypothesis; confirm it with an experiment.
learn_items: Cohorts: group users by first activity week or month, or by acquisition channel
Retention definitions: N-day (on exactly day N), unbounded (on or after day N) and bracketed (within a range)
Cohort table: read the triangle chart by row (one cohort over time) and by column (cohorts at the same age)
Retention curves: flattening versus decaying curves and what each says about product fit
Churn and resurrection: users who stop and users who come back, and how they change active-user counts
Feature adoption and segmentation: compare retention of users who used a feature with those who did not
Cohort SQL: compute a weekly retention table from an events table with date truncation and a self-join

tasks.title: Build a weekly retention cohort table and curve from a learning app’s events table in SQL or pandas

topics.title: Vectors, matrices and matrix multiplication
topics.summary_md: In ML a data point is a **vector** of features and a dataset is a **matrix** with one row per example. Most model maths is matrix multiplication, so you must be able to predict the shape of every product before you compute it. The dot product measures how aligned two vectors are and underlies similarity search and every linear layer.
key_points: An (m x n) matrix times an (n x p) matrix gives (m x p); the inner sizes must match.
Dot product a·b = |a||b|cos θ: positive when aligned, zero when orthogonal.
A dataset X has shape (n_samples, n_features); predictions of a linear model are X @ w.
learn_items: Vectors: a list of numbers as a point or direction; add, subtract and scale element-wise
Norms: L2 length sqrt(sum of squares), L1 sum of absolute values; normalise to unit length
Dot product: sum of element-wise products; a·b = |a||b|cos θ; cosine similarity divides by both norms
Matrices: shape (rows, columns), transpose swaps them, identity matrix leaves vectors unchanged
Matrix multiplication: (m x n)(n x p) = (m x p); entry (i, j) is row i dot column j; AB is not BA
Data as a matrix: rows are examples, columns are features; X @ w gives one prediction per row
NumPy: np.array, .shape, @ for matmul, * for element-wise, broadcasting a (n,) vector across rows

tasks.title: In NumPy, create random matrices of shapes (4,3) and (3,2), predict each product shape, then compute and check it
Write a cosine similarity function without loops and use it to find the most similar of five short word-count vectors

topics.title: Linear maps, rank, inverses and eigenvectors
topics.summary_md: A matrix is a **linear map** that rotates, scales or squashes space. Rank tells you how many independent directions survive, and only square full-rank matrices have an inverse. **Eigenvectors** are directions a matrix only stretches, which is the idea behind PCA and many stability arguments in deep learning.
key_points: Columns are linearly independent when none is a combination of the others; rank counts independent columns.
A square matrix is invertible only if its determinant is non-zero (full rank).
Av = λv: an eigenvector v keeps its direction and is scaled by the eigenvalue λ.
Prefer np.linalg.solve(A, b) to computing inv(A) @ b: it is faster and more stable.
learn_items: Linear map: matrix times vector transforms space; columns show where the basis vectors land
Linear independence and span: which vectors can be built from a set by scaling and adding
Rank: number of independent columns; duplicated or derived features make a data matrix rank-deficient
Determinant: area/volume scale factor; zero means space is squashed and no inverse exists
Inverse and solving Ax = b: use np.linalg.solve; normal equations w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy for linear regression
Eigenvectors and eigenvalues: Av = λv; compute with np.linalg.eig, or eigh for symmetric matrices
Symmetric matrices: covariance matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors

tasks.title: Fit a line to 50 noisy synthetic points by solving the normal equations with np.linalg.solve and plot the result
Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a 2x2 symmetric matrix by hand, then verify Av = λv in NumPy

topics.title: Derivatives, partial derivatives and the chain rule
topics.summary_md: Training a model means asking how the loss changes when each parameter changes, which is a **derivative**. With many parameters you take **partial derivatives** and collect them into the **gradient**. The **chain rule** lets you differentiate functions built from simpler functions, and it is exactly what backpropagation automates.
key_points: The derivative is the slope: how much the output changes per small change in the input.
The gradient is the vector of partial derivatives and points in the direction of steepest increase.
Chain rule: d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x)) · g′(x); backpropagation applies it layer by layer.
learn_items: Derivative as slope: limit of (f(x+h) − f(x)) / h; know the rules for x^n, e^x, ln x, sums and products
Partial derivatives: differentiate with respect to one variable while holding the others fixed
Gradient: vector of all partial derivatives; it points uphill and is zero at a minimum or maximum
Chain rule: d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x))·g′(x); with several paths, add the contributions of each path
Useful derivatives: sigmoid σ′ = σ(1 − σ); ReLU′ = 1 for x > 0 else 0; d/dw of (wx − y)² = 2x(wx − y)
MSE gradient for linear regression: ∇w = (2/n) Xᵀ(Xw − y); check the shape matches w
Numerical gradient check: compare with (f(x+h) − f(x−h)) / 2h for a small h such as 1e-5

tasks.title: Derive the MSE gradient for a linear model by hand, implement it in NumPy and verify it with a numerical gradient check

topics.title: Gradient descent, learning rates and convexity
topics.summary_md: **Gradient descent** repeatedly moves parameters a small step against the gradient of the loss: w ← w − η∇L. The learning rate η decides whether training crawls, converges or diverges. Stochastic and mini-batch variants estimate the gradient from a few examples so each step is cheap, and convex losses guarantee that the minimum found is the global one.
key_points: Update rule: w ← w − η · ∇L(w); stop when the loss stops improving.
Too large a learning rate makes the loss bounce or explode; too small makes training very slow.
Mini-batch gradients are noisy estimates of the full gradient but far cheaper per step.
Convex losses (linear and logistic regression) have one global minimum; neural network losses do not.
learn_items: Update rule: w ← w − η∇L(w); one epoch is one full pass over the training data
Learning rate: plot loss per step for several values (for example 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1) and spot divergence
Batch vs stochastic vs mini-batch: full data per step, one example per step, or a small batch per step
Feature scaling: unscaled features make the loss surface elongated and gradient descent zig-zag
Convexity: any local minimum is global; non-convex losses have local minima and saddle points
Momentum: keep a running average of gradients to speed up along consistent directions
Adam: adapts a per-parameter step size from running means of gradients and squared gradients

tasks.title: Implement batch gradient descent for linear regression in NumPy and plot the loss for three learning rates
Change your implementation to mini-batch SGD with batch size 16 and compare its loss curve with full-batch descent

topics.title: Probability, distributions and maximum likelihood
topics.summary_md: Models output probabilities and losses come from probability. Know conditional probability and **Bayes' theorem**, the common distributions, and expectation and variance. **Maximum likelihood** picks the parameters that make the observed data most probable, and it explains why regression uses squared error and classification uses log loss.
key_points: Bayes: P(A|B) = P(B|A) · P(A) / P(B); the prior matters when events are rare.
Maximising a Gaussian likelihood is the same as minimising mean squared error.
Maximising a Bernoulli likelihood is the same as minimising binary cross-entropy (log loss).
learn_items: Probability rules: joint, marginal and conditional probability; independence means P(A and B) = P(A)P(B)
Bayes' theorem: posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence; work a rare-disease test example by hand
Distributions: Bernoulli, binomial, categorical, uniform and normal (Gaussian) with mean and variance
Expectation and variance: E[X], Var(X) = E[X²] − E[X]²; standard deviation is the square root
Likelihood: probability of the observed data as a function of the parameters; use log-likelihood sums
Maximum likelihood: Gaussian noise gives MSE; Bernoulli labels give binary cross-entropy
Entropy and cross-entropy: average surprise; KL divergence measures how one distribution differs

tasks.title: Simulate a rare-disease screening test in NumPy and check P(disease | positive) against Bayes' theorem
Plot the log-likelihood of a coin's heads probability for 100 simulated flips; check it peaks at the observed ratio

topics.title: Covariance, SVD and principal component analysis
topics.summary_md: The **covariance matrix** describes how features vary together. **PCA** finds the orthogonal directions of greatest variance, which are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, and projects data onto the top few. In practice PCA is computed with the **singular value decomposition** of the centred data matrix.
key_points: Always centre the data (subtract each column mean) before PCA; scale it too if units differ.
Principal components are eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, ordered by eigenvalue.
SVD: X = UΣVᵀ; the rows of Vᵀ are the principal directions of centred X.
learn_items: Covariance: average product of centred features; covariance matrix = XᵀX / (n − 1) for centred X
Correlation: covariance divided by both standard deviations, always between −1 and 1
PCA idea: rotate to directions of maximum variance; components are orthogonal and uncorrelated
Explained variance ratio: eigenvalue / sum of eigenvalues; keep enough components for your goal
SVD: X = UΣVᵀ with orthogonal U and V; singular values squared over (n − 1) equal the eigenvalues
scikit-learn PCA: fit on training data only, then transform validation and test data with it

topics.title: The ML workflow: framing, data splits and baselines
topics.summary_md: Every ML project starts by turning a business question into a prediction task: what is the target, what are the features, and is it **classification** or **regression**? Split the data into **train, validation and test** sets before looking closely, build a trivial **baseline**, and only then try real models. The test set is used once, at the end.
key_points: Supervised learning learns from labelled examples; unsupervised finds structure without labels.
Fit on train, tune on validation, report once on test; never tune on the test set.
A baseline (predict the mean or the majority class) tells you whether a model learned anything.
Split by time for time-dependent data so the model never sees the future.
learn_items: Supervised vs unsupervised vs reinforcement learning: labels, no labels, rewards from actions
Classification vs regression: predicting a category vs a number; pick the task from the target column
Features and target: X is a table of inputs, y the column to predict; each row is one example
Train/validation/test split: fit on train, tune on validation, report once on test
train_test_split: test_size, random_state for reproducibility, stratify=y to keep class ratios
Baselines: DummyClassifier (most frequent) and DummyRegressor (mean) set the bar to beat
scikit-learn API: every estimator has fit(X, y), predict(X), and score(X, y)

topics.title: Linear regression, error metrics and regularisation
topics.summary_md: **Linear regression** predicts a number as a weighted sum of features plus a bias, fitted by minimising mean squared error. Evaluate it with MAE, RMSE and R². When there are many or correlated features, **regularisation** shrinks the weights: Ridge (L2) keeps all features small and Lasso (L1) can set some to exactly zero.
key_points: RMSE punishes large errors more than MAE and is in the same units as the target.
R² compares the model with always predicting the mean; it can be negative on new data.
Ridge (L2) shrinks weights; Lasso (L1) can zero them out and so selects features.
Scale features before regularised models so the penalty treats them equally.
learn_items: Model: ŷ = w·x + b; each weight is the change in prediction per unit change in that feature
Fitting: minimise MSE via the normal equations or gradient descent; LinearRegression in scikit-learn
Metrics: MAE (average absolute error), RMSE (root mean squared error) and R² (variance explained)
Residual plots: residuals vs predictions should look like random noise with no pattern
Polynomial features: PolynomialFeatures adds x², x·z terms so a linear model can fit curves
Ridge (L2) and Lasso (L1): alpha sets penalty strength; larger alpha means simpler models
Scaling for regularisation: StandardScaler before Ridge or Lasso so the penalty treats features equally

tasks.title: Fit LinearRegression, Ridge and Lasso on the California housing dataset and compare their test RMSE and R²
Plot how many Lasso coefficients are exactly zero as alpha increases from 0.001 to 10

topics.title: Logistic regression and classification metrics
topics.summary_md: **Logistic regression** passes a linear score through the sigmoid to output a probability, then a threshold turns it into a class. Accuracy hides problems on **imbalanced** data, so read the **confusion matrix** and use precision, recall, F1 and ROC or PR curves. The threshold is a business choice: missing fraud and blocking a good payment have different costs.
key_points: Precision: of predicted positives, how many were right. Recall: of actual positives, how many were found.
With 1% positives, predicting "negative" always gives 99% accuracy and zero recall.
Moving the threshold trades precision against recall; the default 0.5 is rarely optimal.
PR AUC is more informative than ROC AUC when positives are rare.
learn_items: Logistic regression: p = σ(w·x + b); trained with log loss; predict_proba gives probabilities
Confusion matrix: true/false positives and negatives; confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred) in scikit-learn
Precision, recall and F1: TP / (TP + FP), TP / (TP + FN), and the harmonic mean of the two
Threshold tuning: pick a threshold on validation data that meets a recall or precision target
ROC curve and AUC: true positive rate vs false positive rate over all thresholds
Precision-recall curve and average precision: preferred when the positive class is rare
Imbalance handling: class_weight="balanced", stratified splits, and resampling only the training set
Multiclass: softmax or one-vs-rest; macro vs weighted averaging of precision and recall

tasks.title: Train logistic regression on the breast cancer dataset in scikit-learn, print the confusion matrix and plot the PR curve
Choose the threshold that gives at least 95% recall on the validation set and report the precision you pay for it

topics.title: Decision trees, random forests and gradient boosting
topics.summary_md: A **decision tree** splits the data with yes/no questions on features, choosing splits that make the groups purer. Single trees overfit, so ensembles combine many: a **random forest** averages deep trees trained on bootstrap samples, and **gradient boosting** adds shallow trees one at a time, each fixing the previous errors. Boosted trees are the usual first choice for tabular data.
key_points: Trees need no feature scaling and handle non-linear patterns and interactions naturally.
Random forests reduce variance by averaging; boosting reduces bias by correcting errors in sequence.
Limit max_depth or min_samples_leaf, or a single tree will memorise the training set.
For boosting, a smaller learning rate with more trees and early stopping usually generalises better.
learn_items: Decision tree splits: Gini impurity or entropy for classification, squared error for regression
Overfitting controls: max_depth, min_samples_leaf, and cost-complexity pruning with ccp_alpha
Bagging and random forests: bootstrap samples plus a random subset of features at each split
Out-of-bag score: each tree is tested on the rows it did not see, giving a free validation estimate
Gradient boosting: each new tree fits the residual errors; key knobs are learning_rate, n_estimators, depth
Boosting libraries: HistGradientBoostingClassifier in scikit-learn; XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost
Feature importance: impurity importance is biased; prefer permutation_importance on validation data

tasks.title: On the Titanic dataset, compare a depth-limited decision tree, a random forest and HistGradientBoosting by validation F1
Plot a depth-3 decision tree with sklearn.tree.plot_tree and explain its top three splits in plain words

topics.title: Cross-validation, bias-variance and tuning
topics.summary_md: One validation split can be lucky, so **k-fold cross-validation** averages scores over k different splits. The **bias-variance trade-off** explains under- and overfitting: learning curves show which one you have and whether more data would help. Tune hyperparameters with grid or random search inside cross-validation, then confirm once on the test set.
key_points: Underfitting: both train and validation scores are poor (high bias).
Overfitting: train score much better than validation score (high variance).
Use StratifiedKFold for classification and TimeSeriesSplit for time-ordered data.
Every preprocessing step must be fitted inside each fold, or the scores leak.
learn_items: k-fold cross-validation: k train/validation splits; report the mean and spread of the scores
CV tools: cross_val_score and cross_validate with StratifiedKFold, GroupKFold or TimeSeriesSplit as cv
Bias vs variance: too simple a model underfits, too flexible a model overfits
Learning curves: train and validation score vs training size; a large stable gap means variance
Validation curves: score vs one hyperparameter (for example max_depth) to find the sweet spot
GridSearchCV and RandomizedSearchCV: param grids, scoring, best_params_, refit on all training data
Data leakage: features that encode the target, or scaling fitted on all data before splitting

tasks.title: Tune a random forest with RandomizedSearchCV and 5-fold stratified CV on the breast cancer dataset; test once
Plot a learning curve for logistic regression and a deep decision tree and say which one would gain from more data

topics.title: Feature engineering and scikit-learn pipelines
topics.summary_md: Real data has missing values, categories and text, and models need numbers. Impute, encode and scale with transformers, and combine them per column type with a **ColumnTransformer** inside a **Pipeline**. The pipeline makes preprocessing part of the model, so cross-validation and deployment apply the exact same steps without leakage.
key_points: One-hot encode nominal categories; ordinal encoding implies an order the model will use.
Fit imputers, encoders and scalers on training data only; a Pipeline enforces this.
Set handle_unknown="ignore" so categories unseen in training do not crash predictions.
learn_items: Missing values: SimpleImputer (median for numbers, most_frequent for categories) plus a missing flag
Categorical encoding: OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore") for nominal, OrdinalEncoder for ordered
Scaling: StandardScaler for linear models, SVMs and kNN; tree models do not need it
Derived features: ratios, date parts (day of week, month), counts and log of skewed amounts
ColumnTransformer: apply different steps to numeric and categorical columns by column name
Pipeline: chain preprocessing and model; pass it to cross_val_score or GridSearchCV as one estimator
Saving models: joblib.dump the fitted pipeline and joblib.load it to predict on new rows

topics.title: Clustering with k-means and DBSCAN
topics.summary_md: Unsupervised learning finds structure without labels. **k-means** places k centroids and assigns each point to the nearest one, so it suits round, similar-sized clusters and needs scaled features. **DBSCAN** groups dense regions, finds clusters of any shape and labels outliers as noise. With no labels, judge clusters with the silhouette score and by whether they make sense.
key_points: k-means needs k chosen in advance; try several and compare inertia (elbow) and silhouette.
Scale features first: distance-based methods are dominated by large-valued features.
DBSCAN needs eps and min_samples, not k, and marks outliers with the label -1.
learn_items: k-means algorithm: assign to nearest centroid, move centroids to the mean, repeat until stable
k-means++ initialisation and n_init: several restarts avoid poor local solutions
Choosing k: elbow plot of inertia_ and silhouette_score (from −1 to 1, higher is better)
DBSCAN: core points have at least min_samples neighbours within eps; others are border or noise
Hierarchical clustering: agglomerative merging and reading a dendrogram
Uses: customer segmentation, anomaly detection, and cluster IDs as features for supervised models

tasks.title: Cluster a table of customer income and spending score with k-means, pick k by silhouette, describe each segment

topics.title: kNN, SVMs and Naive Bayes
topics.summary_md: Three classic models still appear in interviews and small projects. **k-nearest neighbours** predicts from the closest training points, **support vector machines** find the widest-margin boundary and use kernels for curved boundaries, and **Naive Bayes** applies Bayes' theorem assuming independent features, which works well for text. Know when each fits and what to tune.
key_points: kNN stores the training set; prediction is slow on large data and needs scaled features.
SVM: C trades margin width against training errors; the RBF kernel gives non-linear boundaries.
Naive Bayes is fast and strong for word-count text features despite its independence assumption.
learn_items: kNN: choose k by cross-validation; small k overfits, large k oversmooths; scale features first
Distance metrics: Euclidean, Manhattan and cosine; the curse of dimensionality weakens distances
Linear SVM: maximum-margin hyperplane, support vectors, hinge loss; C controls regularisation
Kernel SVM: RBF kernel with gamma; large gamma gives wiggly boundaries that can overfit
Naive Bayes: MultinomialNB for word counts, GaussianNB for continuous features; alpha smoothing
Text classification: CountVectorizer or TfidfVectorizer followed by MultinomialNB or LinearSVC

topics.title: Neural networks: neurons, layers and activations
topics.summary_md: A neural network stacks **layers**, each a linear transform followed by a non-linear **activation**. Without activations any stack of layers collapses into one linear model. The output layer and loss depend on the task: a single linear output with MSE for regression, logits with cross-entropy for classification.
key_points: A dense layer computes activation(W x + b); W has shape (out_features, in_features) in PyTorch.
Without non-linear activations, many layers are equivalent to one linear layer.
ReLU is the default hidden activation; sigmoid and tanh saturate and pass small gradients.
Softmax turns logits into class probabilities that sum to 1.
learn_items: Perceptron and neuron: weighted sum plus bias, then an activation; a layer is many neurons in parallel
Multilayer perceptron: input, hidden and output layers; width = neurons per layer, depth = layers
Activations: ReLU, Leaky ReLU, GELU, sigmoid and tanh; know their shapes and output ranges
Why non-linearity: composing linear maps gives a linear map; activations let networks fit curves
Output layers: linear for regression, one logit with sigmoid for binary, k logits with softmax
Losses: MSE for regression, binary cross-entropy, categorical cross-entropy for multiclass
Parameter count: a dense layer from n to m units has n × m weights plus m biases

topics.title: Backpropagation and computational graphs
topics.summary_md: **Backpropagation** computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight by applying the chain rule backwards through the **computational graph**. The forward pass stores intermediate values and the backward pass multiplies local derivatives from the loss to the inputs. Products of many small derivatives cause **vanishing gradients**, which shaped modern choices like ReLU and residual connections.
key_points: Forward pass computes and caches values; backward pass applies the chain rule from the loss down.
Each node only needs its local derivative; gradients are multiplied along paths and summed at joins.
For softmax with cross-entropy, the gradient on the logits is simply p − y.
learn_items: Computational graph: nodes are operations, edges carry tensors; draw one for L = (w·x + b − y)²
Forward pass: compute outputs and cache inputs needed for the derivatives
Backward pass: start with dL/dL = 1 and multiply by local derivatives node by node
Gradient at a branch: when a value feeds several nodes, add the gradients flowing back from each
Dense layer gradients: dL/dW = δ xᵀ, dL/db = δ, dL/dx = Wᵀ δ where δ is the upstream gradient
Softmax + cross-entropy: gradient with respect to the logits is p − y (predicted minus one-hot)
Vanishing and exploding gradients: long chains of small or large factors; gradient clipping helps

topics.title: PyTorch tensors, autograd and nn.Module
topics.summary_md: PyTorch represents data and weights as **tensors** that can live on a CPU or GPU. Setting `requires_grad=True` makes **autograd** record operations so `loss.backward()` fills in `.grad` for every parameter. Models are classes that subclass `nn.Module`, define layers in `__init__` and the computation in `forward`.
key_points: Tensors and models must be on the same device; move both with .to(device).
loss.backward() accumulates into .grad; it adds to old gradients rather than replacing them.
Wrap inference in torch.no_grad() (or torch.inference_mode()) to skip graph building.
Layers assigned as attributes in __init__ are registered, so model.parameters() finds them.
learn_items: Tensors: torch.tensor, zeros, randn, dtype (float32, int64), .shape, reshape and view, indexing
Devices: torch.cuda.is_available(), device = "cuda" or "cpu", tensor.to(device), .cpu().numpy()
Autograd: requires_grad=True, loss.backward(), reading .grad, and why .detach() stops tracking
nn.Module: subclass it, create nn.Linear and activation layers in __init__, compute in forward
Sequential and parameters: nn.Sequential for simple stacks; model.parameters() lists trainable weights
Common shape bugs: batch dimension first, (N, features) for nn.Linear; check shapes with print
Evaluation mode: torch.no_grad() or inference_mode() skip gradients; model.eval() vs model.train()

tasks.title: Use PyTorch autograd to compute the gradient of a small MSE loss and check it against your NumPy gradient

topics.title: The training loop: data loaders, losses and optimisers
topics.summary_md: Training in PyTorch is a loop you write yourself: for each mini-batch from a **DataLoader**, run the forward pass, compute the loss, call `zero_grad()`, `backward()` and `step()`. After each epoch, evaluate on validation data in eval mode without gradients. Track both losses to see when the model starts overfitting.
key_points: Per batch: optimizer.zero_grad(), outputs = model(x), loss = loss_fn(outputs, y), loss.backward(), optimizer.step().
nn.CrossEntropyLoss expects raw logits and integer class labels; do not apply softmax first.
Shuffle the training loader, not the validation loader.
Switch to model.eval() and torch.no_grad() for validation, then back to model.train().
learn_items: Dataset and DataLoader: __len__ and __getitem__; batch_size, shuffle=True for training, num_workers
torchvision datasets and transforms: load MNIST or Fashion-MNIST with ToTensor and Normalize
Loss functions: nn.CrossEntropyLoss (logits, int labels), nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss, nn.MSELoss
Optimisers: torch.optim.SGD with momentum and AdamW; learning rate and weight_decay arguments
Loop order: zero_grad, forward, loss, backward, step; log the average loss per epoch
Validation loop: model.eval(), torch.no_grad(), compute accuracy with argmax over logits
Saving: torch.save(model.state_dict(), path); load with model.load_state_dict(torch.load(path))

topics.title: Training well: initialisation, normalisation, dropout
topics.summary_md: Getting a network to train well is mostly about a handful of tools. Good **initialisation** and **batch or layer normalisation** keep activations in a healthy range, **dropout**, weight decay, augmentation and **early stopping** fight overfitting, and **learning rate schedules** help convergence. Debug by first overfitting a tiny batch, then regularise.
key_points: First check the model can overfit a single small batch; if it cannot, there is a bug.
Dropout and BatchNorm behave differently in train and eval mode; always call model.eval() to evaluate.
AdamW applies weight decay correctly for Adam; it is a strong default optimiser.
Stop training when validation loss stops improving and keep the best checkpoint.
learn_items: Initialisation: He (Kaiming) for ReLU, Xavier (Glorot) for tanh; PyTorch layers have sensible defaults
BatchNorm: normalises over the batch, uses running statistics in eval mode; LayerNorm normalises per example
Dropout: randomly zeroes activations with probability p during training only; nn.Dropout(p=0.5)
Weight decay: L2-style penalty that shrinks weights; set weight_decay in AdamW
Early stopping: track the best validation loss, stop after a patience of a few epochs without gain
Learning rate schedules: StepLR, CosineAnnealingLR and OneCycleLR; warm-up for large models
Debugging recipe: overfit one batch, check the initial loss (about ln k for k classes), watch gradients

tasks.title: Overfit one batch of 32 Fashion-MNIST images to near-zero loss, then add dropout and compare validation curves
Train the same model with a constant learning rate and with CosineAnnealingLR and compare final validation accuracy

topics.title: Convolutional neural networks
topics.summary_md: A **convolution** slides small learned filters over an image, so the same weights detect a pattern anywhere. Stacking convolutions with **pooling** builds features from edges to textures to object parts while keeping the parameter count low. Know how kernel size, stride and padding change the output shape, because shape errors are the most common CNN bug.
key_points: Output size per side = (W − K + 2P) / S + 1 for input W, kernel K, padding P, stride S.
A Conv2d layer has K × K × C_in × C_out weights plus C_out biases, independent of image size.
PyTorch images are (N, C, H, W): batch, channels, height, width.
learn_items: Convolution: a K×K filter slides over the input, computing dot products; weights are shared
Channels: each filter spans all input channels and produces one output feature map
Stride and padding: output = (W − K + 2P)/S + 1; padding="same" keeps the size with stride 1
Pooling: MaxPool2d(2) halves height and width; global average pooling before the classifier head
Receptive field: deeper layers see larger regions of the input image
Conv2d in PyTorch: nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size, stride, padding) on (N, C, H, W)
A small CNN: [Conv-BatchNorm-ReLU-Pool] × 2 or 3, then flatten or pool, then a Linear head

topics.title: Sequence models: embeddings, RNNs, LSTMs and attention
topics.summary_md: Text and time series arrive as **sequences**. Tokens become dense vectors via an **embedding** layer, and **RNNs** read a sequence step by step while carrying a hidden state. **LSTMs** and GRUs add gates to keep information over longer spans. **Attention** lets every position look directly at every other one, which is why transformers replaced RNNs for most language work.
key_points: nn.Embedding maps integer token IDs to learned vectors; it is a trainable lookup table.
Plain RNNs struggle with long-range dependencies because of vanishing gradients.
LSTM gates (input, forget, output) control what the cell state keeps or discards.
Attention weights are softmax(QKᵀ / √d) and mix the value vectors.
learn_items: Tokenisation basics: map words or subwords to integer IDs; pad sequences to a fixed batch length
Embeddings: nn.Embedding(vocab_size, dim); similar tokens end up with similar vectors
RNN: h_t = tanh(W x_t + U h_(t−1) + b); same weights at every time step
LSTM and GRU: gates and a cell state; nn.LSTM(batch_first=True) input shape (N, T, features)
Sequence tasks: many-to-one (sentiment), many-to-many (tagging), sequence-to-sequence (translation)
Scaled dot-product attention: softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V; queries, keys and values are learned projections
Why transformers won: attention runs in parallel over positions and links distant tokens directly

tasks.title: Train an embedding + LSTM sentiment classifier on the IMDB movie reviews dataset and report validation accuracy
Implement scaled dot-product attention for a 4-token toy sequence in NumPy and check each attention row sums to 1

topics.title: GPU training, mixed precision and checkpoints
topics.summary_md: Real projects train for hours, so efficiency and robustness matter. Keep the GPU busy with a good DataLoader, use **mixed precision** to cut memory and speed up maths, and try `torch.compile` in PyTorch 2. Save full **checkpoints** (model, optimiser, epoch) so you can resume, and fix random seeds so experiments are reproducible.
key_points: torch.autocast with bfloat16 or float16 runs most maths in lower precision; float16 needs a GradScaler.
If the GPU runs out of memory, lower the batch size or use gradient accumulation.
A checkpoint saves model and optimiser state_dicts plus the epoch, so training can resume.
learn_items: GPU utilisation: watch nvidia-smi; raise num_workers and set pin_memory=True if the GPU waits for data
Mixed precision: torch.autocast(device_type="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16); torch.amp.GradScaler for float16
torch.compile(model): compiles the model graph for speed; check correctness and time it
Gradient accumulation: call step() every k batches to mimic a batch k times larger
Gradient clipping: torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
Checkpoints: save model, optimiser and scheduler state_dicts and the epoch; resume from them
Reproducibility: torch.manual_seed, seeds for NumPy and Python random, and log every hyperparameter

topics.title: Images as arrays and classic image processing
topics.summary_md: A digital image is an array of pixel values: height × width × channels, usually 8-bit integers from 0 to 255. Before deep learning, vision used hand-made operations such as resizing, blurring, thresholding and edge detection, and these remain useful for preprocessing. **OpenCV** loads images in **BGR** order while most other libraries use RGB, a frequent source of bugs.
key_points: OpenCV and NumPy use (H, W, C); PyTorch models expect (C, H, W) floats.
cv2.imread returns BGR; convert with cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB).
Convolution with a small kernel is the core of blurring, sharpening and edge detection.
learn_items: Pixels and channels: grayscale (H, W), colour (H, W, 3); uint8 values 0 to 255
Colour spaces: RGB vs BGR in OpenCV; HSV makes colour-based masking easier
Basic operations: crop by array slicing, cv2.resize with interpolation, rotate and flip
Filtering: Gaussian blur to remove noise; kernels are small matrices convolved with the image
Thresholding and masks: cv2.threshold and Otsu method; combine masks with bitwise operations
Edges and contours: cv2.Canny for edges, cv2.findContours for object outlines and bounding boxes
Converting for models: to float, scale to 0–1, normalise, transpose to (C, H, W)

topics.title: Image classification and CNN architectures
topics.summary_md: Image classification assigns one label per image. Modern CNNs follow a few ideas: **VGG** showed that stacks of small 3×3 convolutions work well, **ResNet** added **skip connections** so very deep networks train, and efficient families such as MobileNet and EfficientNet trade a little accuracy for speed on phones. Know the ideas, and use pretrained implementations from torchvision rather than writing them.
key_points: Residual block: output = F(x) + x, which lets gradients flow through very deep networks.
Depthwise separable convolutions make MobileNet-style models much cheaper to run.
Report top-1 accuracy on a held-out set and read the confusion matrix for confused classes.
learn_items: Classification pipeline: images, labels, train/val/test split, CNN, softmax over classes
Stacks of 3×3 convolutions: two 3×3 layers see a 5×5 region with fewer weights than one 5×5
ResNet: residual blocks with skip connections and BatchNorm; ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 are common
Efficient models: depthwise separable convolutions (MobileNet) and compound scaling (EfficientNet)
torchvision.models: load an architecture by name, inspect its layers and the final fc or classifier
Evaluation: top-1 and top-5 accuracy, per-class accuracy and a confusion matrix of misclassified images

topics.title: Transfer learning and data augmentation
topics.summary_md: With a few thousand images or fewer, start from a model **pretrained** on ImageNet instead of training from scratch. Replace the final layer, train only the new head first (**feature extraction**), then optionally unfreeze deeper layers with a small learning rate (**fine-tuning**). **Data augmentation** adds random flips, crops and colour changes to training images so the model generalises.
key_points: Use the same resize and normalisation the pretrained weights were trained with.
Freeze the backbone with requires_grad = False, train the new head, then fine-tune with a lower learning rate.
Augment only the training set; validation and test use a fixed resize and centre crop.
Choose augmentations that keep the label true: no vertical flips for digits or road signs.
learn_items: Why transfer works: early layers learn generic edges and textures that suit most photos
Loading weights: models.resnet18(weights=ResNet18_Weights.DEFAULT) and weights.transforms()
Replacing the head: model.fc = nn.Linear(model.fc.in_features, num_classes)
Feature extraction vs fine-tuning: freeze all but the head, then unfreeze later layers at a lower LR
Augmentation with torchvision.transforms.v2: RandomResizedCrop, RandomHorizontalFlip, ColorJitter
ImageFolder: one sub-folder per class for train and val; DataLoader with shuffle for training only
Signs of trouble: validation far below training means more augmentation or less unfreezing

topics.title: Object detection: boxes, IoU, NMS and YOLO
topics.summary_md: **Object detection** finds every object in an image and returns a class and a **bounding box** for each. Boxes are compared with **IoU** (intersection over union), duplicate predictions are removed with **non-maximum suppression**, and detectors are scored with **mAP**. Two-stage detectors such as Faster R-CNN propose regions first; single-stage detectors such as the YOLO family predict boxes in one pass and suit real-time use.
key_points: IoU = area of overlap / area of union; 0 means no overlap, 1 means identical boxes.
NMS keeps the highest-scoring box and drops others that overlap it above an IoU threshold.
mAP averages precision over recall levels and classes, at one or several IoU thresholds.
Single-stage detectors trade a little accuracy for much faster inference.
learn_items: Box formats: (x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max) vs (x_center, y_center, width, height); convert carefully
IoU: compute intersection and union areas by hand for two boxes; used for matching and evaluation
Non-maximum suppression: sort by score, keep the best, drop overlaps above IoU 0.5; torchvision.ops.nms
Two-stage vs single-stage: region proposals then classification (Faster R-CNN) vs one pass (YOLO)
Anchors and anchor-free heads: predicting offsets from reference boxes vs predicting centres directly
Metrics: precision and recall at an IoU threshold, AP per class, mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95
Annotations: COCO JSON and YOLO text formats; label consistently and keep a held-out test set

tasks.title: Write IoU and NMS functions from scratch in NumPy and check them against torchvision.ops.box_iou and nms
Run a COCO-pretrained Faster R-CNN from torchvision on five of your photos and draw labelled boxes with scores

topics.title: Semantic and instance segmentation
topics.summary_md: **Segmentation** labels every pixel. **Semantic segmentation** gives each pixel a class (road, car, sky), while **instance segmentation** also separates individual objects (car 1, car 2). Encoder-decoder networks such as **U-Net** downsample to capture context and upsample with skip connections to recover detail; Mask R-CNN adds a mask head to a detector.
key_points: Semantic segmentation ignores which object a pixel belongs to; instance segmentation does not.
U-Net skip connections pass fine detail from the encoder to the decoder.
Evaluate masks with IoU (Jaccard) or Dice; pixel accuracy misleads when the background dominates.
learn_items: Task types: semantic, instance and panoptic segmentation; output is a mask of shape (H, W)
Encoder-decoder: downsample for context, upsample with transposed convolutions or interpolation
U-Net: symmetric encoder and decoder with skip connections; strong on medical and satellite images
Instance segmentation: Mask R-CNN predicts a box, a class and a per-object mask
Losses: per-pixel cross-entropy, Dice loss, or both for small foreground regions
Metrics: mean IoU across classes and the Dice coefficient = 2|A∩B| / (|A| + |B|)
Augmenting masks: apply the same geometric transform to image and mask; never colour-jitter the mask

tasks.title: Train a small U-Net on the Oxford-IIIT Pet foreground masks and report mean IoU on the validation split

topics.title: Vision transformers and foundation models
topics.summary_md: A **vision transformer (ViT)** cuts an image into fixed-size patches, embeds each patch as a token and runs a standard transformer over them. Pretrained at scale, ViTs match or beat CNNs. **Foundation models** reuse this idea: CLIP learns a shared image-text embedding for zero-shot classification and search, and promptable models such as Segment Anything produce masks from a point or box.
key_points: ViT: image → patches (for example 16×16) → linear embeddings + position embeddings → transformer.
ViTs have weaker built-in image assumptions than CNNs, so they need large pretraining or strong augmentation.
CLIP scores images against text prompts, enabling classification without task-specific training.
learn_items: Patch embedding: a 224×224 image in 16×16 patches gives 196 tokens plus a class token
Position embeddings: tell the transformer where each patch came from
CNN vs ViT: convolutions build in locality; ViTs learn it from data and scale well with pretraining
CLIP: contrastive training on image-caption pairs; zero-shot classification with "a photo of a {label}"
Segment Anything style models: promptable segmentation from points, boxes or a rough mask
Using pretrained ViTs: timm or torchvision vit_b_16 weights; fine-tune the head as in transfer learning

tasks.title: Use a pretrained CLIP model to classify 20 of your own photos zero-shot with five text labels and note its mistakes
Fine-tune a pretrained ViT-B/16 head on CIFAR-10 and compare accuracy and training time with your ResNet-18

topics.title: Text as data: tokens and embeddings
topics.summary_md: Models never see words: a **tokeniser** splits text into subword tokens and maps each to an integer id, and an **embedding** layer turns each id into a vector. Subword schemes such as BPE and WordPiece keep the vocabulary small while still covering rare and new words. Contextual models then give the same token different vectors in different sentences.
key_points: Text → tokens → integer ids → embedding vectors; every model step works on vectors.
Subword tokenisers (BPE, WordPiece) split rare words into known pieces, so nothing is truly out of vocabulary.
Token count, not word count, sets context limits and API cost.
Static embeddings give one vector per word; contextual embeddings depend on the sentence.
learn_items: Classic preprocessing: lower-casing, stop words, stemming vs lemmatisation, and why transformers mostly skip them
Bag of words and TF-IDF: build a document-term matrix and say why word order and meaning are lost
Subword tokenisation: how BPE merges frequent pairs and how WordPiece marks word pieces with ##
Special tokens: [CLS], [SEP], [PAD], [UNK] and beginning/end-of-sequence tokens and what each is for
Token ids and vocabulary size: why a larger vocabulary means fewer tokens per sentence but a bigger embedding table
Word embeddings: word2vec idea (predict neighbours), vector arithmetic and cosine similarity between words
Contextual embeddings: why "bank" gets different vectors in "river bank" and "bank loan"

tasks.title: Tokenise five sentences with two pretrained tokenisers and compare token counts, pieces and ids
Build a TF-IDF search over 50 short texts with scikit-learn and rank them by cosine similarity to a query

topics.title: Self-attention and the transformer block
topics.summary_md: **Self-attention** lets every token build its new representation as a weighted mix of all tokens. Each token produces a query, a key and a value; scores are `softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k)` and the output is those weights times V. A transformer block stacks multi-head attention and a feed-forward layer, each wrapped in a residual connection and layer normalisation.
key_points: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k) · V; the √d_k keeps softmax from saturating.
Multi-head attention runs several attention heads in parallel so each can track a different relation.
Attention has no sense of order, so positional information (sinusoidal, learned or rotary) is added.
Cost grows with the square of sequence length, which is why context windows are limited.
learn_items: Why RNNs struggled: sequential processing, slow training and fading long-range dependencies
Query, key and value: each is a learned linear projection of the token embedding
Scaled dot-product attention: compute QKᵀ, divide by √d_k, softmax each row, multiply by V; work one 3-token example by hand
Multi-head attention: split into h heads, attend in parallel, concatenate and project back
Positional encoding: sinusoidal vs learned vs rotary (RoPE) and why attention alone ignores order
Transformer block: attention → add & layer norm → feed-forward → add & layer norm
Causal mask: hide future tokens in decoders by setting their scores to minus infinity before softmax
Complexity: O(n²) memory and time in sequence length and what that means for long inputs

tasks.title: Implement scaled dot-product attention with a causal mask in NumPy and check every row of weights sums to 1

topics.title: Encoders, decoders and encoder-decoders
topics.summary_md: Transformers come in three shapes. **Encoder-only** models (BERT family) read the whole input in both directions and suit classification, tagging and embeddings. **Decoder-only** models (GPT family) predict the next token and power chat and generation. **Encoder-decoder** models (T5, BART) map one sequence to another, for example translation or summarisation.
key_points: Encoder-only: bidirectional attention, trained with masked language modelling; best for understanding tasks.
Decoder-only: causal attention, trained on next-token prediction; best for generation.
Encoder-decoder: the decoder cross-attends to the encoder output; suits sequence-to-sequence tasks.
Pretrain on huge unlabelled text once, then fine-tune or prompt for each task.
learn_items: Masked language modelling: hide about 15% of tokens and predict them from both sides
Next-token prediction: the causal language-modelling objective behind every chat model
Cross-attention: decoder queries attend to encoder keys and values in encoder-decoder models
Sentence representation: [CLS] token vs mean pooling over token vectors for classification and embeddings
Task mapping: classification, NER, QA, summarisation, translation, chat; pick the architecture for each
Pretraining vs fine-tuning vs prompting: what each stage changes and what data it needs
Model size: parameters, layers, hidden size and heads; read them from a model config file

tasks.title: For eight NLP tasks write which architecture you would use and one sentence on why, then check with a pipeline
Run a fill-mask encoder and a text-generation decoder on the same sentences and note how their outputs differ

topics.title: Running pretrained models with Hugging Face
topics.summary_md: The `transformers` library loads thousands of pretrained models with the same few calls. `pipeline` is the quickest way to try a task; `AutoTokenizer` and `AutoModel` classes give full control over batching, padding and outputs. Learn to run inference correctly: evaluation mode, no gradients, the right device and the attention mask.
key_points: Always load the tokeniser that matches the model checkpoint.
Batching needs padding and an attention mask so padded positions are ignored.
Use model.eval() and torch.no_grad() for inference; it saves memory and disables dropout.
Logits are raw scores; apply softmax to get probabilities.
learn_items: pipeline(): run sentiment, NER, zero-shot classification and summarisation in one line each
AutoTokenizer: call with padding=True, truncation=True, max_length and return_tensors="pt"; inspect input_ids and attention_mask
AutoModel vs AutoModelForSequenceClassification: base hidden states vs a task head with logits
Inference hygiene: model.eval(), torch.no_grad(), moving model and tensors to the same device
Outputs: logits, softmax probabilities, argmax label, and id2label from the model config
Sentence embeddings: mean-pool last hidden states using the attention mask, then L2-normalise
Model cards: read licence, training data, intended use and limitations before using a model

tasks.title: Classify 100 product reviews in batches with a pretrained sentiment model and save label and confidence to CSV
Compute mean-pooled sentence embeddings by hand and find the most similar pair among ten sentences

topics.title: Fine-tuning an encoder for text classification
topics.summary_md: Fine-tuning adds a small classification head to a pretrained encoder and trains the whole network briefly on labelled examples. With a few thousand labels it usually beats training from scratch by a wide margin. Use a validation split, a small learning rate and the right metric, and watch for overfitting and class imbalance.
key_points: Keep a held-out validation set and pick the checkpoint by validation metric, not training loss.
Fine-tuning uses a small learning rate (around 2e-5 to 5e-5) for a few epochs.
Use macro F1 when classes are imbalanced; accuracy can hide a useless model.
Compare against a simple TF-IDF plus logistic regression baseline.
learn_items: datasets library: load a dataset, inspect columns, train/validation/test split with a fixed seed
Tokenising: dataset.map(batched=True), then pad per batch with DataCollatorWithPadding
Model head: AutoModelForSequenceClassification with num_labels, id2label and label2id set
TrainingArguments: learning rate, epochs, batch size, weight decay, evaluation and save strategy
Trainer: compute_metrics returning accuracy and macro F1; read the confusion matrix
Overfitting signs: training loss falls while validation loss rises; fix with fewer epochs or more data
Class imbalance: stratified splits, class weights and per-class precision and recall
Save and reload: save_pretrained for model and tokeniser, then run inference on new text

tasks.title: Fine-tune a small encoder on a public sentiment or news-topic dataset in a free notebook GPU and report macro F1
Train a TF-IDF plus logistic regression baseline on the same split and compare its F1 with the fine-tuned model

topics.title: Text generation and decoding strategies
topics.summary_md: A decoder produces one token at a time from a probability distribution, and the **decoding strategy** decides which token to pick. Greedy and beam search are deterministic; temperature, top-k and top-p sampling trade accuracy for variety. A **KV cache** keeps past keys and values so each new token does not recompute the whole prefix.
key_points: Greedy picks the most likely token each step; beam search keeps several candidate sequences.
Temperature below 1 sharpens the distribution; above 1 flattens it and adds randomness.
Top-p samples from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p.
Generation stops at an end token or max_new_tokens; set both deliberately.
learn_items: Autoregressive loop: logits → probabilities → pick a token → append → repeat
Greedy decoding vs beam search: determinism, repetition and when beam search helps (translation)
Temperature: divide logits by T before softmax; effect of T = 0.2 vs 1.0 vs 1.5
Top-k and top-p (nucleus) sampling: how each truncates the distribution
generate() controls: repetition penalty, stop sequences and max_new_tokens
KV cache: store keys and values of earlier tokens so each step only processes the new token
Chat templates: how a tokeniser formats system, user and assistant turns for an instruction model

tasks.title: Generate from one prompt with greedy, beam, and three temperature and top-p settings, and compare the outputs

topics.title: Calling an LLM API and writing clear prompts
topics.summary_md: An LLM API takes a list of **messages** (system, user, assistant) and returns generated text, billed and limited by tokens. Good prompts state the task, the audience, the format and the constraints, give one or two examples, and separate instructions from data with clear delimiters. Keep API keys on a server and handle rate limits and timeouts.
key_points: The system message sets role and rules; user messages carry the request and data.
Be specific: task, context, output format, length and what to do when unsure.
Few-shot examples steer format and tone better than long descriptions.
Never ship an API key in client code; call the model from your backend.
learn_items: Messages: system, user and assistant roles, and why the whole conversation is resent each call
Tokens and context window: input plus output must fit; estimate cost from input and output tokens
Parameters: temperature, max output tokens and stop sequences, and when to set temperature low
Prompt structure: role, task, context, constraints, output format, and an explicit "if unsure, say so"
Delimiters: wrap user data in tags or fences so the model does not treat it as instructions
Few-shot prompting: two or three input-output examples that show the exact format you want
Reasoning prompts: ask for step-by-step working on hard tasks, then a separate final answer
Production basics: keys in environment variables on the server, timeouts, retries with backoff, streaming

tasks.title: Build a small backend endpoint that summarises pasted text with an LLM API, with a timeout and retry
Rewrite a vague prompt three ways (constraints, examples, format) and compare outputs on five inputs

topics.title: Structured output and tool calling
topics.summary_md: Apps need data, not prose: request **structured output** that matches a JSON schema and validate it in code before using it. **Tool calling** lets the model ask your app to run a function, such as a database lookup, and then answer from the real result. Your code stays in charge: it validates arguments, runs the tool and decides what the model may do.
key_points: Define the output with a schema and validate every response (Pydantic or zod); retry or fail on invalid output.
The model only proposes a tool call; your code executes it and returns the result.
Validate tool arguments like any user input and limit what each tool can do.
Ground facts such as prices, dates and stock in tool results, not model memory.
learn_items: JSON mode vs schema-constrained output: what each guarantees and what you must still validate
Schema design: required fields, enums for categories, nullable fields for unknowns instead of guesses
Validation: parse with Pydantic or zod, and on failure retry once with the error message, then fail cleanly
Tool definitions: name, clear description and a JSON schema for arguments
Tool-call loop: model returns a call → app validates and runs it → app sends the result → model answers
Parallel and multiple tool calls: handle several calls in one turn and match results by call id
Safety: allow-list tools, check permissions, and ask the user before any action that changes data

tasks.title: Extract title, company, location and skills from ten job posts into a validated schema, rejecting bad output
Add one tool (for example a local database lookup) and implement the full tool-call loop with argument checks

topics.title: Evaluating LLM features and guarding outputs
topics.summary_md: You cannot improve what you do not measure: build an **eval set** of realistic inputs with expected outputs or checks before tuning prompts, and rerun it on every change. Use code checks where possible and an LLM judge with a rubric where not. Guard the feature against **prompt injection**, hallucinated facts, leaked personal data and runaway cost.
key_points: Collect 30 to 100 realistic cases, including edge cases and failures you have already seen.
Prefer deterministic checks (schema, exact match, contains) over judgement where possible.
An LLM judge needs a clear rubric and a spot-check against human labels.
Treat retrieved text and user input as untrusted; it can carry injected instructions.
learn_items: Eval set: inputs, expected outputs or pass criteria, tags for case type; store it in version control
Code-based checks: schema validity, exact match, keyword or regex checks, length and refusal checks
LLM-as-judge: rubric with a 1 to 5 scale or pass/fail, pairwise comparison, and checking it against your own labels
Regression runs: score every prompt or model change on the whole set and compare with the last run
Prompt injection: direct vs indirect (via documents or web pages) and mitigations such as least-privilege tools
Hallucination controls: ground in sources, ask for citations, allow "I don’t know", verify links and numbers
Cost and latency: log tokens and time per call, cache repeated requests, use smaller models for easy steps

tasks.title: Write a script that runs 30 eval cases against your prompt, applies code checks and prints a pass rate per tag
Craft five prompt-injection inputs against your summariser and add a defence that blocks at least three

topics.title: Agent loops and multi-step LLM workflows
topics.summary_md: A **workflow** chains LLM calls along a path you define; an **agent** lets the model choose its next tool call in a loop until it decides it is done. Start with the simplest workflow that works, and add agent autonomy only when the steps cannot be known in advance. Every agent needs step limits, state, logging and human approval for risky actions.
key_points: Prefer fixed workflows (chain, route, parallelise) before open-ended agents.
An agent loop is: think → call a tool → observe the result → repeat or finish.
Cap steps, tokens and time, and log every step so failures can be debugged.
Require human confirmation before sending, paying, deleting or publishing anything.
learn_items: Workflow patterns: prompt chaining, routing to specialised prompts, parallel calls and aggregation
Agent loop: reason, act with a tool, observe, repeat; stop on a final answer or a step limit
State and memory: conversation history, a scratchpad, and summarising history to fit the context window
Orchestration libraries (for example LangGraph): graphs of steps with explicit state and checkpoints
Tool servers: what the Model Context Protocol standardises between an app and its tools
Failure modes: loops, wrong tool choice, compounding errors; detect them with traces and evals
Human-in-the-loop: pause for approval on actions with side effects and show what will happen

tasks.title: Build an agent with two local tools (file search and calculator), a five-step limit and a printed trace of each step

topics.title: Embeddings and vector similarity search
topics.summary_md: An **embedding model** maps text to a fixed-length vector so that similar meanings land close together. Search then becomes "find the nearest vectors", measured by cosine similarity or dot product. Exact search compares against every vector; **approximate nearest neighbour** indexes such as HNSW trade a little recall for large speed-ups, and vector databases add storage, filters and updates.
key_points: Embed queries and documents with the same model, or the vectors are not comparable.
On L2-normalised vectors, cosine similarity equals the dot product.
ANN indexes (HNSW, IVF) are fast but approximate; tune them for recall.
Store metadata next to each vector so you can filter by source, date or user.
learn_items: Embedding models: text in, fixed-size vector out; dimension, max input tokens and language coverage
Similarity: cosine, dot product and Euclidean distance; normalise vectors and compare by hand on three examples
Exact k-nearest-neighbour search with NumPy: one matrix product and argsort over all vectors
Approximate search: HNSW graph and IVF clusters, and the recall vs latency trade-off
Vector stores: FAISS (library), Chroma (embedded), pgvector (PostgreSQL extension); when to use each
pgvector basics: a vector column, the <=> cosine distance operator, ORDER BY distance LIMIT k, an HNSW index
Metadata filtering: restrict search by tenant, document type or date before or during the vector search

tasks.title: Embed 200 FAQ entries with a free local embedding model and answer queries with exact top-5 NumPy search
Index the same vectors in FAISS or Chroma and measure how often its top 5 matches the exact top 5

topics.title: Building a RAG pipeline end to end
topics.summary_md: **Retrieval-augmented generation** answers from your own documents. Offline you load, clean, **chunk** and embed documents and store the chunks with metadata. At query time you embed the question, retrieve the top-k chunks, and send them to the model with instructions to answer only from them, cite sources and say when the answer is not there.
key_points: Chunk size trades precision (small chunks) against context (large chunks); overlap avoids cut-off sentences.
Keep source, title and position with every chunk so answers can cite it.
Tell the model to answer only from the context and to say when the context lacks the answer.
Re-embed changed documents and delete stale chunks, or answers go out of date.
learn_items: Ingestion: load PDFs, HTML and Markdown, extract clean text, drop navigation and boilerplate
Chunking: fixed-size with overlap vs splitting on headings and paragraphs; size chunks to the embedding model
Chunk metadata: document id, title, section, page and updated date for citations and filters
Retrieval: embed the query, fetch top-k (start with 4 to 8), optionally drop results below a score threshold
Prompt assembly: system rules, numbered context chunks, the question, and a required citation format
Grounding rules: answer only from context, cite chunk numbers, reply "not found in the documents" otherwise
Updates: re-index on change with a content hash, and delete chunks of removed documents

tasks.title: Build a RAG question-answering script over your own course notes that prints the answer with cited chunk sources
Try three chunk sizes on the same 10 questions and record which size retrieves the right passage most often

topics.title: Hybrid search, reranking and RAG evaluation
topics.summary_md: Vector search misses exact terms such as error codes and names, while keyword search (BM25) misses paraphrases; **hybrid search** runs both and merges the results. A **cross-encoder reranker** then reorders the top candidates more accurately. Evaluate retrieval (did the right chunk come back?) separately from generation (is the answer faithful and relevant?).
key_points: Hybrid search merges BM25 and vector results, often with reciprocal rank fusion.
Rerank the top 20 to 50 candidates with a cross-encoder, then keep the best few.
Measure retrieval with recall@k and MRR on questions whose source chunk is known.
Measure answers for faithfulness to the context and relevance to the question.
learn_items: BM25 keyword search: term frequency, inverse document frequency and why it wins on exact identifiers
Reciprocal rank fusion: score each document by the sum of 1 / (k + rank) across result lists
Rerankers: bi-encoder (separate embeddings) vs cross-encoder (scores query and chunk together); speed vs accuracy
Query transformation: rewrite follow-up questions into standalone queries; split multi-part questions
Retrieval eval set: questions paired with the ids of the chunks that answer them
Retrieval metrics: recall@k (was a correct chunk in the top k) and MRR (how high was the first one)
Answer metrics: faithfulness (every claim supported by context), answer relevance and citation accuracy

tasks.title: Add BM25 to your RAG retriever, fuse it with vector results by reciprocal rank fusion and compare recall@5
Write 20 questions with known source chunks and report recall@5 and MRR before and after adding a reranker

topics.title: When to fine-tune and how to prepare data
topics.summary_md: Fine-tune only after prompting and retrieval fall short. Fine-tuning is good at teaching a **format, style or narrow task** and making a small model reliable at it; it is poor at adding fresh facts, which retrieval handles better. Results depend mostly on the training data: clean, consistent, representative examples in the model’s chat format, with a held-out test set.
key_points: Ladder: better prompts → retrieval → fine-tuning; climb only when the step below is measured and short.
Fine-tuning teaches behaviour and format; use RAG for knowledge that changes.
A few hundred consistent, high-quality examples beat thousands of noisy ones.
Split off a test set before training and check it shares no duplicates with training data.
learn_items: Decision: list what prompting and RAG already achieve on your eval set before choosing to fine-tune
