Good fits: fixed output format, domain tone, classification or extraction with a small model, lower cost per call
Supervised fine-tuning data: instruction and response pairs or multi-turn chats in JSONL
Chat templates: format examples with the base model’s own template and special tokens
Data quality: deduplicate, fix inconsistent labels, remove personal data, balance task types
Splits and leakage: train, validation and test sets with no near-duplicates shared between them
Base model choice: size vs available GPU memory, licence terms, and base vs instruction-tuned checkpoints

tasks.title: Turn 150 raw examples into a deduplicated chat-format JSONL with train, validation and test splits
Score a prompted small open model on your test split so you have a baseline to beat

topics.title: LoRA and QLoRA: parameter-efficient fine-tuning
topics.summary_md: Full fine-tuning updates every weight and needs a lot of GPU memory. **LoRA** freezes the base model and learns a small low-rank update `BA` for chosen weight matrices, so only a tiny share of parameters train. **QLoRA** loads the frozen base in 4-bit precision and trains LoRA adapters on top, which makes fine-tuning possible on a single consumer or free notebook GPU.
key_points: LoRA learns W + (alpha / r) · BA with small matrices A and B; the base weights stay frozen.
B starts at zero, so training begins exactly from the base model.
QLoRA = 4-bit quantised frozen base + LoRA adapters trained in 16-bit.
An adapter is a small file; one base model can serve many adapters.
learn_items: Memory maths: parameters × bytes per parameter for weights (16-bit = 2 bytes, 4-bit = 0.5), plus optimiser state
Low-rank update: W (d × k) gets B (d × r) times A (r × k); count trainable parameters for r = 8 and r = 16
LoRA hyperparameters: rank r, lora_alpha, dropout, and target modules such as attention q/k/v/o projections
PEFT library: LoraConfig, get_peft_model and print_trainable_parameters
QLoRA pieces: 4-bit NF4 quantisation, double quantisation, 16-bit compute dtype, paged optimisers
Fitting memory: gradient checkpointing, small batches and gradient accumulation
Adapters vs merged weights: load an adapter on a base, or merge_and_unload into one model

tasks.title: Wrap a small open model with LoRA, print trainable parameters for three ranks and explain the difference
Load a small open model in 4-bit with QLoRA settings in a free notebook GPU and run one training step

topics.title: Running a fine-tune and evaluating the result
topics.summary_md: A practical run uses a supervised fine-tuning trainer with LoRA, a modest learning rate and one to three epochs, computing loss only on response tokens. Watch training and validation loss, then judge the model on the held-out test set against the prompted baseline. Also check that it has not lost general ability it needs (**catastrophic forgetting**).
key_points: Mask prompt tokens so loss is computed only on the responses the model should learn.
LoRA runs use larger learning rates than full fine-tuning (often around 1e-4 to 2e-4).
A fine-tune counts only if it beats the prompted baseline on the same test set.
Overfitting shows as validation loss rising; reduce epochs or add varied data.
learn_items: SFT trainer setup (for example TRL’s SFTTrainer): dataset, chat template, LoRA config and max sequence length
Completion-only loss: mask instruction tokens with the ignore index so only responses train
Hyperparameters: learning rate, epochs, effective batch size via gradient accumulation, warm-up, scheduler
Monitoring: log training and validation loss each N steps; stop when validation loss stops improving
Task evaluation: exact match, F1 or schema-valid rate on the test split, side by side with the baseline
Forgetting check: run a few general prompts before and after and compare answers
Saving and loading: save the adapter, reload on the base model, and record data and config versions

tasks.title: Fine-tune a small open model with LoRA on your JSONL dataset in a free notebook GPU and save the adapter
Score the base and fine-tuned models on the same test split and write a short table of results and failures

topics.title: Preference tuning and serving fine-tuned models
topics.summary_md: After supervised fine-tuning, **preference tuning** teaches the model which of two answers people prefer. RLHF trains a reward model and optimises against it; **DPO** learns directly from chosen and rejected pairs and is simpler to run. To ship, quantise the model for inference and serve it with an engine that batches requests and can load several LoRA adapters.
key_points: Preference data is a prompt with a chosen and a rejected answer.
DPO skips the separate reward model and RL loop of classic RLHF.
Quantised weights (8-bit or 4-bit) cut serving memory at a small quality cost.
Serving engines batch requests continuously and can swap LoRA adapters per request.
learn_items: RLHF stages: supervised fine-tune → reward model from human rankings → policy optimisation against the reward
DPO: train on chosen/rejected pairs with a frozen reference model; the beta parameter controls drift from it
Preference data: collect pairs from model samples ranked by people or a judged rubric; keep them consistent
Inference quantisation: 8-bit and 4-bit weights, quality checks after quantising, file formats for local runners
Serving: an inference server with continuous batching, streaming and an API compatible with common clients
Multi-adapter serving: one base model in memory with per-request LoRA adapters

tasks.title: Write 30 chosen/rejected pairs for your task and explain the rule that decides which answer wins
Serve your merged or quantised fine-tuned model locally behind an HTTP endpoint and send it five test prompts

topics.title: Reproducible experiments and tracking with MLflow
topics.summary_md: A model is only useful if you can say exactly how it was made. Pin the environment, fix random seeds, version the data and log every run: parameters, metrics, artefacts and the code commit. **MLflow tracking** records this per run and lets you compare runs side by side instead of relying on notebook memory.
key_points: Reproducible = same code commit + same data version + same environment + same seed.
Log params, metrics and artefacts for every run, including failed ones.
Version large data with a tool such as DVC or by recording a content hash, not in plain git.
Compare runs in the tracking UI before choosing a model.
learn_items: Reproducibility checklist: requirements lock file, random seeds, data version or hash, git commit id
MLflow concepts: experiment, run, parameters, metrics (with steps), artefacts and tags
Tracking API: set_experiment, start_run, log_param, log_metric, log_artifact; and autolog for scikit-learn
Tracking UI: run mlflow ui locally, filter runs, compare metrics and parallel-coordinate plots
Logging models: log_model with a signature and an input example so the model can be reloaded anywhere
Data versioning: why git struggles with large files and how DVC stores pointers in git and data elsewhere
Project layout: separate data, src, configs and notebooks; drive runs from a config file, not edited cells

tasks.title: Train three scikit-learn models on one dataset, log each run to a local MLflow server and pick the best in the UI
Rerun your best run from a fresh environment using only the logged params, commit and data hash

topics.title: Registering, packaging and serving a model
topics.summary_md: A trained model becomes a product when it has a version, a clear input schema and an API. Register models in a **model registry** and point an alias such as `champion` at the version in production. Serve it from a small web service that loads the model once, validates input and returns predictions, packaged in a Docker image so it runs the same everywhere.
key_points: The registry gives each model a version history; aliases point at the one to serve.
Load the model once at start-up, never per request.
Validate request input with a schema and return clear errors for bad input.
Choose batch inference for scheduled scoring and online inference for per-request answers.
learn_items: Serialisation: joblib or pickle for scikit-learn (same library versions needed), ONNX for portable models
MLflow model registry: register a run’s model, versions, aliases like @champion, load by models:/name@alias
Serving API: a FastAPI app with a Pydantic request model, a /predict endpoint and a /health endpoint
Start-up loading: load the model in a lifespan or start-up hook and keep it in memory
Docker: slim Python base image, pinned requirements, copy the model or fetch it at start, run with uvicorn
Batch vs online inference: scheduled scoring of a table vs per-request latency targets
Basic load test: measure latency percentiles (p50, p95) and throughput with a simple load tool

tasks.title: Serve your best MLflow model through a FastAPI /predict endpoint with input validation and a /health check
Package the model service in a Docker image, run it locally and measure p50 and p95 latency for 200 requests

topics.title: Monitoring models in production and detecting drift
topics.summary_md: A deployed model slowly goes stale as the world changes. **Data drift** is a change in input distributions; **concept drift** is a change in the relationship between inputs and the right answer. Log inputs and predictions, compare live distributions with the training data using statistical tests, track real accuracy once labels arrive, and alert on thresholds.
key_points: Log every prediction with its inputs, model version and timestamp.
Data drift can be checked at once; concept drift needs labels, which often arrive late.
Use PSI or a KS test per feature and watch the prediction distribution too.
Alert on sustained drift or quality drops, then retrain or roll back.
learn_items: Service metrics vs model metrics: latency, errors and uptime vs input drift, prediction drift and accuracy
Drift types: data drift vs concept drift vs training-serving skew, with one real example of each
Prediction logging: inputs, outputs, model version, request id; join with labels later by request id
Drift tests: Kolmogorov-Smirnov for numeric features, chi-squared for categories, PSI with binned values
Reference windows: compare a recent window with the training data or a stable past window
Drift reports: generate a per-feature drift report with a library such as Evidently
Response plan: thresholds, alerts, investigation, retraining trigger and rollback to the previous version

tasks.title: Shift one feature of a test set on purpose and detect it with a KS test and PSI computed in Python
Log predictions from your model service to a file and generate a weekly per-feature drift report from it

topics.title: CI/CD for ML and automated retraining
topics.summary_md: Mature teams treat training as a pipeline, not a notebook. Every change runs tests on code and data, retrains, and must pass **quality gates** against the current production model before promotion. New versions roll out gradually through shadow or canary deployments with an easy rollback, and retraining runs on a schedule or when drift alerts fire.
key_points: Test code, data and model: unit tests, data checks and a minimum quality gate.
Promote a model only if it beats the current champion on the same evaluation data.
Shadow and canary deployments limit the damage of a bad model.
A feature store or shared feature code prevents training-serving skew.
learn_items: Tests for ML: unit tests for feature code, data checks on training input, model tests on known cases
CI pipeline: on push, run tests, train on a sample, evaluate, and fail the build if metrics drop
Promotion: compare challenger and champion on a fixed evaluation set, then move the registry alias
Deployment strategies: shadow (log only), canary (small share of traffic), blue-green, and rollback
Retraining triggers: schedule, drift alert, or enough new labels; guard against training on bad data
Feature stores: one definition of each feature for training and serving, with point-in-time correct joins
Pipeline tools: run steps as an orchestrated pipeline (for example Airflow, Prefect or Kubeflow)

tasks.title: Add a CI workflow that trains on a sample, evaluates and fails if accuracy is below the champion’s

topics.title: Pipeline basics: ETL, ELT, batch and idempotency
topics.summary_md: A data pipeline extracts data from sources, transforms it and loads it where it is used. **ETL** transforms before loading; **ELT** loads raw data into the warehouse first and transforms there with SQL. Good batch pipelines are **idempotent** (rerunning a day gives the same result), partition data by date and store it in columnar formats such as Parquet.
key_points: Idempotent tasks overwrite or merge a partition instead of blindly appending.
Partition by date so reruns, backfills and reads touch only the days they need.
Parquet is columnar and compressed: queries read only the columns they use.
Keep raw data unchanged and build cleaned layers from it.
learn_items: ETL vs ELT: where transformations run and why cloud warehouses made ELT common
Batch vs streaming: scheduled chunks vs continuous events, and when each is worth its complexity
Layers: raw (as received), cleaned (typed and deduplicated), and curated tables for analytics or ML
Idempotency: delete-and-insert or overwrite a date partition, or MERGE on a key, so reruns are safe
Full vs incremental loads: watermark columns such as updated_at, and handling late-arriving records
File formats: CSV vs JSON vs Parquet; columnar storage, compression and column pruning
Partitioning: folder layout such as dt=2026-01-15, partition pruning, and avoiding too many small files

tasks.title: Write a Python ETL script that loads one day of CSV data, cleans it and writes a date-partitioned Parquet folder
Run the script twice for the same date and prove the output row count does not change

topics.title: Spark DataFrames with PySpark
topics.summary_md: **Apache Spark** splits data into partitions and processes them in parallel on executors, coordinated by a driver. DataFrame **transformations** are lazy and only build a plan; an **action** such as `count`, `show` or `write` runs it. Learn the core DataFrame API and Spark SQL on your laptop with a local session before touching a cluster.
key_points: Transformations (select, filter, join) are lazy; actions (count, collect, write) trigger work.
The driver plans the job; executors process partitions in parallel.
Never collect() a large DataFrame to the driver; write it out instead.
Prefer built-in functions over Python UDFs; they run inside the engine and are optimised.
learn_items: Architecture: driver, executors, partitions, jobs, stages and tasks
Local start: SparkSession.builder with master("local[*]"), and reading CSV and Parquet with a schema
Lazy evaluation: transformations build a plan; actions run it; read the plan with explain()
DataFrame API: select, filter, withColumn, when/otherwise, groupBy().agg(), orderBy and joins
Built-in functions: col, lit, to_date, date_trunc, coalesce and window functions with Window.partitionBy
Spark SQL: createOrReplaceTempView and running the same query in SQL and DataFrame form
Writing output: write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("dt").parquet(path), and dynamic partition overwrite

tasks.title: With local PySpark, load a public trips or sales dataset and write daily totals per category as partitioned Parquet
Rewrite three DataFrame queries as Spark SQL and confirm both give identical results

topics.title: Orchestrating pipelines with Airflow DAGs
topics.summary_md: **Apache Airflow** runs pipelines defined as Python **DAGs**: tasks with dependencies, a schedule and retry rules. Each run covers a **data interval** identified by a logical date, which tasks use to process exactly that slice, so reruns and backfills are safe. Prefect and similar tools follow the same ideas with flows and tasks written as decorated Python functions.
key_points: A DAG defines tasks and their order; the scheduler creates a run per interval.
Use the run’s logical date (for example {{ ds }}) to choose the data slice; never use “now”.
Set retries and retry delays; tasks must be idempotent to retry safely.
XCom passes small values between tasks; pass file paths, not datasets.
learn_items: Core concepts: DAG, task, operator, scheduler, executor, DAG run and task instance states
TaskFlow API: @dag and @task decorators, return values as XComs, and >> for explicit dependencies
Scheduling: schedule (cron or presets such as @daily), start_date, catchup, and the data interval
Templating: use the logical date ({{ ds }}) in paths and queries so each run processes its own day
Reliability: retries, retry_delay, timeouts, SLAs or alerts on failure, and idempotent tasks
Backfills and reruns: clear a task or run a date range to reprocess history
Running locally: airflow standalone or Docker Compose, the UI graph view and task logs
Prefect comparison: @flow and @task, runs from plain Python, deployments for schedules

tasks.title: Write a daily Airflow DAG with extract, transform (your ETL script) and load tasks that use the logical date
Backfill your DAG for the last seven days and confirm each day’s output folder is written once

topics.title: Data validation and quality gates
topics.summary_md: Bad data breaks dashboards and models silently, so pipelines must check data the way tests check code. Validate **schema**, nulls, uniqueness, ranges, row counts and freshness at each stage, and decide per check whether to fail the run, quarantine bad rows or just warn. Agree these rules with the data’s producers as a **data contract**.
key_points: Check schema, nulls, uniqueness, value ranges, row counts and freshness.
Fail the run on critical checks so bad data never reaches consumers.
Quarantine invalid rows with a reason instead of dropping them silently.
Track row counts per run; a sudden drop is often the first sign of a broken source.
learn_items: Check types: schema and types, not-null, unique keys, accepted values, ranges and referential integrity
Volume and freshness: compare row counts with recent runs; alert when the latest partition is late
Validation libraries: declare checks in code with pandera or Great Expectations and run them in the pipeline
Severity: error (stop the pipeline) vs warn (log and continue); choose per check
Quarantine pattern: write failing rows to a separate table with the failed rule and run id
Placement: validate on ingest, after transforms and before publishing; add the check as an Airflow task
Data contracts: an agreed schema and rules with the producing team, versioned and reviewed on change

tasks.title: Add a validation task to your DAG with five checks, failing the run on errors and quarantining bad rows

topics.title: Spark performance: partitions, shuffles and joins
topics.summary_md: Most slow Spark jobs come from **shuffles**, skewed keys and badly sized partitions. Wide operations such as `groupBy` and `join` move data across the network, so reduce what you shuffle, **broadcast** small tables in joins, and fix skew. Read the Spark UI and `explain()` output to find the slow stage before changing settings.
key_points: Narrow transformations stay within a partition; wide ones (groupBy, join) shuffle data.
Broadcast a small table to every executor to avoid shuffling the large one.
Skew: one hot key makes one task run far longer than the rest.
repartition shuffles to any count; coalesce only reduces partitions without a full shuffle.
learn_items: Narrow vs wide: which transformations shuffle data and how shuffles split a job into stages
Spark UI: jobs, stages, task durations, shuffle read and write sizes and spill to disk
Partition sizing: spark.sql.shuffle.partitions, repartition vs coalesce, and the small-files problem on write
Join strategies: broadcast hash join vs sort-merge join, and the broadcast() hint for small tables
Skew handling: spot one long task, salt the hot key, or rely on adaptive query execution skew splitting
Reading less: filter and select columns early, and rely on partition pruning
Caching: cache or persist only DataFrames reused by several actions, then unpersist
Table formats: Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg add ACID writes, MERGE and time travel on Parquet files

tasks.title: Join a large and a small DataFrame with and without broadcast() and compare plans with explain() and run times
Create a skewed key on purpose, observe the slow task in the Spark UI, then fix it by salting

topics.title: Answering product design questions
topics.summary_md: Product sense is the ability to pick the right user problem and shape a solution with clear trade-offs. Interviewers test it with prompts such as "design a product for…" or "improve this app". Use a repeatable structure: clarify the goal, choose a **user segment**, rank **pain points**, brainstorm solutions, pick one with explicit trade-offs, then define **success metrics** and risks.
key_points: Clarify the goal and constraints before proposing anything.
Go deep on one user segment instead of designing for everyone.
Rank pains by frequency and severity, then solve the top one.
Close with metrics, risks and what you would build first.
learn_items: Clarify: ask about the goal (growth, engagement, revenue), platform, market and constraints before answering
Users: list 3–4 segments (e.g. first-time vs daily users) and pick one, saying why it matters most
Jobs to be done: state what the user is trying to get done in their context, not which feature they want
Pain points: list 3–5 pains for the chosen segment and rank them by frequency × severity
Solutions: brainstorm at least three, from simple to bold, then compare them on impact, effort and risk
Trade-offs: name what your chosen solution gives up and why that is acceptable for this goal
Metrics: give one success metric, one or two input metrics and a guardrail that must not get worse
Teardown: for any app, note who it serves, its core loop, what works, what frustrates and one improvement

tasks.title: Answer "design a product to help first-time UPI users in small towns" aloud in 20 minutes, then write it up
Write a one-page teardown of a food delivery app: users, core loop, three pains and one improvement

topics.title: Success metrics and diagnosing metric changes
topics.summary_md: The second half of most product sense interviews is about metrics: how to measure success and why a number moved. Pick a **North Star metric** that captures value delivered, break it into input metrics the team can move, and protect it with guardrails. When a metric drops, rule out data problems first, then segment the change before guessing causes.
key_points: A good North Star reflects value delivered to users, not just activity.
Pair every success metric with a guardrail metric.
For a metric drop: check the data, then timing, segments, internal and external causes.
learn_items: North Star metric: one number reflecting user value, e.g. orders delivered per week, not app opens
Input metrics: the 3–4 levers that drive the North Star, such as new users, frequency and conversion
Guardrail metrics: numbers that must not worsen while you optimise, such as cancellations or support tickets
Funnels: define each step (visit, add to cart, pay, success) and measure conversion between steps
Retention: read a cohort table; know D1, D7 and D30 retention and why retention beats sign-ups
HEART framework: Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, Task success, each with goals and signals
Metric drop diagnosis: check tracking bugs, sudden vs gradual, segment by platform, region and version
External causes: seasonality, festivals and holidays, competitor launches, outages and policy changes

tasks.title: Write a step-by-step diagnosis for "weekly orders on a food delivery app fell 15% this week"
Define a North Star, three input metrics and two guardrails for a ride-hailing app

topics.title: User interviews that reveal real problems
topics.summary_md: Discovery reduces the risk of building something nobody needs. The core skill is the **user interview**: ask about specific past behaviour rather than opinions or hypothetical futures, because people are poor at predicting what they would do. Listen far more than you talk, dig into the last real instance of the problem, and keep your solution out of the conversation.
key_points: Ask "tell me about the last time…", never "would you use…".
Compliments and promises are not evidence; past actions and money spent are.
Talk to 5–8 people per segment before drawing conclusions.
Keep your idea out of the interview until the end, if at all.
learn_items: Research goal: write the decision the interviews must inform and 3–5 questions you need answered
Recruiting: screen for people who had the problem recently; 5–8 per segment usually shows clear patterns
Past behaviour: "Tell me about the last time you…" and "What did you do next?" beat opinion questions
Leading questions: not "Wouldn't it help if…?" but "How do you handle this today?"
Follow-ups: ask why, ask for an example, and use silence to let people keep talking
Workarounds: spreadsheets, WhatsApp groups and paid fixes show that a pain is real and costly
Notes: capture verbatim quotes and observed actions separately from your interpretation
Ethics: get consent to record, explain how notes are used and never pressure people

tasks.title: Write a 10-question guide on how college students split shared expenses, using only past-behaviour questions
Interview two classmates with your guide and write up quotes, workarounds and surprises

topics.title: Synthesis: affinity maps, jobs to be done and personas
topics.summary_md: Raw interview notes become useful only after synthesis. Cluster observations into themes on an **affinity map**, turn the strongest themes into **jobs to be done** and problem statements, and summarise distinct behaviour patterns as personas. Every insight should trace back to quotes or observations, not to what the team already believed.
key_points: One observation per note; cluster bottom-up, then name the clusters.
Job statement: When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome].
Personas describe behaviour and goals, not invented demographics.
learn_items: Affinity mapping: one quote or observation per note, group similar notes, then name each group as an insight
Insight vs observation: an observation is what happened; an insight explains why it matters
Job statement: "When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [expected outcome]"
Kinds of jobs: functional (get a task done), emotional (feel a certain way) and social (be seen a certain way)
Personas: 2–3 based on behaviour patterns from research; include goals, frustrations and context
Problem statement: user, need and insight in one sentence, with no solution inside it
How might we: reframe a problem as "How might we…?" to open several solution directions
Opportunity solution tree: outcome at the top, opportunities below, solutions and tests under each

tasks.title: Affinity-map 30 interview notes (yours or a sample) into themes and write three job statements

topics.title: Testing assumptions with cheap experiments
topics.summary_md: Interviews show problems; experiments test whether your solution will work before you build it fully. List the assumptions behind an idea, find the **riskiest** ones (desirability, viability, feasibility, usability) and test each with the cheapest experiment that gives real evidence. Decide the success threshold before running the test so results cannot be explained away.
key_points: Test first the assumption that would kill the idea if it were wrong.
Set a pass or fail threshold before the experiment starts.
Prefer behaviour (sign-ups, payments) over stated intent in surveys.
learn_items: Assumption mapping: plot assumptions by importance and evidence; test important ones with little evidence
Four risks: desirability (want it), viability (works for the business), feasibility (can build), usability
Fake door test: show a button or page for a feature that does not exist yet and measure clicks honestly
Concierge MVP: deliver the service by hand to a few users to learn what they value before automating
Wizard of Oz: users see a working product interface while people do the work behind it
Surveys: use them to measure how common a known problem is, not to discover new problems
Success criteria: write "we will build it if at least X of Y users do Z" before the test
A/B tests: need enough traffic and one primary metric; low-traffic products should use qualitative tests

tasks.title: List ten assumptions behind a hostel food subscription idea and design tests for the riskiest two

topics.title: Market sizing: TAM, SAM, SOM and guesstimates
topics.summary_md: Market sizing estimates how big an opportunity is. **TAM** is total demand for the category, **SAM** the part your product can actually serve, and **SOM** the share you can realistically win in the next few years. Build estimates **bottom-up** (customers × usage × price) and state every assumption; interviewers care more about structure than about the final number.
key_points: TAM ⊃ SAM ⊃ SOM: each is a narrower, more realistic slice.
Bottom-up beats quoting a report: customers × frequency × price.
Say assumptions aloud, round numbers and sanity-check the answer.
learn_items: TAM, SAM, SOM: total market, the part you can serve (segment, region, channel), and the share you can win
Top-down: start from a large figure and narrow by percentages; quick but easy to get wrong
Bottom-up: target customers × purchases per year × average price; preferred for product decisions
Guesstimate steps: clarify, choose a formula, segment the population, estimate each part, multiply, check
Segmenting: split by urban vs rural, age group or income band when behaviour differs a lot between them
Sanity check: compare the result with a known anchor and ask whether the order of magnitude is plausible
Rounding: use round numbers (India has roughly 1.4 billion people) and say they are approximations

tasks.title: Estimate the yearly market for second-hand engineering textbooks in India bottom-up, writing every assumption

topics.title: Competitive analysis and positioning
topics.summary_md: Competitive analysis shows where a product can win. Map **direct** competitors, **indirect** ones and substitutes (including doing nothing or using WhatsApp and spreadsheets), compare them on what customers actually value, and find a position that is both different and defensible. Public signals such as app store reviews, pricing pages and job posts show what rivals do well and badly.
key_points: Include substitutes and the status quo, not just look-alike apps.
Compare on attributes customers value, not on feature counts.
A position is useful only if it is different and hard to copy.
learn_items: Competitor types: direct (same product), indirect (same job, different product), substitutes, doing nothing
Feature matrix: competitors as rows, customer-valued attributes as columns; mark strengths and gaps honestly
Positioning map: plot competitors on two axes customers care about, e.g. price vs speed, to find open space
SWOT: strengths and weaknesses are internal; opportunities and threats are external
Five forces: rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power and supplier power shape industry profit
Moats: network effects, switching costs, scale, brand and proprietary data make a position defensible
Public signals: app reviews, pricing pages, release notes and job posts reveal priorities and weaknesses

tasks.title: Build a feature matrix and a two-axis positioning map for three quick-commerce grocery apps

topics.title: Structure of a PRD: problem, goals and scope
topics.summary_md: A product requirements document (PRD) aligns the team on **why** and **what** while leaving **how** to engineering and design. A good PRD opens with the problem and its evidence, states goals with measurable success metrics, defines scope and explicit **non-goals**, and lists risks and open questions. Keep it short, cite evidence and update it as decisions change.
key_points: Start with the problem and evidence, not the solution.
Non-goals prevent scope creep as much as goals guide the work.
A PRD is a living document: record decisions and open questions.
learn_items: Problem statement: who has the problem, how often, the impact, and the evidence (interviews, data, tickets)
Goals and metrics: one primary success metric with a target, plus guardrail metrics
Scope and non-goals: what is in this release and what is deliberately left out
Users and use cases: the target segment and the main scenarios the feature must support
Requirements: functional needs as user stories; non-functional needs such as speed, security, accessibility
Risks, dependencies and open questions: what could fail, who you depend on, what is still undecided
Rollout: phased release, feature flags, and how you will measure and decide whether to expand
One-pager: for small features, a single page with problem, goal, scope and metric is enough

tasks.title: Write a two-page PRD for "split bill" in a UPI payments app: problem, goals, metrics, scope, non-goals, risks

topics.title: User stories, acceptance criteria and edge cases
topics.summary_md: User stories turn requirements into small, testable pieces of value: "As a [user], I want [action], so that [benefit]". Each story needs **acceptance criteria**, often written as Given/When/Then, that tell engineers and testers exactly when it is done. Good PMs also list edge cases (empty, error, slow network, permissions), because that is where most bugs and confused users come from.
key_points: Story format: As a [user], I want [action], so that [benefit].
Acceptance criteria make "done" testable: Given, When, Then.
Split big stories by workflow step or rule, not by technical layer.
Always cover empty, error, loading and offline cases.
learn_items: User story: "As a [user], I want [action], so that [benefit]"; the benefit explains why it matters
INVEST: stories are Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable
Acceptance criteria: Given [context], When [action], Then [outcome]; one scenario per rule
Splitting: split by workflow step, business rule, data type or happy path vs edge cases
Edge cases: empty states, invalid input, network failure, timeouts, duplicates and permission denied
Epic, story, task: an epic groups stories; tasks are the technical steps inside a story
Definition of done: a shared checklist such as tested, reviewed, accessible, tracked and documented

tasks.title: Write six user stories with Given/When/Then criteria for booking a seat in a college library app
List every edge case for a UPI payment that times out after the user enters their PIN

topics.title: Scoring work with RICE, ICE and value vs effort
topics.summary_md: Prioritisation frameworks make trade-offs explicit so a team can compare ideas on the same scale. **RICE** scores reach × impact × confidence ÷ effort, **ICE** is a lighter version, and a **value vs effort** grid gives a quick visual sort. **Cost of delay** asks what you lose for each week an item waits. Scores inform judgement; they do not replace it.
key_points: RICE = reach × impact × confidence ÷ effort.
Use the same time window and units for every item you score.
Quick wins (high value, low effort) first; question big low-value work.
Revisit scores when new evidence arrives.
learn_items: RICE: reach (users per period) × impact (e.g. 0.25–3) × confidence (%) ÷ effort (person-months)
ICE: impact × confidence × ease, each scored 1–10; fast for early ideas, but more subjective
Value vs effort 2×2: quick wins, big bets, fill-ins and money pits; drop the money pits
Cost of delay: value lost per unit of time an item waits; urgent items have a steep cost of delay
WSJF: cost of delay ÷ job duration; do short work with a high cost of delay first
Confidence: lower it when an estimate rests on opinion, raise it when backed by data or research
Pitfalls: inflated impact, ignored dependencies, and treating a score as more precise than its inputs

tasks.title: Score eight feature ideas for a campus marketplace app with RICE in a table and explain the top three

topics.title: Scoping releases with MoSCoW, Kano and MVPs
topics.summary_md: Once you know what matters, you must decide how much of it ships. **MoSCoW** sorts scope into Must, Should, Could and Won't for a given release; the **Kano model** separates basic expectations from performance features and delighters; and an **MVP** is the smallest release that tests your riskiest assumption. Saying no clearly, with reasons, is part of the job.
key_points: Must-haves are only what the release cannot launch without.
Missing basics cause anger; having them causes little delight.
An MVP tests learning, not a cut-down version of everything.
learn_items: MoSCoW: Must (launch blocker), Should (important, not vital), Could (nice to have), Won't (not this time)
Must test: ask "would we delay the launch without this?"; if not, it is not a Must
Kano basic needs: expected features (e.g. payment receipts) that anger users when missing
Kano performance and delighters: more is better (faster delivery); delighters are unexpected and pleasing
Kano drift: delighters become expected over time, so today's delighter is tomorrow's basic need
MVP: the smallest product that tests the riskiest assumption with real users
Saying no: explain the trade-off, point to the goal, and say when it could be reconsidered
Opportunity cost: every yes delays something else; name what gets pushed out

tasks.title: Sort 15 requested features for the first release of a hostel mess feedback app into MoSCoW and justify each Must

topics.title: Scrum: roles, events and artefacts
topics.summary_md: Agile teams deliver in small increments and adjust from feedback. **Scrum** runs fixed sprints of up to a month (often two weeks) with three accountabilities (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers), five events and three artefacts. As a PM or product owner you own the **product backlog**, its order and the value of each sprint goal.
key_points: A sprint has one goal; scope can be renegotiated, the goal should not be.
The daily scrum is a 15-minute plan for the next day, not a status report.
The review shows working product; the retrospective improves how the team works.
learn_items: Accountabilities: Product Owner orders the backlog, Scrum Master coaches the process, Developers build
Events: the Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum (15 min), Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective
Artefacts: Product Backlog (with a Product Goal), Sprint Backlog (with a Sprint Goal) and the Increment
Definition of Done: the shared quality bar every increment must meet before it counts as done
Backlog refinement: break down, clarify and estimate upcoming items so planning stays quick
Story points: relative estimates of effort and uncertainty, often on a Fibonacci-like scale
Planning poker: everyone reveals an estimate at once, then the highest and lowest explain their reasoning
Velocity: points finished per sprint; useful for a team's own forecasting, never for comparing teams

tasks.title: Plan a two-week sprint for a college fest ticketing app: sprint goal, ten backlog items, estimates, Definition of Done

topics.title: Kanban, flow metrics and shipping safely
topics.summary_md: **Kanban** manages continuous flow instead of fixed sprints: visualise work on a board, limit **work in progress** (WIP) and measure how long items take. It suits support, operations and teams with unpredictable work. Whatever the method, ship small: feature flags, staged rollouts and clear release notes let teams release often while keeping risk low.
key_points: Lower WIP usually means shorter cycle times: stop starting, start finishing.
Measure cycle time and throughput, not hours worked.
Feature flags separate deploying code from releasing a feature.
learn_items: Kanban board: a column per workflow stage (to do, in progress, review, done) with explicit entry rules
WIP limits: cap items per column; when a column is full, help finish work instead of starting more
Cycle time vs lead time: cycle time starts when work begins; lead time starts when the request is made
Throughput: items finished per week; forecast from throughput history rather than from estimates
Little's law: average WIP = throughput × average cycle time, so less WIP means faster delivery
Scrum vs Kanban: sprints and set roles vs continuous flow; many teams mix the two
Feature flags and staged rollout: release to a small share of users, watch metrics, expand or roll back
Release notes: say what changed for users in plain words and what they need to do, if anything

tasks.title: Design a Kanban board with WIP limits for a three-person team supporting a student app, and explain each limit

topics.title: Vision, strategy and where to play
topics.summary_md: Strategy is a small set of choices about **where to play** (which users, problems and markets) and **how to win** there. A vision describes the future you want; a strategy explains why your approach will get there despite competitors and constraints. Good strategy is as clear about what the team will not do as about what it will.
key_points: Vision is where you are going; strategy is the choice of path.
A strategy must say what you will not do.
Diagnose the key challenge before choosing actions.
learn_items: Vision: an inspiring picture of the future for users, stable for years, e.g. "every graduate finds work"
Strategy kernel: a diagnosis of the challenge, a guiding policy, and coherent actions that follow from it
Where to play: target segments, use cases, regions and channels; narrower choices are easier to win
How to win: the advantage, such as lower cost, better experience, network effects or distribution
Bad strategy signs: fluffy goals, a list of everything, no hard choices and no diagnosis
Strategy vs plan: a plan lists activities; a strategy explains why those activities will win
Trade-offs: write down the segments and features you are explicitly not pursuing, and why

tasks.title: Write a one-page strategy for a job app for tier-2 city graduates: diagnosis, where to play, how to win, what not to do

topics.title: OKRs and outcome-based roadmaps
topics.summary_md: Strategy becomes actionable through goals and a roadmap. **OKRs** pair a qualitative objective with 2–5 measurable key results that describe outcomes, not tasks. An **outcome-based roadmap** groups work by the problems to solve, often as **Now, Next, Later**, so teams commit to results while staying free to change the solutions as they learn.
key_points: Key results measure outcomes ("activation from 30% to 40%"), not outputs ("ship onboarding").
Now, Next, Later avoids fake precision about dates far in the future.
Roadmaps communicate priorities; they are not promises of features on dates.
learn_items: Objective: a qualitative, inspiring goal for a quarter, e.g. "Make first payments effortless"
Key results: 2–5 measurable outcomes with a baseline and a target; if it is a task, it is not a key result
Outputs vs outcomes: outputs are things shipped; outcomes are changes in user behaviour or business results
Now, Next, Later: detailed and committed now, problems to solve next, broad themes later
Themes: group roadmap items under the problem or goal they serve, not under teams or features
Dates: commit to dates only for near-term or externally fixed items, such as a festival sale
Audiences: leadership wants goals and trade-offs, engineering wants sequence, sales wants timing

tasks.title: Write one quarter's OKRs and a Now, Next, Later roadmap for a college placement-prep app

topics.title: Business models, pricing and unit economics
topics.summary_md: Products succeed only if the business works. Know the common **business models** (subscription, transaction fee, marketplace take rate, advertising, freemium), how **pricing** is set, and the **unit economics** that show whether each customer is profitable. In price-sensitive markets such as India, pricing, packaging and payment method (UPI, small low-priced plans) often matter as much as features.
key_points: Lifetime value (LTV) must comfortably exceed acquisition cost (CAC).
Price on value to the customer, not only on your cost.
Freemium works when free users are cheap to serve and some upgrade.
learn_items: Business models: subscription, transaction fee, marketplace take rate, advertising, licensing, freemium
CAC: total sales and marketing spend ÷ new customers acquired in the same period
LTV: average revenue per user × gross margin × expected lifetime (or ÷ churn rate)
Contribution margin: revenue per order minus variable costs such as delivery, discounts and payment fees
Pricing approaches: cost-plus, competitor-based and value-based; value-based captures most when value is clear
Packaging: tiers (free, pro, premium), usage limits and small plans for price-sensitive users
Payback period: months of margin needed to recover CAC; shorter payback means less cash needed to grow

tasks.title: Build a unit economics sheet for one grocery delivery order: revenue, costs, contribution margin, CAC, payback

topics.title: Mapping stakeholders and communicating decisions
topics.summary_md: PMs lead without formal authority, so influence comes from trust and clarity. Map who is affected by your work and how much influence they have, agree who decides what using RACI or DACI, and keep people informed with short, regular written updates. Share bad news early: surprises damage trust far more than problems do.
key_points: Manage closely those with high power and high interest.
Name one decision owner for every decision.
Write decisions down with context, options and rationale.
learn_items: Stakeholder list: everyone affected, such as engineering, design, sales, support, legal and leadership
Power-interest grid: manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor
RACI: Responsible does the work, Accountable owns the outcome (only one), then Consulted and Informed
DACI: Driver runs the decision, Approver decides, Contributors advise, Informed are told the result
Written updates: a weekly note with progress against goals, risks, decisions needed and next steps
Decision log: date, decision, options considered, rationale and owner, so debates are not repeated
Pre-wiring: talk to key people one-on-one before a big meeting so there are no surprises in the room

tasks.title: Map stakeholders on a power-interest grid for launching cash on delivery in a food app, and write a RACI
Write a 200-word weekly update for a delayed feature that states the risk, its cause and the decision needed

topics.title: Handling disagreement, pushback and saying no
topics.summary_md: Conflict is normal when goals compete. Separate the people from the problem, uncover the interest behind each position, and anchor discussions on shared goals and data. Once a decision is made, **disagree and commit**; when you must say no, explain the trade-off and the goal it protects. Escalate only after trying to resolve things directly, and escalate together.
key_points: Positions are what people ask for; interests are why they ask.
Say no to the request, not to the person, and give the reason.
Once decided, commit fully even if you argued against it.
learn_items: Positions vs interests: ask "what problem would this solve for you?" to find the need behind a request
Shared goals: frame trade-offs against the agreed goal or metric, not personal preference
Data over opinion: bring evidence, and agree in advance what evidence would change minds
Saying no: acknowledge the need, explain the trade-off, offer an alternative or a time to revisit
Disagree and commit: argue your view, then fully support the decision once it is made
Escalation: try direct resolution first, then escalate jointly with both views written fairly
Engineers and designers: bring problems and constraints, and let them shape the solutions

tasks.title: Script saying no to a sales lead who wants a custom feature for one large client this sprint, then role-play it

topics.title: Visual hierarchy and Gestalt grouping
topics.summary_md: Good interfaces guide the eye to what matters first. Build **visual hierarchy** with size, weight, colour, contrast and position so the most important element clearly wins. **Gestalt principles** explain how people group what they see: items close together, similar in look or inside a shared region are read as related. Use them to make structure obvious without extra lines and boxes.
key_points: One primary action per screen should stand out clearly.
Proximity is the cheapest way to show that things belong together.
Use fewer borders: spacing and alignment can do the grouping.
learn_items: Hierarchy levers: size, weight, colour, contrast, position and whitespace; combine two or three at once
Squint test: blur or squint at the screen; the most important element should still stand out
Proximity: related items sit close together, unrelated items farther apart
Similarity: elements that look alike (colour, shape) are read as having the same function
Common region: a shared background or card groups content without extra dividers
Figure-ground: modals and menus need clear separation from what is behind them
Continuity and closure: eyes follow lines and complete partial shapes, e.g. a cut-off card hints at scrolling
De-emphasis: make secondary text lighter or smaller instead of making primary text louder

tasks.title: Redesign a cluttered product card from a shopping app using only size, weight, colour and spacing

topics.title: Alignment, whitespace, contrast and consistency
topics.summary_md: Polished screens follow a few habits. **Align** every element to a shared edge or grid line, use **whitespace** generously and on purpose, create **contrast** only where meaning differs, and keep patterns **consistent** so users can predict how things work. Familiar conventions beat novelty, because users spend most of their time in other apps.
key_points: Fewer alignment lines make a layout look calmer.
Whitespace is not wasted space; it groups and separates.
If two things look different, they should behave differently.
learn_items: Alignment: snap elements to a few shared edges; avoid centred text in long blocks
Whitespace: more space around groups than inside them; try adding space before cutting content
Contrast: make differences big enough to notice; small differences look like mistakes
Repetition: reuse the same styles for the same roles, so all secondary buttons look alike
Consistency: internal (within your product) and external (platform conventions such as back gestures)
Jakob's law: users expect your app to work like the apps they already use; follow common conventions
Balance: distribute visual weight so screens do not feel lopsided; symmetry is optional
Critique: describe what you see, link it to a user goal, then suggest a specific change

tasks.title: Critique two screens of a banking app for alignment, whitespace, contrast and consistency, with three fixes each

topics.title: Type scales, hierarchy and readable text
topics.summary_md: Most interface content is text, so typography carries much of the design. Choose sizes from a **type scale** (each step multiplied by a ratio such as 1.25), keep body text around 16px with a line height near 1.5, and limit line length to roughly 45–75 characters. Create hierarchy with size and weight before reaching for colour.
key_points: Use a type scale: a handful of sizes, not dozens.
Body: about 16px, line height about 1.5, 45–75 characters per line.
Headings need tighter line height than body text.
learn_items: Type scale: sizes from a base × ratio, e.g. 16, 20, 25, 31 with ratio 1.25; limit to 5–7 sizes
Ratios: 1.125 or 1.2 for dense apps, 1.25 or 1.333 for more contrast on marketing pages
Body text: 16px or larger on screens; smaller only for captions and secondary labels
Line height: about 1.4–1.6 for body text, 1.1–1.3 for large headings
Line length: 45–75 characters per line; set a maximum width on text containers
Weights: two or three (regular, medium or semibold, bold) are usually enough
Letter spacing: tighten large headings slightly; add tracking to small all-caps labels
Units: use rem in code so text respects the user's browser font size setting

tasks.title: Build a 1.25 type scale and use it to set an article page and a settings screen in Figma

topics.title: Choosing and pairing typefaces for interfaces
topics.summary_md: Typeface choice affects readability and personality. For interfaces, prefer typefaces with a large **x-height**, open letter shapes and a full range of weights; many teams use the system font stack or one well-made sans serif. Pair at most two families with clear contrast, and for Indian products check support for scripts such as Devanagari, Tamil or Bengali early.
key_points: One family with several weights is often enough.
Pair families that contrast clearly, e.g. a serif heading with a sans serif body.
Use tabular figures for numbers in tables and prices.
learn_items: Classification: serif, sans serif, monospace and display; keep display faces for large headings only
X-height: taller lowercase letters read better at small sizes on screens
Pairing: contrast in structure (serif with sans) and similar proportions; never two near-identical sans serifs
System font stack: fast, native feel and no download; a good default for product interfaces
Variable fonts: one file holds a range of weights and widths, reducing downloads
Indic scripts: confirm the family covers every script you need; test conjuncts, matras and line height
Numbers: tabular figures align digits in tables; format amounts as ₹1,00,000 where users expect it
Licensing: check that the font licence allows app embedding and web use before shipping

tasks.title: Create three heading and body font pairings for a news app with English and Hindi text, and pick one with reasons

topics.title: Colour models, palettes and semantic roles
topics.summary_md: Build colour systems by **role**, not by picking hues screen by screen. Start with a brand or primary colour, add neutrals for text and surfaces, and semantic colours for success, warning, danger and information, each with a range of shades. Models such as HSL and **OKLCH** make it easier than raw hex codes to create even steps of lightness.
key_points: Most of an interface is neutral; colour is for emphasis and meaning.
Name colours by role (primary, surface, danger), not by hue.
Generate shades with even lightness steps, e.g. a 50–900 scale.
learn_items: HSL: hue (0–360°), saturation and lightness; easy to reason about, but lightness is not perceptually even
OKLCH: lightness, chroma and hue tuned to human perception, so equal steps look equally different
Shade scale: 9–11 steps from light to dark (50 to 900) for each colour, used consistently
Neutrals: greys (often slightly tinted) for text, borders and surfaces make up most of the UI
Semantic roles: primary, surface, text, border, success, warning, danger and info
60-30-10: a dominant neutral, a secondary colour and a small accent; a rough guide, not a rule
Meaning: red can signal error or loss; check cultural and domain context, e.g. in finance apps
Brand vs UI: a bright brand colour may fail contrast as text; use a darker shade for text and links

tasks.title: Create a palette for a student finance app: primary, neutral and four semantic colours, each with five shades

topics.title: Contrast, accessibility and dark mode
topics.summary_md: Colour must work for everyone and in every theme. WCAG AA requires a **4.5:1** contrast ratio for normal text and **3:1** for large text and for essential parts of controls and icons. Never use colour as the only signal, since many people cannot tell red from green. Design dark mode from the same semantic roles, with dark grey surfaces and slightly softened colours rather than inverted ones.
key_points: Text 4.5:1; large text and UI parts 3:1 (WCAG AA).
Pair colour with an icon, text or pattern.
Dark mode is a separate set of values for the same roles, not an inversion.
learn_items: Contrast ratio: ranges from 1:1 to 21:1; AA needs 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text
Large text: at least 24px regular or about 18.7px bold; AAA raises normal text to 7:1
Non-text contrast: input borders, focus rings and meaningful icons need 3:1 against what is next to them
Colour blindness: red-green confusion is the most common type; add icons, labels or patterns
Checking: run a contrast checker plugin and a colour-blindness simulator on every key screen
Dark surfaces: use dark greys, show elevation with lighter surfaces, and soften pure white text
Dark mode colours: reduce the saturation of bright colours so they do not glow or vibrate
Tokens: map each role (text, surface, primary) to a light and a dark value so themes switch together

tasks.title: Audit a sign-up screen for contrast and colour-only signals, then make a dark mode version from the same roles

topics.title: Spacing scales and the 8-point system
topics.summary_md: Consistent spacing makes a screen feel designed. Pick a **spacing scale** based on 8 (4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64) and take every margin, padding and gap from it. Use smaller values inside components and larger ones between sections, so spacing itself shows how content is grouped.
key_points: Every gap comes from the scale; no random 13px values.
Spacing inside a group is smaller than spacing between groups.
Use 4 for fine adjustments inside small components.
learn_items: 8-point system: sizes and spacing in multiples of 8, with 4 for small details such as icon gaps
Spacing scale: 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64; name them as tokens (space-1, space-2 and so on)
Internal vs external: padding inside a component is smaller than the margin around it
Grouping by space: tight within related items, wider between groups, widest between sections
Component heights: buttons and inputs at 40 or 48px keep rhythm and comfortable tap targets
Baseline rhythm: set line heights in multiples of 4 so text lines up with the spacing system
Spacing in code: map the scale to CSS variables or utility classes so design and code match

tasks.title: Re-space a settings screen so every gap comes from an 8-point scale, noting each value you used

topics.title: Column grids and responsive layouts
topics.summary_md: A **column grid** gives layouts a shared structure across screen sizes. Common choices are 4 columns on phones, 8 on tablets and 12 on desktops, with fixed gutters and outer margins. Content spans whole columns, and **breakpoints** decide when the layout changes. Layout grids in Figma map closely to CSS grid and flexbox, which makes handoff easier.
key_points: 4, 8 and 12 columns for phone, tablet and desktop is a safe default.
Gutters and margins come from the spacing scale.
Design at least a mobile and a desktop layout for key screens.
learn_items: Grid anatomy: columns, gutters (gaps between columns) and margins (space at the outer edges)
Defaults: 4 columns with 16px margins on phones, 8 on tablets, 12 on desktop with 24–32px gutters
Fluid vs fixed: fluid grids stretch with the screen; fixed grids cap content at a maximum width
Breakpoints: change the layout where content breaks, often somewhere near 600, 900 and 1200px wide
Spanning: e.g. a card spans 4 of 12 columns on desktop and all 4 on mobile; keep spans consistent
Layout grids in Figma: add column and row grids to frames and snap elements to them
Code mapping: CSS grid-template-columns: repeat(12, 1fr) with a gap matches a 12-column design grid

tasks.title: Lay out a job listings page on a 12-column desktop grid and a 4-column mobile grid in Figma

topics.title: Figma basics: frames, layers and shapes
topics.summary_md: Figma is the standard interface design tool, used in the browser or the desktop app with real-time collaboration. Everything lives in **frames**, which act as screens or containers; inside them you place shapes, text and images as **layers**. Learn to name and organise layers cleanly, use constraints, and work with keyboard shortcuts from the start.
key_points: Use frames, not groups, for screens and containers.
Name layers by purpose; messy layer trees slow everyone down.
Learn the core shortcuts in your first week.
learn_items: Workspace: canvas, layers panel (left), properties panel (right), toolbar, and pages to organise work
Frames vs groups: frames have size, fill, clipping, constraints and layout grids; groups only bundle layers
Device frames: start from phone or desktop presets and keep the same size across a flow
Shapes and vectors: rectangle, ellipse and pen tool; boolean operations combine shapes
Text: auto width, auto height or fixed size boxes; set font, size, line height and letter spacing
Constraints: pin layers to edges or the centre so they behave correctly when a frame resizes
Shortcuts: F frame, R rectangle, T text, Ctrl+G group, Ctrl+Alt+G frame selection, Shift+A auto layout
Images and export: place images with fill modes; export as PNG, JPG, SVG or PDF at 1x or 2x

tasks.title: Recreate the home screen of a food delivery app in Figma with named layers and sensible constraints

topics.title: Styles, libraries, collaboration and handoff
topics.summary_md: Reusable **styles** for colour, text, effects and grids keep a file consistent: change a style once and every use updates. Shared **libraries** publish styles and components across files. Figma is also where teams collaborate through comments, version history and branching, and **Dev Mode** lets developers inspect measurements and export assets.
key_points: Never hardcode a colour or text setting that should be a style.
Organise files with clear pages: cover, flows, components, archive.
Mark finished frames ready for development and annotate edge cases.
learn_items: Styles: colour, text, effect and layout grid styles; apply them instead of raw values
Variables: store colours, numbers and strings and support modes such as light and dark
Libraries: publish styles and components from one file and enable them in others; review updates
File organisation: pages for cover, work in progress, final flows, components and archive
Collaboration: comments with mentions, observation mode, and version history with named versions
Branching: explore big changes in a branch and merge them after review (available on paid plans)
Dev Mode: developers inspect sizes, spacing, styles and code snippets, compare changes and export assets
Handoff notes: annotate interactions, states and edge cases next to frames marked ready for development

tasks.title: Turn every colour and text setting in your food app screen into styles and add handoff annotations

topics.title: Auto layout: direction, gap, padding and resizing
topics.summary_md: **Auto layout** makes Figma frames behave much like CSS flexbox: children stack horizontally or vertically, or wrap onto new lines, with set gaps and padding, and the frame resizes as content changes. Each layer can **hug** its contents, **fill** the container or stay **fixed**. Nesting auto layout frames is how you build buttons, cards and whole screens that adapt to real content.
key_points: Hug fits the content, fill takes available space, fixed stays put.
Build from the inside out: button, then row, then card, then screen.
Gaps and padding should come from your spacing scale.
learn_items: Adding auto layout: Shift+A on a selection; set the direction to horizontal, vertical or wrap
Gap and padding: space between items and inside the frame; "space between" spreads items evenly
Alignment: align children to start, centre or end on both axes, like justify and align in flexbox
Resizing: each layer can hug contents, fill the container, or use a fixed width and height
Min and max width: stop a fill element from becoming too narrow or too wide
Absolute position: lift one child (such as a badge) out of the flow while keeping it in the frame
Nesting: combine vertical and horizontal frames, e.g. a card is a vertical stack holding a horizontal row
Text: set text layers to fill width with auto height so long strings wrap instead of overflowing

tasks.title: Build a job listing card with nested auto layout that copes with long titles, many tags and a missing logo

topics.title: Components, variants and component properties
topics.summary_md: A **component** is a reusable main element; each copy is an **instance** that updates when the main component changes. **Variants** group related versions (size, state, type) into one component set, and **component properties** (boolean, text, instance swap, variant) let designers change an instance from the properties panel without detaching it. Combined with auto layout, this gives flexible and consistent building blocks.
key_points: Edit the main component; instances follow while keeping their overrides.
Avoid detaching instances: it breaks the link to future updates.
Name variant properties like code: size=sm|md|lg, state=default|hover.
learn_items: Main component and instances: Ctrl+Alt+K creates a component; instances inherit changes, keep overrides
Variants: combine versions into a component set with properties such as type, size and state
Boolean property: show or hide a layer, e.g. the leading icon on a button
Text property: expose label text so it can be edited from the properties panel
Instance swap property: replace a nested instance, e.g. choose which icon a button shows
Nested instances: expose nested properties so people configure children from the parent
Interactive components: link variants with hover or press interactions for realistic prototypes
Naming: slash naming (Button/Primary) and property names that match the names used in code

tasks.title: Build a button component with variants for type, size and state, plus icon and label properties

topics.title: Design tokens: primitives, semantics and modes
topics.summary_md: A design system is the shared language of design and engineering, and **tokens** are its smallest pieces: named values for colour, type, spacing, radius and shadow. Keep two layers: **primitive** tokens hold raw values, and **semantic** tokens describe purpose and point to primitives. Modes such as light and dark swap the values behind semantic tokens without touching components.
key_points: Components use semantic tokens, never raw primitives.
Name by purpose: color.text.muted, not grey-500.
Modes switch values; names stay the same.
learn_items: Token: a named design decision, e.g. space.4 = 16px or color.text.default = gray.900
Primitive tokens: the raw palette and scales (blue.600, size.16) with no meaning attached
Semantic tokens: purpose-based aliases (color.action.primary, color.surface.raised) that reference primitives
Naming pattern: category.property.variant.state, e.g. color.border.input.focus; stay consistent
Figma variables: one collection for primitives, one for semantics; modes for light, dark or brand themes
Scoping: limit each variable to the fields where it belongs (fills, gaps, radius) to prevent misuse
Coverage: colour, typography, spacing, radius, elevation, motion duration and breakpoints

tasks.title: Create primitive and semantic colour and spacing variables with light and dark modes for a college events app

topics.title: Building and documenting a component library
topics.summary_md: Components turn tokens into reusable UI: buttons, inputs, selects, cards, dialogs and navigation. Each needs every state designed, accessibility built in and clear usage guidelines, so others use it correctly without asking. Start from the components your product repeats most, and document when to use each one and when not to.
key_points: Build the most-used components first; do not design for imaginary needs.
Document states, variants, do and don't examples, and accessibility for each component.
Prefer composing small parts over one giant configurable component.
learn_items: Inventory: screenshot existing screens, group duplicates and pick which components to standardise
Composition: small parts (icons, labels) build components, which build patterns such as forms
States: default, hover, focus, pressed, disabled, loading, error and selected where relevant
Accessibility: visible focus rings, 3:1 non-text contrast, labels for icon buttons, keyboard behaviour
Documentation: purpose, anatomy, variants, states, spacing, do and don't examples and content rules
Patterns: document combinations such as forms, empty states and confirmation flows, not just pieces
Flexible content areas: let cards and dialogs hold any content instead of adding endless variants

tasks.title: Design a text input component with all its states and write a one-page usage guideline for it

topics.title: Syncing with code, versioning and governance
topics.summary_md: A design system only works if design and code match. Teams export tokens as JSON, often in the Design Tokens Community Group format, transform them into CSS variables and platform code with build tools, and version releases with **semantic versioning**. Governance decides who can add or change components, and how teams contribute and hear about updates.
key_points: One source of truth for tokens, transformed for each platform.
Semantic versioning: breaking changes bump the major version.
A clear contribution process prevents forks and one-off components.
learn_items: Token pipeline: tokens as JSON → build tool → CSS variables plus Android and iOS values from one source
Token format: the Design Tokens Community Group JSON format gives each token a $value and a $type
Parity: the same names in Figma and code; link components to their code with snippets in Dev Mode
Semantic versioning: MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new features, PATCH for fixes
Changelog and deprecation: announce changes and mark old components deprecated before removing them
Governance models: a central team, federated contributors, or a hybrid with a review process
Adoption signals: share of screens built from system components and the number of detached instances

tasks.title: Write your colour and spacing tokens as JSON and map them by hand to CSS custom properties
Draft a one-page contribution process for proposing a new component

topics.title: User flows and low-fidelity wireframes
topics.summary_md: Before visual design, map how users reach a goal and sketch the structure of each screen. A **user flow** shows the steps, decisions and screens between an entry point and a goal; a **wireframe** shows layout, content and hierarchy in greyscale without polish. Staying low-fidelity keeps feedback on structure and makes it cheap to throw ideas away.
key_points: Start from the user goal and entry point, then map the steps.
Wireframes use realistic content, not lorem ipsum.
Sketch several options quickly before committing to one.
learn_items: User flow: entry point → steps → decisions → success, with error and back paths shown
Flow symbols: rectangles for screens, diamonds for decisions, arrows for user actions
Task flow vs user flow: a task flow is one linear path; a user flow includes branches and user types
Paper sketches: draw 6–8 rough layout ideas in a few minutes (crazy eights) before using software
Wireframe content: real labels and realistic text lengths reveal layout problems early
Fidelity: low (boxes and lines), mid (greyscale with real layout), high (full visual design)
Annotations: note behaviour, rules and data sources next to the wireframe

tasks.title: Draw the user flow for booking a doctor's appointment in a health app, including payment failure and rescheduling
Sketch eight layout ideas for the doctor list screen in eight minutes, then wireframe the best one

topics.title: Screen patterns for mobile and web wireframes
topics.summary_md: Most screens reuse a small set of proven patterns: lists and detail views, forms, search and filters, dashboards and onboarding. Knowing these patterns and the platform conventions for mobile and web lets you wireframe quickly and spend your thinking time where your product is actually different. Design for the smallest screen first, then expand.
key_points: Reuse proven patterns; innovate only where it matters.
Mobile first: decide what truly fits on a small screen.
Put primary actions within easy thumb reach on phones.
learn_items: List and detail: scannable rows with key information, and a detail screen for everything else
Forms: one column, labels above fields, related fields grouped, the primary button at the end
Search and filters: search at the top, filters as chips or a sheet, result counts and a clear-all option
Navigation: a bottom tab bar for 3–5 top destinations on mobile; top navigation or a sidebar on desktop
Thumb zone: put frequent actions in the lower middle of phone screens, not in the top corners
Mobile first: wireframe the phone layout, then add columns and side panels for larger screens
States: wireframe the empty, loading, error and full states of each key screen, not just the happy path

tasks.title: Wireframe five mobile screens for a second-hand book marketplace: home, search results, detail, chat, sell form

topics.title: Clickable prototypes: flows, links and fidelity
topics.summary_md: A prototype lets people experience a design before anyone writes code. In Figma, connect frames with **interactions** (on tap, navigate to), set a starting point for each flow and present it on a device. Build only the paths you need to answer your question, and match fidelity to that question: low for flow and structure, high for visual and interaction details.
key_points: Decide which question the prototype must answer first.
Build the happy path plus the one or two branches you will test.
Test on a real phone when the product is mobile.
learn_items: Purpose: exploring ideas, testing usability or showing stakeholders; each needs a different fidelity
Flows and starting points: one starting frame per flow so testers begin in the right place
Interactions: a trigger (on tap, on drag, while hovering, after delay) plus an action (navigate, overlay, back)
Overlays: open menus, bottom sheets and dialogs as overlays positioned over the current frame
Scrolling: set overflow scrolling on frames and fix headers or tab bars so they stay in place
Transitions: instant, dissolve, move in, push and slide; keep them short and consistent
Presenting: use present mode with the right device frame, or the Figma mobile app on a real phone

tasks.title: Prototype the doctor booking flow from your wireframes: list, detail, slot choice, payment and confirmation

topics.title: Smart animate, variables and realistic prototypes
topics.summary_md: Realistic prototypes need state and motion. **Smart animate** animates matching layers between frames, **interactive components** let a button or toggle handle its own states, and **variables with conditionals** let a prototype remember values such as a cart count or a signed-in flag. Use them to test detailed interactions, but do not try to build the whole app in Figma.
key_points: Smart animate matches layers by name across frames.
Interactive components cut the number of frames you need.
Stop when the prototype answers the question; it is not production code.
learn_items: Smart animate: animates position, size, opacity and rotation of same-named layers between two frames
Easing: ease-out for entering elements, ease-in for leaving ones; keep most transitions to 150–300 ms
Interactive components: wire variants (off and on, default and pressed) so every instance works
Variables in prototypes: a "set variable" action on click stores values like quantity or the selected tab
Conditionals: if/else on variable values shows different outcomes, such as an empty cart
Device testing: try gestures (drag, swipe) on a phone, because mouse clicks hide touch problems
Prototype hygiene: name flows, delete unused links and click through every path before a session

tasks.title: Prototype an add-to-cart flow with a quantity stepper and a cart badge using variables and smart animate

topics.title: Feedback, affordances and component states
topics.summary_md: Interaction design shapes how a product responds to people. Controls must look like what they do (**affordances** and **signifiers**), every action needs visible **feedback**, and every component needs designed states for hover, focus, pressed, disabled, loading and error. Make targets large and easy to reach, and let people undo mistakes instead of only warning them.
key_points: Every action gets feedback, ideally within about 100 ms.
Design all the states, not just the default.
Prefer undo over "Are you sure?" dialogs for reversible actions.
learn_items: Affordance and signifier: what an element allows, and the cue (shape, underline, shadow) that shows it
Feedback: pressed states, spinners, toasts and inline messages confirm that an action happened
Component states: default, hover, focus, pressed, disabled, loading, error, success and selected
Target size: at least 24×24 CSS px under WCAG 2.2 AA; 44–48px is the usual mobile guideline
Fitts's law: bigger and closer targets are faster to hit; place key actions near the user's focus
Hick's law: more choices take longer to decide; reduce or group options for frequent decisions
Error prevention and recovery: constrain input, confirm destructive actions and offer undo
Keyboard: logical tab order, visible focus, Enter or Space to activate and Esc to close

tasks.title: Design every state of a "Pay ₹499" button and a UPI ID input, including loading, error and success

topics.title: Motion, loading states and response times
topics.summary_md: Timing shapes how fast and trustworthy a product feels. About **0.1 s** feels instant, about **1 s** keeps the user's flow of thought, and beyond about **10 s** attention drifts, so match the loading pattern to the wait. Use motion to explain changes (where something came from or went), keep it short, and respect the reduced-motion setting.
key_points: Under about 1 s: no spinner needed; 1–10 s: an indicator; longer: progress and an estimate.
Motion should explain, not decorate.
Honour reduced motion: replace movement with fades or nothing.
learn_items: Response time limits: 0.1 s feels instant, 1 s keeps the flow of thought, 10 s is the limit of attention
Loading patterns: skeleton screens for content, spinners for short waits, progress bars for long tasks
Optimistic UI: show the result at once (a like, a sent message) and roll back with a message if it fails
Motion purpose: show relationships, continuity and state changes, e.g. a card expanding into a page
Duration and easing: about 100–300 ms for most UI motion; ease-out to enter, ease-in to exit
Micro-interactions: trigger, rules, feedback, and loops and modes, e.g. pull to refresh or a toggle
Reduced motion: respect the OS setting (prefers-reduced-motion) and avoid large parallax and zooms

tasks.title: Design loading, empty, error and success states for a train ticket search results screen
Prototype a like-button micro-interaction with smart animate, plus a reduced-motion version

topics.title: Planning and running a moderated usability test
topics.summary_md: Usability testing means watching real people try realistic tasks with your design. Recruit about five representative users per round, write task scenarios that give a goal without hinting at the interface, ask participants to **think aloud**, and observe without helping. Several small rounds with fixes in between find more problems than one large study.
key_points: Test tasks, not opinions: watch what people do.
Do not lead or rescue; ask "what would you do next?".
About five users per round, then fix and test again.
