learn_items: Test plan: goals, participant profile, 4–6 tasks, success criteria, prototype version and team roles
Recruiting: screen for real target users; friends who know the product give biased results
Task scenarios: realistic goals ("Book a cab to the station for 6 am") without naming buttons or menus
Think aloud: ask people to say what they look for and expect; prompt gently when they go quiet
Moderation: stay neutral, answer questions with questions, and help only if someone is fully stuck
Observing: note where people hesitate, backtrack, misread or fail; a note-taker frees the moderator
Moderated vs unmoderated: live sessions allow follow-up questions; unmoderated tests scale but lose context
Pilot: run the full session once with a colleague to fix confusing tasks and broken links

tasks.title: Write a usability test plan with five task scenarios for your doctor booking prototype
Run the test with three people and record where each one hesitated or failed

topics.title: Heuristic evaluation and analysing findings
topics.summary_md: A **heuristic evaluation** reviews a design against established usability principles and catches obvious problems before you test with users. After testing, turn observations into findings: group repeated problems, rate their **severity** and recommend specific fixes. Report a few clear, prioritised issues with evidence rather than a long list nobody acts on.
key_points: Heuristics find likely problems; tests confirm real ones.
Severity depends on how often a problem occurs, its impact and whether it persists.
Each finding: what happened, evidence, severity and a fix.
learn_items: Heuristics 1–5: visibility of status, match with the real world, user control, consistency, error prevention
Heuristics 6–10: recognition over recall, flexibility, minimalist design, error recovery, help and docs
Running an evaluation: 3–5 evaluators review alone, then merge their issues and remove duplicates
Severity scale: 0 not a problem, 1 cosmetic, 2 minor, 3 major, 4 catastrophic
Metrics: task success rate, time on task, errors per task and a questionnaire such as SUS
Synthesis: list issues per task, count how many participants hit each, and attach quotes or clips
Report: top issues first with evidence and a concrete recommendation; note what worked well too

tasks.title: Run a heuristic evaluation of a railway ticket booking app and rate each issue on the 0–4 severity scale

topics.title: Organising content: card sorting and sitemaps
topics.summary_md: **Information architecture** (IA) decides how content is grouped, labelled and connected so people can find things. Learn how your users think about the content with **card sorting**, choose an organisation scheme that matches their tasks, and record the structure in a **sitemap**. Labels should use the users' words, not internal team jargon.
key_points: Organise around user tasks and mental models, not the org chart.
Open card sorts discover groups; closed sorts test existing ones.
Balance breadth and depth; do not bury content many levels down.
learn_items: IA parts: organisation (grouping), labelling (names), navigation (moving) and search (finding)
Organisation schemes: by topic, task, audience, time or alphabet; mix them only for clear reasons
Open card sort: users group cards and name the groups themselves, revealing their mental models
Closed card sort: users place cards into predefined groups, checking a proposed structure
Analysing sorts: look for cards often grouped together and for cards with no agreement
Sitemap: a hierarchy diagram of sections and pages, numbered by level (1.0, 1.1, 1.1.1)
Breadth vs depth: a few levels with clear groups is usually easier than a deep, narrow tree

tasks.title: Run an open card sort with 25 cards for a college app with three classmates, then draw a sitemap

topics.title: Navigation design, labelling and tree testing
topics.summary_md: Navigation turns the IA into something people can move through. Choose patterns that fit the platform and the number of destinations, show users where they are, and support both browsing and search. **Tree testing** checks whether people can find items in your structure without visual design getting in the way.
key_points: Users must always know where they are and how to go back.
Tree testing checks findability before visual design.
Search complements navigation; it does not replace a clear structure.
learn_items: Global vs local navigation: global for top sections everywhere, local for options within a section
Patterns: bottom tabs, top tabs, side navigation, drawers, breadcrumbs and hub-and-spoke
Wayfinding: highlight the current section, use clear page titles and add breadcrumbs on deep pages
Tree test: users find items in a text-only hierarchy; measure success rate and directness
First click: where people click first strongly predicts whether they complete the task
Search: show suggestions, tolerate typos and transliterated words, and design a useful no-results state
Labelling: short, specific, parallel labels; avoid vague ones such as "Resources" or "More" where possible

tasks.title: Design and run a tree test with six find-it tasks on your college app sitemap, then revise the structure

topics.title: Buttons, labels and error messages
topics.summary_md: Words are part of the interface. Write buttons as **verbs that describe the outcome**, labels that say exactly what goes in a field, and error messages that explain what happened and how to fix it, without blaming the user. Keep text short, put the key words first and use the same term for the same thing everywhere.
key_points: Buttons: verb plus object, e.g. "Save changes", not "OK".
Errors: what happened, why if useful, and how to fix it.
One term per concept across the whole product.
learn_items: Buttons: verb plus object ("Pay ₹499", "Send invite"); avoid vague "Submit", "OK" or "Click here"
Labels: name the content precisely ("Mobile number"); give format hints outside the placeholder
Error messages: say what went wrong and how to fix it, e.g. "Enter a 10-digit mobile number"
Error tone: no blame, no jargon, no bare error codes; keep what the user typed whenever possible
Front-loading: put the important words first so people who scan still get the meaning
Consistency: pick one term (e.g. "Sign in", not also "Log in") and keep a shared word list
Confirmation dialogs: the title names the action and buttons repeat it ("Delete file" and "Cancel")

tasks.title: Rewrite ten vague buttons and error messages from apps you use, showing before, after and why

topics.title: Empty states, onboarding copy and voice and tone
topics.summary_md: Beyond labels, UX writing guides people through first use, empty screens and sensitive moments. An empty state should explain what will appear and offer the next step; onboarding should show value quickly instead of listing every feature. A defined **voice** keeps the product sounding the same everywhere, while **tone** adapts to the moment: calmer for errors and payments than for celebrations.
key_points: Empty states: what goes here, why it is empty, and one clear action.
Voice stays constant; tone changes with the situation.
Write for translation: simple sentences, no idioms.
learn_items: Empty states: first use, no results and cleared states each need different text and a next action
Onboarding copy: lead with the user benefit, keep steps few, and let people skip and return later
Voice: 3–4 traits with do and don't examples, e.g. "friendly, not childish"
Tone: adjust to context; plain and reassuring for money, failures and account problems
Plain language: short sentences, common words and active voice, written for someone new to the product
Localisation: leave room for longer translations, avoid idioms, and test Hindi and regional languages
Inclusive language: avoid gendered defaults and ableist phrases; use "they" when gender is unknown
Formats: write ₹ amounts, dates and phone numbers in the formats Indian users expect

tasks.title: Write empty-state copy for no saved jobs, no search results and no internet in a job app, each with a next step
Write a voice chart with three traits and do and don't examples for a student finance app

topics.title: Choosing projects and structuring a case study
topics.summary_md: Hiring managers skim portfolios quickly, so show **2–3 deep case studies** rather than many shallow ones. Choose projects that show the kind of work you want next and real problem-solving, even if they are student or self-initiated projects. Every case study follows the same arc: context, problem, your role, process, solution and outcome.
key_points: Quality over quantity: 2–3 strong case studies.
Pick projects that match the roles you apply for.
Self-initiated work counts if the process is real.
learn_items: Project choice: work with real users, constraints and decisions, matched to the roles you want
Case study arc: context, problem, role and team, constraints, process, solution, outcome, learnings
Your role: state exactly what you did versus the team; interviewers will ask
Self-initiated projects: redesign a real flow you can research, such as a college portal, with real users
Constraints: time, technology, business rules and accessibility; showing them explains your decisions
Outcome: measured results if you have them; otherwise test findings and what you would measure
Confidentiality: remove client data and anything under NDA, and describe it at a higher level instead

tasks.title: Pick your two strongest projects and outline each as a case study using the eight-part arc

topics.title: Writing case studies that show process and impact
topics.summary_md: A case study is a story about decisions. Open with a short summary a reader can grasp in seconds, then show the messy middle: research insights, alternatives you explored, trade-offs and why you chose the final direction. Use visuals with captions that explain the point, and keep the text scannable with headings and short paragraphs.
key_points: Lead with a summary: problem, your role, result.
Show alternatives and why you rejected them.
Every image needs a caption that says what to notice.
learn_items: Summary block: one paragraph at the top with the problem, your role, the timeline and the outcome
Research evidence: one or two key insights with a quote, not every sticky note you made
Exploration: early sketches and two or three rejected directions, with the reason for each
Decision points: "We chose X over Y because…" sentences show judgement better than screens alone
Visuals: before and after, flows and annotated screens; captions explain what to look at
Scannable writing: headings, short paragraphs and bold key phrases; aim for about a 5-minute read
Reflection: what you learnt and what you would do differently next time

tasks.title: Write a full case study draft for one project with a summary block, three decision points and captioned images

topics.title: Portfolio site, presentations and design interviews
topics.summary_md: Your portfolio site is itself a design sample: fast, readable on a phone and easy to navigate. Prepare to present one case study live in about 15–20 minutes, and expect interview rounds such as a portfolio review, a design exercise or whiteboard challenge, and an app critique. Practise telling each story aloud and get feedback from working designers.
key_points: The portfolio site must load fast and work well on phones.
Rehearse a 15–20 minute walkthrough of one case study.
In design exercises, ask questions first and narrate your reasoning.
learn_items: Site basics: your name and role, 2–3 case study cards on the home page, an about page and contact details
Formats: a website builder, a simple coded site or a PDF; keep a short PDF version for applications
Accessibility: readable text size, alt text for images and good contrast; reviewers notice
Presentation: 15–20 minutes, slides adapted from the case study, with time left for questions
Design exercise: clarify the brief, define users and goals, sketch options, choose and explain trade-offs
App critique: pick a product, state its goal and user, then discuss what works, what fails and why
Feedback loop: get reviews from working designers and peers, and revise before applying widely

tasks.title: Record yourself presenting one case study in 15 minutes and list three things to tighten
Give a 10-minute spoken critique of a train booking app's search flow and write down your main points

projects.outcome: A deployed one-page site with a header, project cards, an about section and a contact form that validates input, scoring well on accessibility checks.

Connect error text to its input with aria-describedby.

projects.title: Kubernetes deploy with monitoring
projects.pitch: Run a two-service app on a local Kubernetes cluster with deployments, services, config, autoscaling and Prometheus and Grafana dashboards. It covers what platform and SRE teams do every day.
projects.outcome: Manifests that deploy an API and a worker with config, secrets, probes and autoscaling, plus dashboards and an alert for error rate and latency.

stages.title: Cluster and first deployment
stages.goal: The API runs on a local cluster behind a service.

steps.title: Local cluster
steps.detail: Create a local cluster with kind or minikube and load your image.

steps.title: Deployment and service
steps.detail: Write a Deployment with two replicas and a ClusterIP Service.

steps.title: Access
steps.detail: Expose it with port-forward or an ingress and call the health route.

hints: Set resource requests and limits on every container.

acceptance.text: Two replicas run and pass health checks.
Containers have requests and limits.
The service answers through port-forward or ingress.

self_check: What does a Service give you that a Pod IP does not?

stages.title: Config, secrets and probes
stages.goal: Configuration is external and unhealthy pods restart.

steps.title: ConfigMap and Secret
steps.detail: Move settings to a ConfigMap and credentials to a Secret.

steps.title: Probes
steps.detail: Add readiness and liveness probes with sensible delays.

steps.title: Worker
steps.detail: Deploy the worker service using the same config.

hints: Readiness gates traffic; liveness restarts stuck containers.

acceptance.text: No setting is hard-coded in the image.
Readiness and liveness probes are configured.
Killing a pod brings a new one up automatically.

self_check: Readiness versus liveness: what happens when each fails?

stages.title: Autoscaling and rollouts
stages.goal: The API scales with load and updates without downtime.

steps.title: Metrics server
steps.detail: Install the metrics server.

steps.title: HPA
steps.detail: Add a HorizontalPodAutoscaler on CPU and load-test to see it scale.

steps.title: Rolling update
steps.detail: Change the image tag and watch a rolling update; practise a rollback.

hints: maxUnavailable: 0 keeps capacity during rollouts.

acceptance.text: The HPA adds pods under load and removes them after.
A rolling update causes no failed requests.
A rollback restores the previous version.

stages.goal: You can see error rate and latency, and get alerted.

steps.title: Expose metrics

steps.title: Prometheus and Grafana
steps.detail: Install them on the cluster and scrape the API.

steps.title: Dashboard and alert
steps.detail: Build a dashboard for rate, errors and duration, and an alert for a high error rate.

hints: Start with the RED metrics: rate, errors, duration.

acceptance.text: Prometheus scrapes the API metrics.

steps.detail: Delete the cluster, recreate it and apply everything from the README to prove it works.

hints: A runbook entry answers: what broke, how to confirm, how to fix.

acceptance.text: The README explains how to run the stack.

Manifests apply cleanly to a new cluster.
